docs.title: Rev. 1
docs.text: Rev. 1 MONSTER ALIGNMENT GUIDELINES ============================ Introduction: ------------ This purpose of this document is to present suggested guidelines for the alignments assigned to monsters. These guidelines contain recommended values and definitions of each alignment. These guidelines are designed to help prevent the alignment problem experienced during the first half of 1996 and to ensure that all wizards are on the same alignment scale. The administration of Darkwind suggests these ranges of values for monsters. Extreme alignment values are not forbidden, just discouraged due to their effects on players and their respective guild abilities. Alignment Definitions: ---------------------- Saintly - Saintly creatures value nothing more than the pursuit of beauty, kindness, freedom, and truth. In order for this pursuit to succeed, all that is not good must be eliminated. Good - Good creatures strongly believe in beauty, kindness, truth, and freedom. However in their pursuits for truth sometimes certain sacrifices may have to be made in the name of all that is good. Nice - Nice creatures are those that believe in things such as beauty, kindness, truth, and freedom as they will ultimately make the world a better place by bringing maximum benefits to all. Neutral - Neutral creatures look upon all the other alignments as being part of the natural order of things. They think that the alignments must exist in order for the natural balance of of things to hold. Neutral alignment also applies to most natural animals and other creatures that do not care about and have no concept of good and evil. Nasty - Nasty creatures can be those that have just entered a lifestyle of evil pursuits. They are lacking respect for one or more of the following: life, beauty, truth, freedom. They may have also entered into this lifestyle unwittingly, but only value themselves and as much power they can get. Evil - Creatures of this alignment hold things such as life, beauty, truth, freedom, with little value and generally scorn them. These creatures are generally out to gain power and control over others through fear, torture, and any other means necessary. Typical creatures in this range include fiends, devils, lesser warlords, some dragons, and demons. Demonic - Creatures of this alignment have total disdain and scorn for life, beauty, truth, and freedom. Their only purpose is total conquest of the world through any means necessary, most likely at the expense of others. They also believe in the total eradication of good creatures and often capture and manipulate them into being their slaves. It is extremely rare for a normal creature to become this evil without some supernatural or magical assistance. These creatures are generally very powerful demon lords, lords or dukes of other plains of existance, or manifestations brought into the physical world by evil forces. Ethics definitions: ------------------- Lawful - Creatures of lawful alignment are extremely disciplined and live according to rigorous codes of behavior. They tend to have highly regimented social structures, and will follow their superiors with extreme obedience (and expect the same from their inferiors). Examples might be a legendary knight, a stereotypical samurai warrior, or a clan of dark elf warriors. (Note that it is possible to be lawful and evil; in this case, the code of behavior that the creature follows is itself evil.) Orderly - Orderly creatures are those who try to live their lives according to a code. They tend to be very disciplined and methodical, but suffer the occasional lapse. Orderly creatures often live in a regimented society, where they generally defer to those of greater rank and expect respect from those of lesser rank. Examples would include most knights, orcish war-bands, or dark elf commoners. Just - Just creatures are those who believe in a code of behavior and generally try to live according to that code, but who are willing to make "reasonable" exceptions. These creatures believe that the code is a good idea in theory, and necessary for the protection of society, but they overlook smaller details in practice. They tend to be fairly disciplined and organized, but not notably so. Neutral - Creatures with neutral ethics don't particularly care about ethics and codes of honor, or they don't follow any particular code. This includes most natural animals and other creatures who cannot understand the concept of ethics, as well as those who are simply not concerned by the matter. Lawless - Lawless creatures have no use for the ethical codes society imposes. Though they do not go out of their way to break laws, they will if they feel they must, in order to attain their goals. Lawless ethics can also indicate someone who is an individualist and who sees no need for outwardly- imposed rules of behavior. In this way, a lawless creature can still be a good individual, just as a lawful creature can be evil in nature. Entropic - Entropic creatures do not recognize outwardly-imposed rules of behavior. They tend to be disorganized by others' standards, and are seen as too undisciplined to work in large groups, since they do not follow orders well, nor do they acknowledge any permanent leader or ruler. Examples of entropic creatures would include pirates, trolls, and some lesser demons. Chaotic - Chaotic creatures are actively opposed to codes of behavior. They will break laws with abandon, holding only their own judgment important. They will never acknowledge another as ruler willingly, and have difficulty even joining forces with other creatures temporarily. They are extreme individualists. Examples would include some ancient dragons, chaos demon lords, the most infamous pirates, etc. Alignments: Suggested Range: ----------- ---------------- Saintly 1000 - above Good 500 - 999 Nice 300 - 499 Neutral -299 - 299 Nasty -499 - -300 Evil -999 - -500 Demonic -1000 - below Ethics: Suggested Range: --------- --------------- Lawful 1000 - above Orderly 500 - 999 Just 300 - 499 Neutral -299 - 299 Lawless -499 - -300 Entropic -999 - -500 Chaotic -1000 - below Misc. ----- It should be noted that extreme alignment values (above 2000 or below -2000), although not forbidden, should be rare and used with caution. Creatures with these alignments should be legendary on Darkwind as it should be almost all but impossible for mere mortal creatures to have such alignments. However, unworldly creatures from other planes of existence that defy the laws of nature can be known to have such alignments. Conclusions: ------------ The purpose of this doc is not to target any one person or group of people in particular, it is to provide suggested guidelines for the assignment of alignments to monsters. This doc can be revised at any time. Such revision will follow with posts to the wizboards. If you are unsure about anything in this document, please post to the document wiz board. In addition, please provide a variety of alignments in your area as it is unlikely that two creatures would have the exact same alignment. Extreme alignment values are also discouraged because they can have adverse effects on players and their respective guild abilities. Note that everything in this document that applies to alignment applies equally to ethics. Revision History: ----------------- Rev. 1 - Added information on ethics. Fixed typos. Rev. 0 - Initial release

docs.title: Languages
docs.text: Languages ========= Player languages are independent of race, although some player races are accorded extra languages. Languages are specified in the language.h header. A living's language knowledge is either fluent, or non-fluent (regular). At the moment, the distinction only affects whether the say command shows an accent or not. There is also a default language and a native language for each living as well. The default language is the languages used with the 'say' command, and the native language is used by 'rsay'. Adding new languages -------------------- To add a language, alter language.h to include the new language in the ALL_LANGUAGES array, and assign a color to it in LCOLOR. Giving language knowledge ------------------------- void add_language(string) void add_fluent_language(string) Both of these functions give appropriate knowledge of a language. They can also be passed arrays of languages as well. void set_default_language(string) void set_native_language(string) These functions set the say and rsay default languages. void remove_language(string) Removes all knowledge of a language. Checking language knowledge --------------------------- string query_native_language() string query_default_language() These return the appropriate language setting. status query_language(string) status query_fluent_language(string) These return 1 if the language is known. ------ Version 1: Bob - April 13, 2003

docs.title: There are currently 5 different 'types' of guilds, although several types
docs.text: There are currently 5 different 'types' of guilds, although several types have more than one guild within it's category. The different types are: DRUIDS, CLERICS, MAGES, THIEVES, and FIGHTERS. Most classes have restrictions on what type of armours and which type of weapons they are allowed to use. When you design a piece of armour or weapon, the type of armour or weapon and the material it's made of will determine which guilds can use the weapon. The following is a general guildeline as to who can wear and use what: CLASS WEAPON TYPE ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- MAGES Daggers and staves. THIEVES Daggers, some blunt weapons (like a blackjack), medium size swords. No large weapons. FIGHTERS All, except for magic items that are guild specific. DRUIDS Daggers, blunt weapons, and most swords (except things like two-handed swords and such). CLERICS Blunt weapons only. CLASS ARMOUR TYPE ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- MAGES Only very light armours like robes, rings of protection, bracers of defense, etc. THIEVES Similar to mages, but not as strict. Able to wear leather armour, FIGHTERS Anything, unless the item is guild specific. DRUIDS Similar to mages, except able to wear armours made from naturally growing materials, i.e. BarkMail. CLERIC Almost anything, unless it is a class specific item. If you have any questions on what to set an object ask another wizard! There are several examples in the /open/WEAPON and /open/ARMOUR directories that show how to set guilds for weapons and armour. Below is a complete listing of ALL guilds currently in the game and their proper syntax when using them. FIGHTER, GAROU, BARD, NECRO, DRUID, THIEF, MAGE, CHARLATAN CLERIC_MITRA, MORPHER, LUNAR, PSIONICIST, SWASHBUCKLER, NINJA ALL_GUILDS can be used when you wish to have something globally encompass all guilds. // Revised to correct thief restrictions and remove WEREWOLF // from list of guilds. Druid guild exists but is not open. // ---Xnedra 23/08/98---

docs.title: Writing Guild Emotes For Rooms And Channels
docs.text: Writing Guild Emotes For Rooms And Channels ============================================ Guild emotes should use EMOTE_D's guild-scoped emote infrastructure when they are ordinary social actions. That gives them the same room, targeting, perspective, channel, preview, search, and random-emote support as global emotes while restricting use to active members of one guild. Do not implement an ordinary guild social as a command under /cmds/guilds/<guild>/emotes/. A standalone command can still be appropriate when the action moves characters, changes game state, or performs other complex behavior, but the generic channel-emote parser cannot invoke it. Static Guild Emotes =================== Most guild emotes need no LPC object. Register each supported rule directly: addemote -guild Mage motion LIV New message: $N $vmotion to $t to stand still -- toys are coming! The addemote preview shows the actor, target, and room perspectives before the definition is accepted. Repeat the command for each additional rule. The guild argument is matched case-insensitively against GUILD_NAMES. The emote name is lower-cased and may contain letters, numbers, underscores, and hyphens, but must start with a letter. New guild-emote names cannot collide with global emotes, another guild's emotes, or available commands. Variable Guild Emotes ===================== Use a variable emote only when get_emote() must calculate the Message String. Place the object in the guild's lower-case directory under /cmds/soul/: /cmds/soul/mage/motion.c string get_emote(string sArg, object *aoWho) { if (sArg == "LIV") return "$N $vmotion to $t to stand still -- toys are coming!\n"; return ""; } Register the scoped rule, then use a guild redirect as its Message String: addemote -guild Mage motion LIV New message: ->Guild_Mage_motion The guild token in the redirect must match the configured guild name. The object name follows the final underscore and resolves beneath the guild's directory in /cmds/soul/. Inspection And Removal ====================== showemote -guild Mage motion rmemote -guild Mage motion LIV rmemote -guild Mage motion The first removal deletes one rule. The second deletes the entire guild emote. Omitting -guild inspects or changes a global definition instead. Player Discovery And Access =========================== Players can use: feelings guild [<guild>] [<prefix>] semote <emote> emoteapropos guild [<guild>] <text> random [<player>] Guild-channel commands that support colon souls can invoke the same emotes, for example "samchat :jackin". Access is checked every time: leaving the guild or marking that guild inactive immediately removes access. Players cannot list or preview definitions belonging to inaccessible guilds. Persistence =========== Guild definitions are saved with EMOTE_D in /secure/savedir/soul and survive daemon reloads and game restarts. That runtime save is environment-local, so add or migrate the definitions separately in each environment where they are required. See also: help guild emotes, help addemote, help showemote, help rmemote

docs.title: To use the new guild soul inherit, you'll of course need to #include <mudlib.h>
docs.text: To use the new guild soul inherit, you'll of course need to #include <mudlib.h> The #define for the guild soul inherit is, predictably enough, GUILD_SOUL Note that GUILD_SOUL inherits nothing else, so it can be used in multiple inheritance situations with anything on the OBJECT tree (and usually will be). ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The following functions should be called from reset() of the guild_soul: void set_guild(string sName) This function sets the name of the guild, which must be registered with the Guild Daemon. Proper captalization is necessary. Example: set_guild("Paladin"); void set_main_channel(string sChannel) This function tells the guild soul what the name of the main channel is which ALL guild members receive. This channel must be a real, static channel registered in the USER_D, and is usually simply the name of the guild rendered to lower case. Example: set_main_channel("paladin"); void set_guild_path(string sPath OR string * asPaths) This function tells the guild soul what command paths (/cmds/..) the guild deals with. A single string or an array of strings can be passed to this function, and the function can be called several times to add additional paths if the single-string format is preferred. Example: set_guild_path("/cmds/guilds/paladin"); set_guild_path(({"/cmds/guilds/ranger", "/cmds/guilds/ranger/emotes"})); void add_extra_channel(string sChannel, string sDescription, string sColor) This function tells the guild soul to create a dynamic channel for use by this guild, with the given name, description, and color. Whether or not a specific player is added to the channel or not is controlled by overloading can_join_channel(). See the section on overloads. Example: add_extra_channel("mitra","Followers of Mitra discussion",""); add_extra_channel("lord","Lord Paladin Discussion",""); ** Note for those unfamiliar with multiple inheritance in LPC. It is necessary to call BOTH reset() functions in the parent inherits explicitly by use of the scope resolution operator. A similar process must be followed for init(). Example: armour::reset(arg); guild_soul::reset(arg); ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The following functions exist in the guild soul inherit but should be overloaded in any individual guild soul. Failure to overload these properly will usually result in generic defaults. string query_msg_in() string query_msg_out() string query_mmsg_in() string query_mmsg_out() These should return the relavent msg to be applied to members of this guild. Example: string query_msg_in() { return "$N enters proudly from the $D."; } string query_mmsg_in() { return "$N appears out of nowhere."; } string query_guild_header() This should return the header used to mark messages on the main guild channel. Example: string query_guild_header() { return "[PALADIN]"; } string query_death_message() string query_death_general() These functions should return the message to be broadcast on the main guild channel when an individual in the guild dies. $N represents the name of the person killed, and $T represents the living object that killed him. Note that use of $T in query_death_general() is not allowed. Example: string query_death_message() { return query_guild_header() + " Mitra's Paladin $N falls to $T."; } string query_login_message() string query_logout_message() These functions should return the message to be broadcast on the main guild channel when a non-applicant individual in the guild logs in or out. Note that most guild souls should already support this. Example: string query_login_message() { return "\<>Mitra smiles as " + CAP(REAL) + " enters Darkwind. <>"; } int can_join_channel(string sChannelName) This function controls whether or not a player may join a guild's dynamic channel (see add_extra_channel() for how to create such channels). This function is called for every dynamic channel in the guild and a return result of 1 indicates that the channel will be added, while a return of 0 indicates that the channel should be skipped. Since this is done AFTER reloading/move of the guild soul to the player, it may refer to individual player data. Example: int can_join_channel(string sChannelName) { if(sChannelName == "mitra") return 1; return (GLEVEL == 15); } -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Other function information void save_soul() This function causes the soul data to be saved, if the possessor is a PC. void set_default_variables() This function is called when a player enters a guild for the first time (or otherwise lacks a savefile for the guild). It can be overloaded to set up defaults for guild-specific variables. If so, be sure to call the inherited version. void set_timer(int iNumSeconds, string sTimerName) This function sets an individual or group timer that is stored and checked independently of the general power timer. status check_timer(string sType) This function checks an individual or group timer. Return value is 0 if the timer is set and not expired (i.e. attempts to use this category should fail), 1 otherwise. status query_timer(string sType) This function returns the time at which an individual or group timer expires. To include guild-specific code in the setup and guild removal functions, overload void init() and status remove_guild(int iSilently) respectively. Remember to call the inherited version! Do not use init_arg() - monsters do not get init_arg() called when guild souls are created for them! ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Notes on converting existing guild souls: The following code should be removed and/or replaced with standard inherit calls: Death messages Login/out messages Changes to msgin/out Setting/removal of command paths Adding/removal of channels Creation of dynamic channels Setting of attributes on the player Incorrect calls to save Add_actions that force guild soul to save Code that restores the soul from a savefile Code that backs up the guild savefile Basically, all that should be left in individual guild souls is information that is specific to that guild only, and functions to carry out tasks specific to that guild only. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- Doc created by: Kanan Date: 3/29/2003

docs.title: WIZHELP 11.3
docs.text: WIZHELP 11.3 This file is a work in progress. GUILD STANDARDS DAMAGE RATIOS SP:DAMAGE NOTE: Ratios should only hit top level ratios when the player is fully guilded, high level, etc. Standard Guilds: Standard guilds are divided into 3 categories: Melee, Caster, and Combo. These categories are based on their combat adjustments found in guildd.h. Melee guilds (400+): Bard, Cleric, Fighter, Garou, Paladin, Priest. Combo guilds (380-399): Ninja, Psionicist, Swashbuckler, Thief. Caster guilds (360-379): Lunar, Mage Melee: 1:3 - 1:5 Combo: 1:4 - 1:6 Casters: 1:5 - 1:7 Note: The lower ratioed categories MAY bump up the ratio if the spell warrants the increase. eg: Bard wail also damages the player while damaging the mob. Mythic Guilds: 1:4 - 1:8

docs.title: Player races
docs.text: Player races ============ The Basics ---------- Player races are not races in the normal sense, but rather racially based cultures. Each culture is drawn from an in-play area inhabited by that culture. Not all areas in DarkWind contain cultures that are appropriate for a player race, nor are all appropriate cultures included in the set of player races. The minimum criteria for inclusion as a player race are that: 1) The race is drawn from an in-play area. 2) A reasonable population of the race be present in the area. 3) The area contains a city, camp, or other permanent or semi-permanent gathering place for members of that race. Although player races are drawn from npc areas, players and npc do not have the same kind of race attribute. Player races are specific to a particular culture while npc races are broader groupings along more traditional racial divides. For example, the player race "high elf" is drawn from the Elf Kingdom, but the npcs of the kingdom are of the racial type "elf". New player races can be added quite easily, and it is expected that over time the list of available races will grow considerably. Racial Bonuses -------------- Races are balanced according to a point-based power allocation scheme. The point scheme is intended to provide a level of objectivity in balancing each race against the other. It is probably possible to abuse the system. Don't do it, it's bad. Each common race is allowed a total of 100 racial power points worth of extra powers and characteristics. Common races are available to players in the Hall of Races on the appropriate continent. Each exotic race is allowed a total of 125 racial power points. Exotic races should have a separate race room in the originating area where players can reincarnate into that race only. Currently there are the following powers allowed for races: Exp bonus: Bonus to exp gained. Stat bonus/penalty: % bonus/penalty to base stats. Alignment tendencies: Bonus to moves towards, penalty to moves away. Size: Affects relative weapon sizes. Dark vision: Vision in various levels of darkness. Magic/Psi resistance: Resist magic, psionics. Eat/drink bonus: Effectively increases capacity and detox/desate. Damage resistance: Damage reduction vs types. (also vulnerability) Weapon mastery: Unaffected by out-of-spec weapon penalties. Hyperborean: Resistance to Hyper cold effect, resist cold, vulnerable to heat. Souvraeli: Resistance to Souv heat dam, resist heat, vulnerable to cold. Winged: Allows wing piercings. Flight: Allows flight. Race change: Allows free race changes. Breath weapon: Allows use of breath player command. Damage type: Extra damage type on attacks. SP regen rate: Increases the base regen rate of sp. Languages: Free (fluent) languages besides common. Race rooms ---------- Race rooms allow players to describe the races available there and reincarnate into them. DW, Hyper and Souv have race rooms for common races from those continents, whereas exotic races have their own race rooms. Technical information --------------------- The guildd.h header contains information on racial guild restrictions. The race.h header contains most of the information about each race. The RCOLOR define should be deprecated, but is messy to change over. In the future, keys that correspond to the old race set should be removed. The RACE_MAP define contains the details about the new set of races and their powers. DO NOT access RACE_MAP directly to extract racial characteristics. Use the function query_race_data() instead. (see the funhelp for query_race_data() for usage) ------ Version 1: Bob - April 08, 2003

docs.title: Building a New Race
docs.text: Building a New Race ------------------- These are the technical stages to making a new race. 1) Add an RCOLOR for the specific race being added and an RACE_MAP entry. 2) Assign racial power pts (100 for common races, 125 for exotic) according to the cost guide below. Make sure you add an rbit key linking the race to its major race grouping. 3) Set up guild restrictions in guildd.h 4) Write a description for the race and put it in /public/docs/race. The name of the file should be the same as your race name, but with underscores replacing the spaces. (e.g. the "ice ogre" race has the description file /public/docs/race/ice_ogre. For common races, update /public/docs/helpdir/race and /public/docs/helpdir/races appropriately. Exotic races should not do this. Copy the race description file to /public/docs/helpdir as well for common races. 5) If the race is a common race, add it to one of the continent race rooms. (add it to the array passed to set_available_races()), and adjusting the room's long desc slightly. If it's exotic make a race room for it. To do this, inherit RACE_ROOM instead of ROOM and add: set_available_races( ({ "race name" }) ); (replacing "race name" with the name of your race). Racial powers ------------- Power Key Cost size - -1/0/+1: size -55/0/+30 exp bonus: exp +3 per 1% (max 25%) stat bonus - +5%/10/15/20: str, dex etc. +15/+30/+60/+100 stat penalty - -5%/10/15/20: str, dex etc. -15/-30/-60/-90 net stat bonus - +15%/20/25+ --- +10/20/30 dark vision: vision +15, +5 per additional level to 6, +1 per after magic resist: magic_res +5 per 1%, +10 per 1% after 10% psi resist: psi_res +2 per 1%, +4 per 1% after 10% eat/drink: eat, drink +1 per 1%, +2 per 1% after 15 (max 25) damage resistance: resistances +1 per 1% per type +2 per 1% past 25%(max 50%) dam vulnerability: resistances -1 per 1% per type alignment tendency: al_good +1 per +/- 1% (max 25%) al_law weapon mastery: weapon_spec +50 hyperborean: hyperborean +10 souvraeli: souvraeli +5 winged: winged +0 flight: flight +35 racechange: racechange +15 (darkwinders only) languages: languages free breath weapon: breath +30 damage type damtype +50 sp regen rate: spregen +15 per +1 regen per tick (max 3) SIZE EFFECTS ------------ SMALL - weapon size effects rise 1 level: - cannot use huge weapons - all large weapons require 2 hands - can only use 1 medium weapon if dual wielding - should affect guild weapon restrictions - armor size effects [if/when armor sizes are implemented] LARGE - weapon size effects drop 1 level: - cannot use small weapons - if dual wielding, can use 2 large weapons, or 1 huge + 1 large - can wield huge weapons in 1 hand unless explicitly 2 handed, polearm, or missiles - should affect guild weapon restrictions - armor size effects [if/when armor sizes are implemented] STAT ADJUSTMENTS ---------------- - increases/decreases based on the base stats of the player. - NB extra costs for having high net stat bonuses are in addition to the costs of the stat bonuses themselves. ALIGNMENT TENDENCY ------------------ - increase positive (tendency direction) change by % - reduce negative change by % - 1% resistance to related damtype - -1% resistance to opposite damtype - use al_law with a negative value for chaotic - use al_good with negative value for evil - n.b. tendencies to either direction should be costed positively. EAT/DRINK ---------------- - increased detox/desate by % - increased capacity by % - no change in food/drink size DAMAGE RESISTANCE/VULNERABILITY ------------------------------- - the value field of the resistances key is a mapping of the form: TYPE:VALUE, where TYPE is a damage type and VALUE is the amount of resistance. A negative VALUE is a vulnerability to the damage type. WEAPON MASTERY -------------- - no penalty for out-of-spec weapon use HYPERBOREAN ----------- - +10 resist cold - -10 resist fire - +1 resist environmental cold SOUVRAELI --------- - +10 resist fire - -10 resist cold - +2 resist environmental heat dam WINGED ------ - allows wing tattoos FLIGHT ------ - allows flight RACECHANGE ---------- - allows free race changes BREATH ------ - allows special draconian breath spell SP REGEN RATE ------------- - increases the base regen rate for sp LANGUAGES --------- - array of fluent languages - first element in array is the native language - all others count towards total knowable languages ------ Version 1: Bob - April 07, 2003

docs.title: Guild restrictions by Race
docs.text: Guild restrictions by Race -------------------------- Guild restrictions by race are setup in the RACE_RESTRICT #define in the guild header: guildd.h The current moment (when this doc was written) the #define looks something like this: #define RACE_RESTRICT ([ \ "Barbarian" : ({}), \ "Bard" : ({ "ice ogre", }), \ "Charlatan" : ({ "barbarian", "high elf", "silver elf", "stone dwarf", }), \ . . . "Smith" : ({ }), \ "Thief" : ({ "desert dwarf", "stone dwarf", "barbarian" }) \ ]) The keys to the mapping are the string names of the guilds. Each value associated with a key is an string array player race names. The array specifies the races that are NOT allowed to join the guild. Thus any race can join the "Smith" guild, and only "ice ogre"s are disallowed from joining bards. These restrictions have very little to do with whether the race/guild is a good fit or not. Race/guild restrictions should ONLY be checked when actually joining the guild or switching race, not in any other guild code. Adding/removing restrictions should not affect people already in the guild. Every guild should be added as a key into this mapping, even if the race list is empty. Guild coders can modify the restriction list simply by adding/removing items from the race array for their guild. ------ Version 1: Bob - April 07, 2003

docs.title: --Strict Typing--
docs.text: --Strict Typing-- It has come to my attention recently that there are some of you out there who do not fully understand the concept of stricttyping and why we do it. This doc will attempt to explain why we stricttype, and will hopefully give you a better understanding of how to stricttype your functions. The first part : WHY ==================== Why do we stricttype our functions in LPC? It requires more thought, more time, and can turn out to be a general pain in the ass if you don't know how to do it. However, there are several legitimate reasons behind we (the management) requiring you to stricttype your functions. 1) It's more efficient. If you tell the compiler exactly what type of function you are writing, then it doesn't have to go through the code and attempt to determine what kind of function you are writing. Also, stricttyped code uses less memory since the interpreter doesn't have to reserve the maximum amount of space for each variable in the case that it might be large. 2) Better for debugging. There are two sub-sections under this part. a) More verbose error messages. If you incorrectly stricttype a function, you will get more detailed error messages than if you didn't stricttype your function at all. As a matter of fact, if you don't stricttype your functions at all, the compiler may miss some errors BECAUSE your file isn't stricttyped. This incorrect file will update and load correctly, but it will crash at run-time. As any programmer knows, it is MUCH harder to debug a logical (i.e., run-time) error than it is to debug a syntactical (i.e., compile-time) error. This is true if for no other reason than, if you have a compile-time error, the compiler tells you what line you made your mistake on, and what kind of error it is. Once you have seen enough of these errors, you get to know what to look for and where to look without much thought. b) Easier to read. One of the most important things to know about programming is that, most likely, you will NOT be the only person to ever read your own code. You might have trouble trying to do something, or you might have to leave for an extended period of time, or something might come up while you aren't here which someone else has to fix. Therefore, it is important to make your code readable and self-documenting. This is where stricttyping comes in. It is easier for the other human fixing your code to fix it if he/she knows what they are looking for. The second part : HOW ===================== I will start this section off with a list of stricttyping "reserved words" (to borrow a term from Pascal), and continue on with how to implement them. Qualifiers ========== static varargs nomask types ===== void int status object mixed string How to implement these "reserved words" ======================================= The first three, what I will call "qualifiers," are not necessary for all functions, and, in fact, SHOULD NOT be used for all functions. Most of the time, these qualifiers are used in files which many other files inherit (like player.c or living.c or newroom.c). A brief description of each qualifier follows: static - This variable will not change, and this qualifier is for variables only. Variables of this type will not be saved when the object containing them is saved via a save_object() call. Functions of this type cannot be called from outside the object they are defined upon. [NOTE: The first version of this doc incorrectly stated that functions could not be typed "static." That was incorrect. The way it is stated here is correct.] varargs - There are a variable number of arguments to this function. An example of a varargs function which you all should be familiar with is make_object(). If you only want one of the object made, then you don't have to pass a 1 as the third argument to make_object(). Therefore, the third argument is optional; its existence could be said to be variable. This is also used to allow certain functions to compile. For example, if a function is stricttyped, and you attempt to call it with fewer args elsewhere in the code, the compiler will puke nasty error messages at you unless you have stricttyped the function as "varargs." [NOTE: The second paragraph was added in the second version. The first paragraph is correct.] nomask - Functions of this type are typically only used in inheritable files, however, this type can be used anywhere. Typing a function as a nomask is a security procedure. The nomask does not allow any file which inherits that file to change the value of a function. Also, these functions cannot be shadowed, which is another security procedure. For example, in living.c, we have: nomask query_value() { return 0; } This sets the value of any object inheriting living.c to 0, and does not allow the inheriting object to change the value of itself. [NOTE: The first version of this doc incorrectly stated that "nomask" functions were ONLY used in inheritables. That was incorrect. The way it is stated here is correct.] Now, I will move on to the other types of stricttyping "reserved words," what I will call "types." These should be used on every function (but not all at once!) You can tell what type a function is by looking at what kind of value it returns. You are all familiar with statements that return 0; or just return; at certain spots. These return lines will give you clues as to what type your function is. A brief description of each type follows: void - This function does not return a value. Examples of this are reset() and init(). int - This function returns integer values. These can be more useful if you have a function which will determine how you want something to perform in another function. Functions which will only return a 1 or a 0 can also be stricttyped at "status" functions. Those that possibly would return something other than a 1 or a 0 must be stricttyped "int," and are generally more complex (but not necessarily so.) Examples of this are int <or status> north_hook(), buy(). status - As explained above, these functions only return a 1 or a 0 (which can be thought of as "True" and "False" respectively. Examples of this are status <or int> north_hook() and status is_npc(). object - This type is used for functions which return objects. I have mostly seen these type of functions used in code for shops, or code which searches through a player's inventory looking for a specific object. mixed - Type a function mixed when it is possible that more than one of the listed types can be returned. For example, a function that would return an array or a string, depending on what is appropriate for your uses should be typed "mixed." [NOTE: The first version of this doc incorrectly stated that "mixed" functions should be used to return 0 or (for example) an object. That was incorrect. 0 is an acceptable value for any type; it is the "nothing" or "does not exist" value for all types. The way it is stated here is correct.] string - This type of function wiz used to represent strings. A string is a group of letters placed back to back. Every word is a string of characters. Something important to note about strings is that any argument passed into any function is automatically passed as a string. This is important for rooms such as stores where you might want to "buy 42". Since I warned you about this, I should inform you of how to fix it, eh? This is where the function "to_int(string)" comes in. For something like the "buy 42", you would have a function, possibly "int buy(string arg)", and to turn that string arg into an int, you would call "to_int(arg);". If the string that you pass to to_int() can be turned into a number, then to_int() will return it as a number. If, however, you pass something that cannot be turned into an integer (such as a word), then to_int() will return 0. Prototyping functions ===================== You may have heard of this as "forward typing" (I hate to reference Pascal so much, but it is the only language in which I have formal training.) All that it is, is if you make a call to an argument before it is defined, the compiler will barf at you. That's no fun, but it is a syntax error, and therefore easy to fix. To prototype a function, all you have to do is, before you call the undefined function, place the header (declaration line) of the function before you call it. However, you must remember to replace the open brace ( { ) with a semicolon ( ; ). Example: int foo(string str); status bar() { . . . foo("baz"); . . . return 1; } int foo(string str) { . . . return 3; } In most files, there is a prototyping section at the beginning of a file where all the necessary prototyping is done in one spot so you don't have to go searching for it. Also, most of the time, prototyping can be avoided by simply moving the undefined called function to before the calling function. This is no always possible, but most of the time it is. Advanced Stricttyping ===================== Arrays - If you wish to return an array of any type, simply place a * before the name of the function, just as if you were naming an array variable. ------ Version 1.0 by Rodney@Darkwind - 10/21/94 Version 1.1 by Rodney@Darkwind - 10/26/94 - Thanks Malraux. [All comments contained in brackets are editor's notes. They delimit changes between versions 1.0 and 1.1 of this document. I am sorry for any problems anything incorrect from the first version may have caused. Hopefully, everything in here is correct.]

docs.title: --Hungarian Notation--
docs.text: --Hungarian Notation-- Hungarian Variable Naming Notation: Hungarian notation basically encodes the variable type and scope of the variable in the name of the variable itself. There are 4 parts to it: 1) The variable's scope 2) Is it an array? 3) The variable's type 4) The variable's name The variable's scope -------------------- At the basic level, there are two types of scope. - Local scope - Module-level scope If a variable has been declared inside of a function, then its scope is local. Otherwise, the variable can be used anywhere in the file, and it has module-level scope. If the variable has module-level scope, then start your variable name with an "m". If it has local scope, then do not add anything to the variable name. Is it an array? --------------- In LPC, arrays are designated by use of the "*" when declaring variables. For example: int iIndex; // This is not an array. int *aiSize; // This is an array of integers. If your variable is an array, then you add an "a" to the variable name. The "a" goes after the "m" mentioned above if your variable has module-level scope. If your variable is not an array, then do not add anything to the variable name. The variable's type ------------------- Basically, this is taking the variable type (IE, int, string, mixed, etc.) and shortening it to 1 unique letter so that you know what the variable's type is every time you look at it. The LPC Unique letter for each variable type is: i : integer ib : integer used as a bitfield m : mapping o : object s : string t : status x : mixed Whatever type your variable is, add the unique letter to the variable name. The variable type letter goes after the "m" and the "a" if they exist. It is not allowable to not encode the variable type into the name. The variable's name ------------------- This is the easy part. It is what you call your variable. The variable name should be descriptive of the function of the variable, and should use proper case. All that "proper case" means is that you should capitalize the first letter of the variable name as well as all letters of "new words" inside the variable name, and that you should not use underscores to separate the "new words." Examples -------- iCount: local integer variable aiCount: local array of integers maiCount: module level array of integers mIDsToNames: local mapping mmIDsToNames: module level mapping asNames: local array of strings int iCount; int *aiCount; string *asNames; object oPerson; The second part: WHY should I use Hungarian notation? ----------------------------------------------------- At its simplest, because redundancy in variable naming is a good thing. If you have a long file which contains a global variable named something generic without the scope and type encoded in the name, then by the time you reach the end of the file and spot a line which uses that variable, you may have forgotten what kind of variable it is. If, however, your variable uses Hungarian notation, you can look at the variable name and you will immediately know that it is, for example, a module-level array of mappings which you're using to store Responses (IE, mamResponses). ------ Version 1: Malraux, 1997-Aug-26 Version 2: Rodney, 1998-Apr-15

*************************************************************************** Coding Efficiently *************************************************************************** is_clone check: The is_clone check is meant for objects that do not need to refer to their master object. It will prevent the code from setting the various functions, such as the set_long string, on that master object. The check should appear before ::reset(arg) is called, and should be entered as follows: if (!is_clone(this_object())) return; The is_clone check should appear in all cloned objects and monsters, unless the object's master object needs to actually do something/store information. (99% of objects do not.) It should not be used in room files. ------ Version 1: ? Version 2: Edited by Bob - July 16, 2004

*************************************************************************** Bracketing and Indentation *************************************************************************** The sole purpose of good indentation is to make code readable. Poor indentation makes it difficult to find bugs in code, and is otherwise annoying to other people who have to read your code. Bracketing of code happens when braces (i.e. { } ) are used to specify one or more lines of code as being part of a particular execution path. During execution, the execution path may or may not enter the section between the braces. If it does enter, then the code is executed normally. If not, NONE of that code is executed. Sometimes (e.g. in a for loop), after executing the code between braces, the program will return to the start of the braced section. Indentation should always be consistent in your code. Common sizes of indentation are 2, 4 or 8 characters per indentation level (I personally recommend 4.) This means that the first "level" of code is at 0 spaces in, the second is 4 spaces in, the third is 8 spaces in etc. for a 4 space indentation scheme. When do you indent? ------------------- - All code inside a function should be indented one level. - All code inside braces should be indented one level more than the level the braces themselves are at. - Long lines of code that are broken up into multiple lines should have the second and subsequent lines indented one level more than the first line. - Literal text broken into multiple lines (with \) should NOT be indented. ------ Version 1: Bob - July 16, 2004

docs.text: wizhelp trans Command: trans Argument: name Transport a player or NPC to you. Be warned, you are only allowed to trans a player that is within the city limits. docs.title: Command: funhelp
docs.text: Command: funhelp Argument: function name Functions: ---------- There exists two types of functions in LPC, called LOCAL and EXTERNAL functions. A local function is defined in LPC code in an LPC file, and is contained in an object. A local function can be called from LPC code inside the object or from LPC code in another object. Objects communicate with each other by calling functions in each other. A local function can be declared STATIC, meaning that it can only be called from LPC code within the same object. External function are "built in" in LPC, so it has no definition in LPC code. Examples of local functions are the functions set_value and query_value in "/obj/treasure.c". Examples of external functions are write(), time() and add_action(). All external functions are documented in "/public/docs/efun/FUNCTION", where FUNCTION is the name of the function. Many local functions are documented in "/public/docs/lfun/FUNCTION". Not all can be documented, as they are unlimited. You can get information on most of these functions by typing: funhelp <function>

docs.text: ---Editing Files--- 3.6.1 Directory Structure 3.6.2 Manipulating files 3.6.3 Using the online editor To view the help file type wizhelp <number>

docs.title: The file structure is a tree
docs.text: The file structure is a tree ---------------------------- LPmud mimics the file system hierarchy and file handling commands of UNIX. A directory is a set of files, where those "files" can be both normal files and other directories. Everything starts with the so-called root directory, the name of which is "/" (at least from inside Darkwind!). As in UNIX, a file or a directory is referred to by its file name or its path name, i. e. for example "thing.c" and "/players/alarian/thing.c". The rooms in the "core" domain of Darkwind are in the directory "/room", and the objects (like the weapon and monster objects) are in "/obj". Each wizard has his own home directory for example: "/players/alarian". Each area should have its own directory structure, with a separate directory for each of: inherit, room, monster, weapon, armour, and object. The directory structure for an area would look like this: ls /players/alarian/area/island armour/ inherit/ monster/ object/ room/ weapon/ The inherit directory inclues all inheritable files and all header files for the area 'island'

docs.title: Some basic commands for handling files:
docs.text: Some basic commands for handling files: ls <dir> Lists the files directory 'dir'. If no argument is given it lists the files in the current directory. cd <dir> Changes the current directory to 'dir'. If no argument is given it changes to the builder's home directory. rm <filename> - remove a file ed <filename> - edit a file using LPmud's online editor cat <filename> - print the contents of a file on the screen more <filename> - print the contents of a file, one screen at a time tail <filename> - print the last few lines of a file Loading, cloning and updating ----------------------------- "Loading an object" means the process of taking a class description file, for example "/obj/weapon.c", and reading it into the game. This is done as soon as that object is used in any way, for example if a function in the object is called from LPC, or if another object tries to enter it (as when a player walks into a room). When the object is loaded, one instance of the object class is created. If there should be only one instance, as for example for (most) rooms, this is enough. If you need to create several instances of a class of objects, you clone it. Objects can be cloned using the wizard command "clone", as in "clone /obj/torch", and with the LPC function clone_object(), as in this_torch = clone_object("obj/torch"); Cloning an object will cause it to be loaded, if it wasn't already. When you have changed the description of an object by editing the file, and want to load the new version of the object, you can use the wizard command "update". Then load (or clone) the new version. If the object in question is a room, a "goto ROOMNAME" will load the room as well.

docs.title: -=[ ED - Unix Style Line Editor ]=-
docs.text: -=[ ED - Unix Style Line Editor ]=- The online editor is a clone of the Unix ed. This is a rehash of the original ed docs. Only creators have access to the online editor. Ed has two modes, command mode and insert mode. Command mode has the prompt ':', insert mode displasy a * prompt. <Insert Mode Commands> Insert mode has only one command. By typing a single '.' at the beginning of the line you exit insert mode, and enter command mode. Otherwise, each line of text is added to the document. Commands -------- / search forward for pattern ? search backward for a pattern = show current line number a append text starting after this line A like 'a' but with inverse autoindent mode c change, delete line and enter input mode d delete line(s) e replace this file with another file E same as 'e' but works if file has been modified f show/change current file name g Search and execute command on any matching line. h help file (display this message) i insert text starting before this line I indent the entire file (from DGD ed v0.1) j join lines together k mark this line with a character - later referenced as 'a l line line(s) with control characters displayed m move line(s) to specified line n toggle line numbering p print line(s) in range q quit editor Q quit editor even if file modified and not saved r read file into editor at end of file or behind the given line s search and replace set query, change or save option settings t move copy of line(s) to specified line v Search and execute command on any non-matching line. x save file and quit w write to current file (or specified file) W like the 'w' command but appends instead z display 20 lines, possible args are . + - Z display 40 lines, possible args are . + - Most commands in command mode will accept the following format, <line1,line2>command - apply command from line1 to line2 <line1>command - apply command to line1 command - apply command to current line For example: :1,5d - delete from line 1 to line 5 :2d - delete line 2 :d - delete current line If any numbers are out of range the command will fail. For help on ed commands type 'hc' where is the name of the command at the command prompt in ed.

*************************************************************************** Area Building Overview *************************************************************************** Areas are where players go to kill stuff, do quests etc. Creating an area is as much an artistic endeavour as it is a technical one, but the process should not be a haphazard and random. Of course builders can us any process they want to get the job done, but if they use a shitty process, it's their own damned fault, and will get approximately 0 sympathy from me. The procedure and guidelines listed here is a good starting point for beginning builders. *************************************************************************** Planning *************************************************************************** Before writing a single line of code, the area should be planned out. First, pick a theme for the area - a one line description of what the whole area is about. For example: Eves and vikings in a perpetual war. Ruined temple to Athena in some swamps. Settlement of desert dwarves. Dwarven mines that produce metals in Mitra's name. Keep in mind that the theme for Darkwind is fantasy. Your area must fit into this theme to be added to the game. No cyber realms or modern day areas will be considered. Next, flesh out the area with some rough details, again before coding. For example: Area in the underworld with mineral mines and an attached mining town full of dwarves. Dwarves are mining for metals which are used to make weapons for Mitra's holy armies. Monster levels are 10-25 with a few special BS monsters. Are is good/lawful aligned. Astute players will be able to custom make one special exceptional weapon for their own use. Total of about 50 rooms. Next, make a map of the area. The map can be on paper, but a text file is better since you can then include it with your area as supporting documentation. Fill in the map with notes on where mobs are, treasures are, special questy things etc. Lay out the entire area before writing a single line of code. *************************************************************************** Coding *************************************************************************** First, lay out your directory structure and headers. Since you've planned out what will exist, you can create a directory for the area, and subdirectories for things like rooms, monsters etc. Set up a header file that contains #defines to the appropriate directory paths. At no time should a path be hardcoded into the action objects in your area. Next lay down the topology. Basically put down all the rooms and connections (name the rooms correctly right off the bad) without setting up any properties etc. You want to be able to walk around the area even if there's nothing there yet. Once the rooms are there, fill them in with all the setting they need and the descs, but NOT the objects they contain like loot and monsters. Also, don't put in any special code yet - just set up the basic rooms. What you have now is a fully laid out, deserted area. The next step is to populate the area with restocking items (i.e. mobs and room contents that respawn). The difficulty here is that mobs carry items and you haven't made those yet. So now, go and make all the items that exist, but do them in their most basic forms - no add_actions or special stuff outside the reset() function. Then make all the mobs, and make sure they load up the required items. Finally add the restocking items to each of the rooms as appropriate. Now you have a basic, stocked area, but lacking features like add_actions, questy things etc. This area should stand on its own already as a basic, killing area. Now add all the special stuff to make your quests and whatnot work. In the course of this, you may have to alter descs etc. to give out hints, and do other funky stuff. Since you've already filled in the basics of the area you should be able to concentrate on just the special code. The end. Have your mentor check it over, then submit it for review. *************************************************************************** Some Dos and Don'ts ************************************************************************* Do not make deadly traps without hints A player must never die because there was some unforseeable danger in the next room. Of course if there are signs and they ignore them (giant, dragon footprints leading into a cave) it's their own damned fault... Don't make things too good (or bad) There's a balance between challenge and reward. If your area leans too far one way or the other, it's bad. High challenge should net high rewards and vice versa. Remember that the purpose of the game is for it to be fun and enjoyable both for players and for wizards - not to have all players converge on your castle just to get that wc 30 sword. Don't submit an area for review that you KNOW has problems Reviews are for VERIFYING that an area is OK. It's not a bug-fixing step. Don't make a HUGE area and submit it all at once Break it up into smaller, more manageable chunks. It's better that way for both the builder and the reviewer. Each chunk doesn't have to go into play piece by piece - they can get approved and wait for the whole thing to be done. ------ Version 1: ?? Version 2: Bob - May 29, 2004

docs.title: /public/docs/wizard/treasure
docs.text:
/public/docs/wizard/treasure ==================== /* Updated by Rodney - 9/20/94 */ ************************************************************************** IMPORTANT! THIS RULE IS LAW!!! ************************************************************************** If you make a magic item that does ANYTHING except for very minor things THIS COUNTS AS YOUR 1 ITEM PER 100 ROOMS LIMIT!!!!! You are only allowed 1 item per 100 QUALITY coded rooms. I.E., this means only one exceptional OBJECT per 100 rooms, not 1 weapon + 1 armour + 1 whatever per 100 rooms. Also items like this MUST use make_unique_object to ensure that only 1 of these items will be in the game at any one time. *************************************************************************** VERY IMPORTANT ADDITION!! DATE : 9/20/94 THIS TAKES EFFECT NOW!! *************************************************************************** The shops in town are all in the process of changing. We now have an inheritable shop, and they are type-specific, and they will soon be material-specific as well. These accept bitfield arguments, just like the set_new_type() on weapons. For example: set_treasure_type(TYP_MAP|TYP_MAGIC); The following are the legal treasure types (yes, you must include the "TYP_"): TYP_BOOK TYP_FURNITURE TYP_GEM TYP_JEWELRY TYP_STATUE TYP_GLASS TYP_MEAT TYP_DRINK TYP_FOOD TYP_CLOTHING TYP_ART TYP_CONTAINER TYP_SCROLL TYP_TABLET TYP_MAP TYP_BONES TYP_TRASH TYP_MAGIC TYP_TRINKET TYP_LIGHT TYP_POTION TYP_INSTRUMENT TYP_ALLTREASURES This last sets your treasure object to all treasure types. Now...On with the other functions... I never saw the point of making doc files that did not use all of the possible functions callable in stuff like armour/weapons in the doc file itself. If it's a doc file, then it's supposed to help you, right? Not to mention that LPmud 2.4.5's docs are not the greatest in explaining things. So, I took the time to re-write them. Here is the documentation for treasure. -------------------- The first lines in any treasure object should be: #include <mudlib.h> #include <treasure.h> #include <material.h> inherit TREASURE; These lines set up the object to be a treasure object and will allow calls to the treasure master object as defined below. Also, in the reset function, you should include the following line: if(!is_clone(this_object())) return; before calling ::reset(arg). This is a memory-saving measure. The only time when you should not include this line is when the treasure needs to reference the master object for some reason. -------------------- set_name("name"); string name. Adds the name passed in to the id list. set_alias("alias"); string alias. This is another name for the object. It doesn't appear anywhere, but it can be used by the player. set_alt_name("alt_name"); string alt_name. This is yet another name for the object. It doesn't appear anywhere, but it can be used by the player. set_short("short"); string short. This is the description seen in the player's inventory plus a ".
" Sets the short description of the object to short and the long description to "You see nothing special.
" set_long("long.
"); string long. Sets the long description of the object to long. I added the ".
" in the LPC line above to remind you that you should add the period and newline in the long description because LPC doesn't add it in for you. This is what the player will see when they look at the object. set_weight(weight); integer weight. This is the weight of the object. set_value(value); integer value. This is the selling value of the object. The buyback value is twice this value. set_treasure_type(TYPE1|TYPE2|...); bitfield TYPE1, TYPE2, .... set_material(TYPE1|TYPE2|...); bitfield TYPE1, TYPE2, .... set_read("read.
"); string read. This is what the player will see if they read the object. I added the ".
" in the LPC line above to remind you that you should add the period and newline in the long description because LPC doesn't add it in for you. set_info("info.
"); string info. This will be displayed to the owner of the treasure if he identifies the it. I believe there are plans here for something like an identify scroll or possibly an identify spell for one of the guilds, and this info would be displayed to the player at that time. This is a good place to put special information about the treasure. Usually, a hint of the weight is given, as well as if the treasure has any special uses. set_no_buy(n); status n. Set this to 0 if you want people to be able to buy and sell this to and from the store. Set to 1 if you don't. If you dont set this command, it will default to buyable. void set_no_sell(int iX); Pass a 1 as the parameter to have it be refused in stores. Note that this works a bit differently from no_buy, in that the more times you call set_no_sell(1), the more times you then have to call set_no_sell(0) to get it to a sellable state again. This is done so that the creator can set it no_sell, and if a guild uses no_sell to prohibit players from selling checked-out/borrowed items, when the guild calls set_no_sell(0) when the object is done being borrowed, the item will still not be sellable. int query_no_sell(); Returns sellable status. set_steal(n) status n. Set to 1 if you want to make the item unstealable by thieves. Don't abuse this command! It is meant only for things like quest items or objects great importance. If you don't add this command, item defaults to stealable ------------------ Here is a sample treasure for you to look at: #include <mudlib.h> #include <treasure.h> inherit TREASURE; void reset(int iArg) { if(!is_clone(this_object())) return; ::reset(iArg); if(iArg) return; set_id("rodney-hayden"); set_alias("key"); set_short("glowing key"); set_long("\ This key is completely black. However, it also emits a strange blue glow.
"); set_value(565); set_weight(1); set_light(1); set_treasure_type(TYP_GEM); }

docs.title: The first lines in any light source should be:
docs.text:
The first lines in any light source should be: #include <mudlib.h> #include <treasure.h> #include <material.h> inherit LIGHT; These lines set up the object to be a light source and will allow calls to the light master object as defined below. -------------------- set_name("name"); string name. Adds the name passed in to the id list. set_alias("alias"); string alias. This is another name for the object. It doesn't appear anywhere, but it can be used by the player. set_alt_name("alt_name"); string alt_name. This is yet another name for the object. It doesn't appear anywhere, but it can be used by the player. set_short("short"); string short. This is the description seen in the player's inventory. set_long("long.
"); string long. Sets the long description of the object to long. I added the ".
" in the LPC line above to remind you that you should add the period and newline in the long description because LPC doesn't add it in for you. This is what the player will see when they look at the object. set_weight(weight); integer weight. This is the weight of the object. set_treasure_type(TYP_LIGHT|TYPE2|...); Needless to say, you must at the very least set the treasure type to TYP_LIGHT. If there ere other properties to the light, they should be added as well. set_material(TYPE1|TYPE2|...); bitfield TYPE1, TYPE2, .... set_max_fuel(int); The integer amount for the maximum amount of fuel the object can hold. If this line is left out, it will default to 1000. IMPORTANT: This line MUST go before the line set_fuel() line. set_fuel(int); This is the amount of fuel that the light source will start with. For every 1 point of fuel, the light source will stay lit for 2 seconds. So a set_fuel(30) would stay lit for 1 minute. IMPORTANT: This line must go after set_max_fuel(); add_fuel(int); This will add fuel to light source upto a maximum of max_fuel. this function will almost always be called from an external source for the purpose of refilling a light source. set_reusable(int); Is the object reusable, or will it burn itself up in the process of being used. 1 = reusable; 0 = burns up in use. If this line is left out, it will default to burn itself up in use. set_can_light(int); Is the object always on, or can it be turned on and off. The flag is as follows: 1 = can be lit and extinguished. 0 = is always on. If this line is left out, it will default to being able to be lit. If object is always on, you don't need either set_max_fuel, set_fuel, or set_reusable. If an object is always on, this variable needs to be set BEFORE set_power(); set_value(value); integer value. This is the selling value of the object. The buyback value is twice this value. Also, the amount of fuel left in the object will modify the value of the object if it uses fuel. Please note, that the value is determined by a light source with a full supply of fuel. So if you set_value of 100 but then only put 1/4 of the fuel in it to fill it, you will get a reduced price. set_power(int); How much light does the light source give off? Default is 1. set_read("object","message.
"); string read. This is what the player will see if they read the object. I added the ".
" in the LPC line above to remind you that you should add the period and newline in the long description because LPC doesn't add it in for you. set_info("info.
"); string info. This will be displayed to the owner of the object if he identifies it. This line is required on all objects magical or mundane. This is a good place to put special information about the object that a player would not normally have access to. A hint of the weight could be given, as well as if the object has any special uses. If the item is truely a mundane item, state in the set_info that there are no special properties with the item. set_no_buy(n); status n. Set this to 0 if you want people to be able to buy and sell this to and from the store. Set to 1 if you don't. If you don't set this command, it will default to buyable. void set_no_sell(int iX); Pass a 1 as the parameter to have it be refused in stores. Note that this works a bit differently from no_buy, in that the more times you call set_no_sell(1), the more times you then have to call set_no_sell(0) to get it to a sellable state again. This is done so that the creator can set it no_sell, and if a guild uses no_sell to prohibit players from selling checked-out/borrowed items, when the guild calls set_no_sell(0) when the object is done being borrowed, the item will still not be sellable. int query_no_sell(); Returns sellable status. set_steal(n) status n. Set to 1 if you want to make the item unstealable by thieves. Don't abuse this command! It is meant only for things like quest items or objects great importance. If you don't add this command, item defaults to stealable

-=- /public/docs/wizard/container -=- ----------------------------- I never saw the point of making doc files that did not use all of the possible functions callable in stuff like armour/weapons in the doc file itself. If it's a doc file, then it's supposed to help you, right? Not to mention that LPmud 2.4.5's docs are not the greatest in explaining things. So, I took the time to re-write them. Here is the documentation for containers. -------------------- The first few lines in any container should be: #include <mudlib.h> inherit CONTAINER; This line sets up the object to be a container object and will allow calls to the container master object as defined below. -------------------- NOTE: The maximum weight allowed in the container should be no more than five (5) times the weight of the filled container itself. Anything more than this qualifies as a special item that must be created UNIQUE! (I.e., a bag of holding or portable hole.) -------------------- set_name("name"); string name. This is the a name for the object. Also sets the name and short description to name and the long description to name + ".
" set_alias("alias"); string alias. This is another name for the object. It doesn't appear anwhere, but it can be used by the player. set_alt_name("alt_name"); string alt_name. This is yet another name for the object. It also doesn't appear anywhere, but it can be used by the player. set_short("short"); string short. This is the description seen in the player's inventory plus a ".
" Sets the short description of the object to short and the long description to short + ".
" set_long("long.
"); string long. Sets the long description of the object to long. I added the ".
" in the LPC line above to remind you that you should add the period and newline in the long description because LPC doesn't add it in for you. This is what the player will see when they look at the object. set_weight(weight); integer weight. This is the empty weight of the container. set_max_weight(max_weight); integer max_weight. This is the maximum weight of all objects inside the container added together. set_weight_ratio(ratio); integer ratio. The number of weight units that must be put inside a container to increase the weight of the container by 1. Note that if this value is larger than the max_weight, the container will never become heavier, regardless of what is put inside it. The default value is 6. set_value(value); integer value. Sets the selling value of the container to value. Buy back value will be twice this amount. set_read("read.
"); string read. This is what the player will see if they read the object. I added the ".
" in the LPC line above to remind you that you should add the period and newline in the long description because LPC doesn't add it in for you. set_no_buy(n); status n. Set this to 0 if you want people to be able to buy and sell this to and from the store. Set to 1 if you don't. If you dont set this command, it will default to buyable. set_steal(n); status n. Set to 1 if you want to make the item unstealable by thieves. Don't abuse this command! It is meant only for things like quest items or objects great importance. If you don't add this command, item defaults to stealable. -------------------- Some special functions not normally called in reset() update_weight(); This function can be called to make sure the weight of the container is correct. It may become necessary to call this function if objects are moved into or out of the container by means other than the "put" and "get" commands. ie, when a reset clones and moves something into it. fix_weight(player); Don't use this function. Command "fixweight" on the player instead. object player. This function can be called to update the carried weight of a player if objects are moved into or out of the container by means other than "put" and "get". Usually used in conjunction with update_weight(). -------------------- Here is an example container object for you to look at: #include <mudlib.h> inherit CONTAINER; void reset(int iArg) { if(!is_clone(this_object())) return; ::reset(iArg); if(iArg) return; set_name("grape bowl"); set_alias("bowl"); set_alt_name("fruit bowl"); set_short("Grape bowl"); set_long("This bowl originally contained plump grapes.

"); set_weight(2); set_max_weight(6); set_weight_ratio(6); set_value(30); set_read("On the bottom of the bowl reads: Pontius Pilate's

"); set_no_buy(0); set_steal(0); }
