Both this function and the above two will add to the array of verbs, rather than replace them, so which you use is up to you. set_trigger_object(string) Sets the object which will trigger the trap, if any. If the trap is triggered by 'north', this will be blank. If it's triggered by 'pull lever', the trigger_action will be 'pull' and the trigger_object will be 'lever'. If it's triggered by 'search skeleton', the trigger_action is 'search' and the trigger_object is 'skeleton'. Performing the trigger action on a different object, such as 'search for traps' in the third example above, will NOT set off the trap. add_trigger_object(string) Performs the same function as set_trigger_object. set_trigger_objects(array of strings) Performs the same function as the above two, but with an array of strings instead of one string at a time. query_trigger() Returns the string(s) which must be performed to trigger the trap. (trigger_actions, plus trigger_objects if applicable) query_triggers() Returns the same thing as query_trigger. set_trap_func(closure) If you would like the trap to do something other than damage, this function specifies the function to be called when the trap is triggered. It can also be used in addition to the damage functions. set_search_func(closure) If you would like to set a customized search procedure, this function specifies the function to be called. The default search function is based on int, with thieves and (to a lesser extent) bards having a much better chance than other classes. Mages and necros also have a much better chance, but only if the trap is magical (see below). set_search_difficulty(int) Subtracts int from the chance of successfully searching (using the default search function). Used for traps that are particularly difficult or easy to detect. Note that there is a minimum chance of 1%, and a maximum of 95%, in any case. query_search_difficulty() Returns the search difficulty. set_disarm_difficulty(int) Subtracts int from the chance of successfully disarming the trap. The default is based on int and dex, and favors thieves, bards, mages, and necros in much the same way as the default search function. Again there is a minimum chance of 1% and a maximum of 95%. (However, the setter can always disarm his own trap.) query_disarm_difficulty() Returns the disarm difficulty. set_trap_type(int) Set to 1 if the trap is magical, 0 if it's mechanical. This affects the default search function and the disarm function, and also sets the treasure_type to either TYP_MAGIC or TYP_FURNITURE, respectively. remove_trap() Call this to destruct the trap. Included in case of trap- removing uniques or the like. In addition, there are two attributes that apply to traps: "auto_detect_traps" Gives the player a 100% chance of finding the trap (with the default search function). Useful for a 'find traps' spell or item. "immunity_to_traps" If the player has this, the trap will trigger without harming him. A trap can be found with the commands 'search', 'find', or 'detect', and the arguments 'traps', 'trap', 'for traps', or 'for trap'. It can be disabled with the commands 'disarm', 'remove', or 'disable' and the arguments 'trap' or 'traps', but only if the person attempting to disable the trap first succeeded in searching for it. The default search function displays the trigger on a successful search and tells the character that they can attempt to 'disable trap'.

*************************************************************************** Naming and Descriptions *************************************************************************** Note: All literal code in this help document is separated by a bunch of = signs. The = signs are NOT part of the code. For example: ==================== #include <mudlib.h> #include <types.h> #include <material.h> ==================== refers to the three include lines, literally. *************************************************************************** Naming/Desc Basics *************************************************************************** All monster, weapons, armors, and other objects have names. These names are how players and the mudlib refer to the items. Visible objects also have descriptions. These descriptions are how players see these objects. (NOTE: rooms also have descriptions, but not names) The reason for this document is to spell out exactly how to use names in a consistent manner. The following function calls can be used to set the name(s) of an object: ==================== set_name(string sName); set_alias(string sAlias); set_aliases(string* asAliases); ==================== set_name() is used to set the primary name of an object. The primary name of an object may occasionally be shown to a player under certain circumstance. Each object can only have one primary name, and the object can be referred to by that name, by players (for looking etc). set_alias() is used to set an alias name of an object. The alias name never appears to the player, but can be used by the player to refer to an object. Multiple calls to set_alias() can be used to set multiple aliases. set_aliases() is used to set multiple aliases at once. Note that this will clear all previously set aliases. The following function calls can be used to set the desc(s) of an object: ==================== set_long(string sLong); set_short(string sShort); set_short_modifier(string sMod); set_short_modifiers(string* asMod); ==================== set_long() is used to set the long desc of an object. This desc is what is seen when the object is looked at. The long desc in a room is what is seen when a player enters a room with brief mode off. set_short() is used to set the short desc of an object. This desc is what is seen when the player doesn't actually look specifically at the object (for example, a player's inventory lists things by short desc). In rooms, the short desc is what is seen when the player is in brief mode. set_short_modifier() and set_short_modifiers() work in the same was as aliases. Short modifiers alter the short desc line of an object by adding the modifier string in brackets. *************************************************************************** Deprecated Functions *************************************************************************** The following functions are deprecated and should no longer be used. Older code may contain them, and they will still work, but they should not be used in new code: ==================== set_id(string sId); // same as set_name reset_short(string sShort); // same as set_short add_alias(string sAlias); // same as set_alias set_alt_name(string sAltName); // same as set_alias ==================== *************************************************************************** Names *************************************************************************** The name is the main name of an object, and should be something obvious for that item. It should be all-lowercase, except for proper names, and not contain any articles such as 'the' or 'a'. Alias names are other names that may refer to the object. They should always be all lowercase, with no articles. Try to include aliases for all reasonable combinations of an object's short desc, or obvious characteristics. (E.g. a rapier should have a 'sword' alias) In some cases, it is useful for an object to have special aliases so that other code can recognize that that particular object from other, similar ones (Like a special quest sword). In these cases, add a unique alias (not used anywhere else on the mud) that starts with double underscores and the coder's name. E.g. __bob_dwarf_mines_key. *************************************************************************** Descriptions *************************************************************************** Short descs should be short (one line) descriptions of the object. This can be considered a first impression upon seeing it, but it can also be used to give extra implied information. For example: gleaming longsword large goblin Ed the horse are all good short descs. Note that all short descs should be entirely in lowercase letters except for proper names which start with a capital. Do not use articles like 'the' or 'a' in the short desc. (Exception: the short desc for rooms may use articles, and are always first letter capped). N.B. The ENTIRE short desc can be used to refer to an object as well. There is no need to make a separate alias for it. Long descs are a detailed description seen when a player looks at an object/room in detail. Long descs should be in complete English sentences, with appropriate punctuation and capitalization. Short modifiers should be words/short phrases that briefly denote how an object has been modified. For example: hardened chipped broken poisoned are all good modifiers. *************************************************************************** Using Names/Descs *************************************************************************** Sometimes, the name/descs are are used in spam and for other uses in the course of building. There are appropriate queries for each kind of name and desc, and some extras as well. If you need this functionality, this is all encapsulated in the alias.c inherit. If you do not have permissions to read this file, ask an ARCH+. ------ Version 1: Bob - May 29, 2004

docs.title: Profession Drops
docs.text: Profession Drops With professions come profession materials. If you'd like to have rooms or npcs have any of the materials as loot, you can. For Example: #include <professions.h> inherit PROFESSION_MATERIAL; void reset(int iArg) { if(!is_clone(this_object())) return; ::reset(iArg); if(iArg) return; set_short("a bundle of Topaz Shards"); set_long("\ A small bundle of Topaz Shards used for professions.\n"); set_aliases(({"bundle","shard","shards","Topaz Shard","Topaz Shards"})); set_profession_type("special"); set_profession_item("Topaz Shard"); set_profession_quantity(5); } set_profession_type("<type>") must be: bolt, herb, ore, reagent, skin or special. Lower case, and if not one of those, it will do nothing. set_profession_item("<item>") is the profession material. They are case sensitive to match what you'd see in the reagents command. If it doesn't match a known item, it will do nothing. set_profession_quantity(int) is the quantity to add/subtract from the player's total when they pick up the item. Just like standard reagent drops, the code for applying the count is done when the player picks up the item using init(). It also gives them random(100) coins for the item, unless you override it with your own set_value. If you want your own special item added to the special list for an area specific quest or item, please contact an admin to get it added for you. Profession Recipe Along with profession drops, you can create recipe cards. The cards allow the players to create objects with the items they have gathered. For Example: #include <professions.h> #include "ExampleHeaderFile.h" inherit PROF_RECIPE; void reset(int iArg) { if(!is_clone(this_object())) return; ::reset(iArg); if(iArg) return; set_short("Fly Potion Recipe Card"); set_object_file(PROF_DIR+"potions/fly"); set_required_items ( ([ "Hashish":"herb";3, "Mistletoe":"herb";3, ]) ); set_other_items ( ([ "Cow Horn":MYAREAOBJS+"cowhorn";3, "The King's favorite beer":MYAREAOBJS+"budlight";3 ]) ); set_prof_level_required("Alchemy",1,1); set_read_info("\ This recipe creates a Hashish Potion for flight."); set_uses(5); set_value(50); } set_object_file(filepath) is the path to the object that will be created. set_required_items(mapping) is the mapping of the profession materials needed to create the item. It should be: ([ case-sensitive material short: profession type ; quantity ]) set_other_itmes(mapping) is the mapping for any other non-profession materials required to create the item. It should be: ([ string description of the item : object path ; quantity ]) The description could be the short of the item, or a hint to what it is if it's part of a quest combine, or whatever you want them to see when they read the card. set_prof_level_required("<Profession>", min skill to craft, tNoSkillup). Profession should be any of the 8 professions. Min skill is the minimum skill they need in the profession to craft the item. tNoSkillup means that they can't gain a skillup using the card. If the minimum skill is <= 500, the max skill they can gain is minimum skill + 100, otherwise 1000. set_uses(int) is the amount of times the players can use the card.

*************************************************************************** Equipment Power and Gearcheck *************************************************************************** Weapons, armour, implants, and other objects inheriting EQUIP expose a common power-scoring API. The player command "gearcheck" uses this API to compare carried equipment against the equipment and slots a player is currently using. *************************************************************************** Item Level *************************************************************************** Every object inheriting EQUIP can declare its intended progression level: ==================== set_item_level(150); ==================== void set_item_level(int level); Sets the equipment's item level. Values are bounded from 0 through the current player level cap of 250. Level 0 means that legacy or deliberately unranked equipment has no item level. Calling this function, including with 0, is an explicit override of area inference. void clear_item_level(); Removes an explicit override and allows the equipment to infer its level again from the owning area's catalog metadata. int query_item_level(); Returns the explicit item level when one was set. Otherwise, the first query resolves the equipment blueprint's owning area and caches that area's equipment level on the object. This API is shared by weapons, armour, implants, cyberware, relics, and other EQUIP descendants. Item level describes the progression context for which an item was designed. It is not a minimum-use restriction: use set_level_restriction() separately when a real mechanical gate is required. For implants, cyberware, relics, and other non-weapon/non-armour equipment, item level remains descriptive unless the owning mechanic explicitly consumes it. Weapons and armour use item level in physical combat. Their inherent rating is: ==================== min(25, item_level / 10) ==================== A weapon uses the rating as inherent armour penetration. Armour uses it as inherent armour strength. The ratings oppose each other, so equal-level gear preserves the ordinary combat result: ==================== armour factor = 100 + armour strength - weapon penetration armour factor is bounded from 75 through 125 ==================== Level 150 therefore supplies a 15% rating and level 250 supplies 25%. Worn armour strength is weighted by each piece's absorb contribution; a small ring cannot raise an otherwise weak suit to its own item level. Only worn armour's share of physical flat reduction, percentage reduction, and armour-derived absorb chance participates. Intrinsic absorb, temporary absorption, shields, resistances, guild mitigation, boss reduction, dodge, accuracy, and nonphysical damage are unchanged. NPCs without a weapon use their capped monster level as the item level of natural physical attacks. NPC intrinsic armour likewise uses capped monster level when worn armour is not supplying the effective absorb class. When worn armour overtakes the NPC's intrinsic armour floor, the actual worn equipment levels are used instead. These fallbacks do not apply to unarmed or naked players. A source-owned player intrinsic attack may explicitly supply a clamped item level, which provides the same standard level-derived penetration without requiring a hidden weapon object. Boss tier remains separate from item level. The matchup applies after the ordinary physical-armour cap is calculated. DAM_AP then halves the remaining armour contribution. Do not manually add a power feature for inherent penetration or strength; EQUIPMENT_POWER_D scores both automatically. Area-owned equipment normally needs no setter. Its blueprint path resolves through AREA_CATALOG_D, which uses area.json's optional equipment_level or the midpoint of recommended_min_level and recommended_max_level. The result is cached, so combat does not repeatedly query the catalog. Existing objects keep their resolved value; newly cloned objects see refreshed catalog metadata. Use set_item_level() for boss, quest, shop, crafted, generated, shared-path, or otherwise exceptional rewards whose intended progression differs from the surrounding area. Shared-path equipment cannot infer where it was acquired. Use set_item_level(0) to deliberately opt an item out of area inference. Normal structured properties are scored automatically, including weapon class, hit bonus, armour dodge and absorb class, equipment stats, resistances, sigils, item-level armour penetration and strength, standard weapon and armour modifications, generated item procs, implant procs, cyberware strain, durability, and temporary item warnings. *************************************************************************** Hidden Sigil Discovery *************************************************************************** See wizhelp 4.27 for the complete builder-facing sigil guide, including how to mark equipment, add registry entries and effects, wire discovery, and validate the result. The shared sigil registry in <sigils.h> distinguishes public and hidden definitions: ==================== "open mark": SIGIL_DEF(3, 100, "mid", "Its concise effect summary"), "secret mark": HIDDEN_SIGIL_DEF(3, 160, "high", "Its concise effect summary"), ==================== A hidden sigil remains mechanically active and contributes its full equipment power. Its ID, level, summary, and named effect messages are concealed from a character until discovery. Item inspection reports only an uninterpreted marking, gearcheck reports an undiscovered sigil, and the sigils command omits it. Do not use display text or equipment possession as discovery state. The system owning the real criterion reveals it at the successful mutation boundary: ==================== if (player->discover_sigil("secret mark")) /* criterion-specific follow-up, if any */ ==================== discover_sigil() returns true only for a newly learned hidden registry ID, saves player progression immediately, and gives a generic discovery message. Pass a nonzero second argument to suppress that message when the owning quest, encounter, remort, or lore interaction supplies its own presentation. query_sigil_known() reports public or discovered IDs, and query_discovered_sigils() returns a defensive copy of learned hidden IDs. Discovery is an additive player-save field. Existing saves restore with an empty discovery list, and lazy normalization removes malformed, duplicate, public, or retired entries. Hidden definitions should not be added to public wiki tables or other static exhaustive lists. Custom scripted callbacks cannot be executed while an item is being inspected. Running weapon_hit(), wear_func(), or an implant callback during gearcheck could damage something, change state, or otherwise cause side effects. Builders must therefore describe the relative value of custom effects explicitly. *************************************************************************** Declaring Custom Effects *************************************************************************** void add_power_feature(string sId, int iPower, string sDescription, string sCategory); Adds or replaces one explicitly scored feature on the equipment. sId A stable lowercase identifier. Use underscores instead of spaces. Reusing an identifier replaces the previous declaration. iPower The feature's relative power contribution. Positive values make the item stronger; negative values represent a drawback or tradeoff. sDescription Short text describing the mechanical effect being scored. sCategory One of "offense", "defense", "utility", or "reliability". Invalid or omitted categories default to "utility". Example: ==================== add_power_feature("scripted_hit", 300, "Burning cinder on-hit burst", "offense"); ==================== Power values should reflect the effect's expected value over ordinary play, not its maximum possible single activation. Consider damage or healing amount, activation chance, cooldown, duration, targeting limits, reliability, and any cost paid by the player. Compare the result with similar existing items and inspect it with "gearcheck <item>" before release. Do not add declarations for properties already scored automatically. For example, do not manually score weapon class, AC, add_equipment_stat(), resistances, sigils, standard modifications, or structured generated procs. Doing so would count the same power twice. *************************************************************************** Required Scripted Feature IDs *************************************************************************** Use these exact identifiers for the standard opaque equipment hooks: "scripted_hit" A weapon using set_hit_func() or set_hit_obj(). "scripted_wield" A weapon using set_wield_func() or set_wield_obj() when the callback grants a benefit or drawback beyond permission checks and messaging. "scripted_wear" Armour using set_wear_func() or set_wear_obj() when the callback grants a benefit or drawback beyond permission checks and messaging. For an implant proc whose effect is "call_function", use the proc's exact "id" as the power feature identifier. Example implant callback: ==================== add_power_feature("offhand_cleave", 540, "Armour-piercing off-hand cleave", "offense"); add_implant_proc(([ "id" : "offhand_cleave", "trigger" : "combat_hit", "chance" : 17, "cooldown" : 6, "effect" : "call_function", "function" : "execute_offhand_cleave" ])); ==================== If the required declaration is missing, gearcheck marks the item UNCERTAIN. Its visible score still includes all measurable properties, but the scripted effect is omitted from that score. *************************************************************************** Supporting Functions *************************************************************************** void remove_power_feature(string sId); Removes one explicit feature declaration. mapping query_power_features(); Returns a copy of all explicit feature declarations. Each entry contains "power", "description", and "category". int query_power(object oPlayer); Returns the item's final integer power score. Pass the player when player-specific context is available. mapping query_power_profile(object oPlayer); Returns the full scoring explanation used by gearcheck. Important fields include: "score" final non-negative score "item_level" declared progression level, or 0 when unranked "offense" offensive subtotal "defense" defensive subtotal "utility" stats, resources, and general utility "reliability" durability and reliability adjustments "components" individual scored reasons "warnings" restrictions and temporary-item notes "unknown_effects" scripted effects not yet declared "confidence" "high", "uncertain", or "invalid" void set_power_adjustment(int iPower); Adds a general item-specific correction to the final score. Prefer add_power_feature() for named mechanics because it provides a useful explanation. Use this only when a named feature cannot reasonably describe the correction. int query_power_adjustment(object oPlayer); Returns the general correction. An unusual item may override this function when its correction genuinely depends on the player. It must be deterministic and must not change game state. *************************************************************************** Guidelines *************************************************************************** * Power scoring is comparison guidance, not permission to exceed equipment balance, uniqueness, guild, or area-building rules. * Annotation functions must be called during normal item configuration, such as reset() or a tier/grade configuration function. * Scoring functions and overrides must never deal damage, send combat spam, consume resources, roll random outcomes, or modify the player or item. * Keep identifiers stable so saved or restored equipment remains explainable. * When an effect changes by tier or grade, calculate its declared power from that same tier or grade. * Validate the result in game with "gearcheck <item>" and compare it with equipment intended for the same level and slot.

*************************************************************************** Sigils *************************************************************************** Sigils are passive, levelled effects supplied by active equipment or by an explicit inherent source on a living. They modify existing game actions; a sigil should not grant a command of its own. This file covers the builder-facing contracts. Players can use "sigils" to see their active recognized sigils and "sigils catalog" to see the effects their character recognizes. See wizhelp 4.26 for equipment power and gearcheck generally. Applicant-level and higher wizards also have two diagnostic forms: ==================== sigils <player> sigils report ==================== "sigils <player>" shows the same source breakdown for another online living or a saved player. "sigils report" summarizes every currently online non-immortal player, including players with no active recognized sigils. The report excludes NPCs and Applicant-level or higher users. Both forms apply the viewing wizard's normal hidden-sigil discovery rules. The system has four main owners: /secure/include/sigils.h Stable IDs and display/scoring metadata. /inherits/equip.c The API used to place sigils on equipment. /secure/living/equipment.c Active equipment and inherent-source aggregation. /secure/living/sigils.c Shared effect calculations, cooldowns, counters, discovery, and effect messages. Do not put a standard sigil's mechanical implementation on every marked item. The item contributes levels; the shared living layer implements the effect once. *************************************************************************** Putting Sigils on Equipment *************************************************************************** Weapons, armour, implants, and other objects inheriting EQUIP already have the sigil API. Configure a mark with its lowercase registry ID: ==================== set_sigil("rime focus", 1); ==================== An item can carry more than one sigil: ==================== set_sigil("fortified", 1); set_sigil("venom ward", 1); ==================== void set_sigil(string sSigil, int iLevel); Adds or replaces the item's contribution for a registered sigil. The ID is normalized to lowercase. Unknown IDs and levels below 1 remove that entry. Values above the registry maximum are clamped. void remove_sigil(string sSigil); Removes the named contribution from the item. int query_sigil(string sSigil); Returns this item's contribution, or 0 when absent. mapping query_sigils(); Returns the item's valid sigil contributions, clamped to their registry maxima. Use this public query in consumers. The sigil is active only while the item participates in the living's active equipment set. That includes worn armour, main and secondary weapons, and properly activated internal equipment. Merely carrying an item is not enough. Use the normal armour, weapon, or internal-equipment lifecycle; do not make a carried object alter the player's inherent sigil mapping as a shortcut. Contributions from active sources add together and the final level is capped. Excess levels have no effect. Ordinary marked equipment usually contributes one level. A two-level contribution is a deliberate reward and balance choice, not a default. Review the item's slot, acquisition difficulty, item level, and the ease of completing the sigil's cap. Looking at an item automatically shows recognized sigils and their item/max levels. The "sigils" command automatically reports active totals and their equipment sources. Builders do not need to duplicate either display. An explicit successful "get" or "take" calls the living's notify_sigil_pickup() helper. query_sigil_pickup_message() owns the generic text used by that notification. Neither helper names sigils, changes discovery state, or runs during unrelated inventory delivery and restoration paths. Sigils are scored automatically by EQUIPMENT_POWER_D at: ==================== item contribution * registry power per level ==================== Do not add add_power_feature() or set_power_adjustment() for the same sigil. That would count its power twice. Use "gearcheck <item>" to inspect the result; hidden sigils are still scored even when their identity is concealed. *************************************************************************** Inherent Sigil Sources *************************************************************************** Livings have a separate inherent sigil mapping for forms, boons, guild features, and other non-equipment sources: ==================== player->set_sigil("evade", 1); player->remove_sigil("evade"); player->query_inherent_sigil("evade"); ==================== This setter replaces the entire inherent value for that ID. It does not keep independent contributions for several systems. If several features can grant the same inherent sigil, one owning soul, daemon, or inheritable must retain their primitive source state, calculate the combined value, and publish that value through set_sigil(). Do not have unrelated objects race to overwrite or remove each other's contribution. Temporary inherent sources must reapply through their normal restore or activation path and remove their contribution on every exit path, including expiry, form change, guild cleanup, destruction, quit, and reconnect where applicable. Prefer equipment sigils when a concrete equipped object is the actual source; equipment aggregation already owns that lifecycle. Useful living queries are: int query_sigil(string sSigil); Returns the capped effective total from inherent and active-equipment sources. Mechanics should use this query. mapping query_sigils(); Returns all capped effective totals. int query_equipment_sigil(string sSigil); Returns the uncapped sum from active equipment only. mapping query_equipment_sigils(); Returns all uncapped active-equipment sums. int query_inherent_sigil(string sSigil); Returns the living's inherent contribution only. The uncapped source queries are useful for presentation and diagnostics. Game effects should consume query_sigil() so excess sources cannot exceed the mechanical maximum. *************************************************************************** Extending the Registry *************************************************************************** Sigil IDs are player-visible compatibility contracts. Before adding one, search all producers and consumers, confirm that an existing sigil cannot express the design, and settle the effect, cap, progression band, power per level, acquisition plan, and exact integration boundary. Add the definition to SIGILS in /secure/include/sigils.h: ==================== "open mark": SIGIL_DEF(3, 100, "mid", "Its concise player-facing effect summary"), ==================== Each definition supplies: max Maximum effective level. Current effects support a maximum of 3, except Critical Strike and Ruthless, which support 5. A new maximum is not metadata-only: update and test query_sigil() in /secure/living/equipment.c and query_sigil_effect_level() in /secure/living/sigils.c rather than allowing display and mechanics to disagree. power Equipment power per contributed level. Set this from expected value in ordinary play, not the largest possible activation. It is scored automatically as utility by the current power daemon. band The player-facing progression label: "low", "mid", or "high". This is catalog metadata, not an equip restriction. summary Concise player-facing text used by "sigils catalog". Describe what the sigil does, without implementation jargon. hidden Supplied by SIGIL_DEF() or HIDDEN_SIGIL_DEF(). See Hidden Sigils below. Keep the ID lowercase and stable. Renaming an ID changes equipment source, effect, discovery, display, tests, and possibly saved character progression. Preserve an alias or migrate persisted discovery state if a live hidden ID must change. *************************************************************************** Implementing the Effect *************************************************************************** Implement shared behavior in /secure/living/sigils.c. Read levels through query_sigil() or query_sigil_effect_level(); do not rescan worn inventory or reimplement source aggregation. Keep the operation bounded, validate object arguments, and avoid retaining LPC object references in persistent state. Use the narrowest existing integration boundary. Current examples include: /secure/living.c Damage dealt/received, fatal damage, kills, shields, and regen. /secure/living/combat.c Critical-hit and dodge calculations. /secure/living/stats.c Overhealing. /inherits/ash_burner.c Ash yield and autosalvage proceeds. /objects/professions/profession_material.c Profession-material quantity. Prefer a named helper in the sigil effect layer with one call at the owning gameplay boundary. Do not scatter string-ID checks through item files or several unrelated callers. Add a compatible forward declaration in the consumer when that file's compilation style requires one. Runtime cooldowns, counters, object references, and caches must be nosave. Use stable string keys for independent counters and cooldowns. Messages about a hidden effect must pass through the shared hidden-aware presentation helper or provide equivalent concealment; a hidden ID must not leak through combat spam before discovery. When adding a reactive effect, decide and test: * whether it triggers before or after ordinary mitigation; * whether misses, zero damage, reflected damage, and self-damage count; * whether repeated hits retain state across targets or combat; * whether cooldowns are per living, per target, or global to that effect; * whether NPCs and players use the same behavior; * whether the effect can recurse through the event it creates; * what happens on death, linkdeath, reconnect, and destruction. Use catch() only at optional integration boundaries where a sigil failure must not break the owning action. The effect itself should remain deterministic where practical and must not mutate state from a display or power query. *************************************************************************** Hidden Sigils *************************************************************************** Use a hidden definition only when discovering the mark is real progression: ==================== "secret mark": HIDDEN_SIGIL_DEF(3, 160, "high", "Its concise player-facing effect summary"), ==================== Hidden sigils remain mechanically active and fully power-scored. Until a character discovers one, item inspection reports an uninterpretable marking, gearcheck reports an undiscovered sigil, the active list and catalog omit its identity, and generic effect messages must not reveal its name. The system that owns the actual discovery criterion reveals it only after the criterion succeeds: ==================== if (player->discover_sigil("secret mark")) /* criterion-specific follow-up, if any */ ==================== discover_sigil() returns true only for a newly learned hidden ID, persists the player immediately, and normally sends a generic discovery message. Pass a nonzero second argument when the owning quest, encounter, remort, or lore interaction supplies its own message: ==================== player->discover_sigil("secret mark", 1); ==================== query_sigil_known() returns true for public or discovered registry IDs. query_discovered_sigils() returns a defensive copy of learned hidden IDs. Do not use item possession, display text, or an object's alias as discovery state. Do not add hidden definitions to public exhaustive wiki tables. *************************************************************************** Validation *************************************************************************** For ordinary marked gear: * compile the item with both standard LPC checks; * look at it before and after equipping it; * verify "sigils" reports the correct source and capped total; * verify removing, unwielding, or extracting it removes the contribution; * inspect "gearcheck <item>" and confirm the sigil is scored once; * exercise save/login and reconnect when the equipment kind requires it. For a new or changed sigil, extend the focused regression in /secure/obj/sigil_effects_test.c. Validate the registry entry, level 1, the maximum level, one level beyond the cap, and the exact mechanical boundary. Update the regression's expected registry count when adding or retiring an entry. For chance effects, bound the result rather than asserting one random roll. For counters and cooldowns, test one event before activation, activation, and the immediate repeat or reset path. Compile every changed LPC file and representative consumers of a changed shared include or living inheritable. Then exercise the effect through its real gameplay action on a live or test MUD. Compilation alone does not prove equipment activation, cleanup, discovery persistence, or event ordering. ------ Version 1: Codex - Aug 10, 2026

docs.title: Rev. 3
docs.text:
Rev. 3 Coding Monsters =============== Purpose ======= The purpose of this doc is to explain how to properly code monsters in Dakrwind. Instructions ============ The first three lines in any monster object should be: #include <mudlib.h> #include <types.h> inherit MONSTER; These lines set up the object to be a monster object and will allow calls to the monster master object as defined below. Additionally, in the reset() function, before calling ::reset(iArg), you should enter the following line: if(!is_clone(this_object())) return; This is a memory-saving measure. The only time this line should not be entered is when the monster needs to refer to the master object for some reason. ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_name("name"); string name. This is a name for the object. Also sets the alignment to 0, capitalizes the string you pass into set_name and sets the cap_name and short_desc to that, and the long description to "You see nothing special.
" ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_level(level); int level. This function serves many purposes: - Sets the monster's level according to level. - Sets the monster's intrinsic AC to 10/3 of level. Intrinsic AC is defined as that of the monster's "skin" (or scales, or hide, or whatever). This number will be added to any armour which you may clone onto the monster and make it wear. - Sets the monster's hit points to the max of the result of the following equations: 42 + (Con * 8) or (Con + 5) * (Con + 5). - Sets the monster's spell points to the result obtained from the hit points calculation. - Sets the monster's experience points by getting the number from "/domains/darkwind/maincity/adv_guild" NOTE: It is important to call these two functions first. Since these functions set up many of the monster's stats, if you call these functions after you call the ones below, then these functions will override those explained below (only if you call them afterwards.) I should also note that because these two functions set all of the monster's necessary stats, the remaining functions are all optional. ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_alias("alias"); string alias. This is another name for the monster. It doesn't appear anywhere, but it can be used by the player. ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_alt_name("alt_name"); string alt_name. This is another name for the monster. It doesn't appear anywhere, but it can be used by the player. ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_aliases(aliases); string array aliases. Causes the monster to identify to any of the strings in the argument array. add_alias("alias"); string alias. Adds alias to the array of strings which the monster identifies to. ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_race("race"); string race. This is another name for the monster. It doesn't appear anywhere, but it can be used by the player. The race is also often used in dir_hooks in rooms as an identifier for the monster. See /open/INCLUDE/monster_race.h for currently available races. ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_short("short"); string short. This is the description seen when the player walks into the room, looks at the room, or glances. Sets the short description of the monster to short and the long description to the short description + ".
" ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_long("long.
"); string long. Sets the long description of the object to long. I added the ".
" in the LPC line above to remind you that you should add the period and newline in the long description because LPC doesn't add it in for you. This is what the player will see when they look at the monster. ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_size(SIZE); This sets the size of the monster and is mandatory. For backwards compatablility reasons though, if the line is not in the monster, it will default to a size of SIZ_MEDIUM. Legal sizes are: SIZ_NONE SIZ_TINY SIZ_SMALL SIZ_MEDIUM SIZ_LARGE SIZ_HUGE Examples of sizes are: SIZ_NONE: Used for monsters that don't leave corpses when they die. E.g. Ghosts, Air Elementals, etc. SIZ_TINY: Butterflys, Goldfish, Mice, Rats, etc. SIZ_SMALL: Racoons, Dogs, Cats, Kobolds, etc. SIZ_MEDIUM: Humanoids (Dwarves, Humans, Elves, etc.), Wolves, etc. SIZ_LARGE: Bears, Lions, Trolls, Ettins, etc. SIZ_HUGE: Dragons, Elephants, Whales, Titans, etc. It should be noted that if you use SIZ_NONE, no corpse will be left when the monster dies. Anything they are carrying will fall to the ground. Also, when a SIZ_NONE monster dies, it will give you a different death message than just <You Killed X>. However, if you set a different death message on your monster, that will be used in place of the standard one, as usual. query_size(); returns the bit value of the size of the monster. SIZ_NONE = 1 SIZ_TINY = 2 SIZE_SMALL = 4 SIZ_MEDIUM = 8 SIZ_LARGE = 16 SIZ_HUGE = 32 ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_hp(hp); int hp. Sets the monster's hit points and max hit points to hp. Using set_con is preferable, so that in case the hit point formulae are changed your monsters won't be wildly out of whack. ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_ep(ep); int ep. If ep is less than the number of experience points gotten from "/domains/darkwind/maincity/adv_guild" then it sets the monster's experience points to ep. Otherwise, it stays at the value received from "/room/adv_guild.c." Typically this function is only used when you want to make a monster not worth anything on death. ----------------------------------------------------------------- add_dodge_bonus(bonus); This number can be positive or negative. It will make the monster either easier or harder to hit in combat. A monster with dodge bonus 20 would be 20% harder to hit in combat than another monster with the same stats and level. Use this to make the monster better or worse at dodging attacks in combat. It works as a percentage. Small, quick monsters can be given a positive number, while large or clumsy ones can be given a negative number. ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_al(al,et); int al. Sets the alignment of the monster to al. Remember that to make a monster evil, you must use a negative number. int et. Sets the ethics of the monster to et. Remember that to make a monster chaotic, you must use a negative number. If you don't set this, 0 will be assumed (ie, setting ethics is not required when you use set_al). A note with both types of alignment-- The range between -299 and 299 is neutral, more than 1000 or less than -1000 is very extreme (see 'wizhelp 11.1 (alignment and ethics)' for more details). ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_ac(ac); int ac. Sets the monster's intrinsic AC to ac. Do not use this to just arbitrarily set the monster's ac. If you don't know when it should be used or not, ask. ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_str(str); int str. Sets strength to str. set_int(int); int int. Sets intelligence to int. set_dex(dex); int dex. Sets dexterity to dex. set_con(con); int con. Sets constitution to con. set_wis(wis); int wis. Sets wisdom to wis. set_chr(chr); int chr. Sets charisma to chr. The above functions do not need to be set as the monster's level will set them up automatically. You will override those numbers with these funtions. If you don't know when they should be used, ask. ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_move_at_reset(); no arg. Sets move_at_reset (a local int monster variable) to 1, which makes the monster pick an exit in its present location at random each reset and move in that direction. When using this function in a monster, make sure to clone it in the room via make_room_unique (see wizhelp 4.2, coding a room) ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_aggressive(a); int a. If a is 0, the monster is peaceful. If a is 1, the monster will attack any player that enters the room. If a is greater than 1, then a is used as a percentage to determine if the monster will attack. For example, if a is 70 then the monster has a 70% chance of attacking a player entering the room, and a 30% chance of leaving the player alone. int query_aggressive(); This returns the base chance of being aggressive. It is an integer from 0-100 representing the % of attacking on sight. The value 1 is never returned, because that is a special value for backwards compatibility, and is automatically registered as 100 instead. set_aggressive_level(a); int a. The variable "a" is a number that represents the player level after which the monster will attack. If you set it to 29, the monster will only be agressive on players level 30 and above. This function is used in conjuction with set_agressive. ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_steal(a); int a. If a is 0, then the monster can be stolen from. If a is 1, then the monster cannot be stolen from. If a is greater than 1, then the chance of stealing from the monster will be reduced by a% (so a thief would have only a 20% chance of stealing from a monster which set_steal(80)). int query_steal(); Returns the value of set_steal. Note that this function will never return 1, because set_steal(1) and set_steal(100) are equivalent, and this function automatically returns 100 when the monster uses set_steal(1). ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_viking(); no arg. Gives the monster the viking curse. ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_whimpy(); no arg. Will make the monster run away when its hit points get low. set_wimpy_cmd(s); string s. If set, this will cause the monster to always perform the command 's' first when trying to wimpy. You can use this to control which direction a monster attempts to run away. ----------------------------------------------------------------- load_chat(chance, strs); int chance, string *strs. Sets the chance that a monster will talk each heartbeat to chance, and sets the things the monster can say to the array passed into load_chat(). load_a_chat(chance, strs); int chance, string *strs. Same as load_chat, but these messages are said only during battle. ----------------------------------------------------------------- load_cmd(chance, strs); int chance, string *strs. This works exactly like load_chat, except it is a list of commands the monster will perform. You can have an array which includes something like: ({"say who are you?","say I'm Bob!","sing"}) rather than having to do ({"Monstername asks: who are you?
","Monstername exclaims: I'm Bob!
", "Monstername sings a song.
"}) for fairly obvious reasons. Anywhere you place a $N, it will be replaced with the name of a random player character in the room, allowing the monster to do directed emotes. "kick $N" would cause the monster to kick a random player, for instance. load_a_cmd(chance, strs); Same as load_cmd, except works in combat. ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_random_pick(r); int r. Determines if the monster will randomly pick an object from the room's inventory. If the item it picks up is a weapon which has a better WC than its current wielded weapon, then it wields the weapon. If the item is an armour, and it is not already wearing an armour of that type, it will wear the armour. ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_dead_ob(ob); object ob. Usually this_object() is the object passed to set_dead_ob. Use this function in conjunction with monster_died() when you want something done when the monster dies. This function is useful for destructing corpses (Like on Stone Golems...) ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_hit_ob(ob); object ob. Usually this_object() is the object passed to set_hit_ob. Use this function in conjunction with monster_hit() when you want the monster to have a special combat ability. The monster_hit() function should be an integer function which returns an amount of extra damage to be done by the monster that attack. The monster will pass its attacker to monster_hit() as and argument. Monster_hit() can be used for many things other than simply doing damage. It can be used to have the monster talk, run away, heal itself, summon more monsters, steal from the player, etc - what's inside monster_hit is up to the coder. ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_init_ob(ob); object ob. Usually this_object() is the object passed to set_init_ob. If this is defined, the function monster_init will be called by the monster whenever it has its init called. Essentially, this allows you to write a function that is executed whenever your monster meets another monster or player. Monster_init should return 0 or else it will interrupt the normal init process making aggressive monsters not attack and other things. ----------------------------------------------------------------- can_put_and_get(n); optional string n. If n exists, the monster can put and get things. If n does not exist, the monster cannot pick up and drop things. Further examples: can_put_and_get(1); // The monster can pick up and drop things can_put_and_get(yes); // The monster can pick up and drop things can_put_and_get(no); // The monster can pick up and drop things can_put_and_get(); // The monster canNOT pick up and drop things ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_keep_alive(keep_alive); int keep_alive. This function should be used VERY INFREQUENTLY on UNIQUE monsters. This will not turn off the heart_beat in monsters. DO NOT use this unless the object you are creating REQUIRES it. If you are not sure of why you would use this, then DON'T USE IT. ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_death_messages(i_died,you_killed); When the monster dies it will display the you_killed string to the object which killed it and it will display the i_died message to everyone in the room. If these are not set, the default messages will be used. ----------------------------------------------------------------- command("cmd"); string cmd. Forces the monster to perform the command "cmd". The force_us() function isn't always good, because it checks the level of the caller, and this function can be called by a room. ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_wander(int chance, int time); This is similar to the move_at_reset function. It gives the monster a percentage chance equal to 'chance' to move. This chance will be checked every 'time' seconds. For example, set_wander(50,20); would cause the monster to have a 50% to make a random move every 20 seconds. This allows greater flexibility than the move_at_reset does. When using this function in a monster, make sure to clone it in the room via make_room_unique (see wizhelp 4.2, coding a room) ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_match(object,functions,types,matches); You use this to allow your monster to react to what it sees. Object is the object where your functions will be located. Functions, types, and | matches are all string arrays. Each must be exactly the same size as the others, so you should use allocate() and leave the appropriate elements empty. The following example is Fornay's set_match: function = allocate(12); type = allocate(12); match = allocate(12); function[0] = "why_did"; type[0] = "sells"; type[1] = "attack"; type[2] = "left"; match[2] = "the game"; type[3] = "takes"; type[4] = "drops"; function[5] = "must_be_nice"; type[5] = "is now level"; function[6] = "smiles"; type[6] = "smiles"; match[6] = " happily."; function[7] = "say_hello"; type[7] = "arrives"; function[8] = "test_say"; type[8] = "says:"; type[9] = "tells you:"; function[10] = "follow"; type[10] = "leaves"; function[11] = "gives"; type[11] = "gives"; set_match(this_object(),function,type,match); This doesn't make much sense on first glance, but it is fairly clear if a table is made out of it: Array FUNCTION TYPE MATCH position: Execute this function: If monster sees: followed by: 0 why_did sells 1 attack 2 left the game 3 takes 4 drops 5 must_be_nice is now level 6 smiles smiles happily 7 say_hello arrives 8 test_say says: 9 tells you: 10 follow leaves 11 gives gives Anywhere there is a blank spot, the array has a 0 in it, done automatically by allocate(). Every time the monster sees a message it will look through the TYPE array, and scan the message to see if it contains the TYPE. It then sees if the rest of the message contains the MATCH of the same number. If the MATCH string is present in the message, OR if there is no MATCH at all, then the last FUNCTION that it found is executed with the original message as an argument. For example, if Fornay sees the text: "Bill takes our taxes" First, it will find the FUNCTION 'why_did' at position 0 and save it, but won't do anything else because "Bill takes our taxes" does not contain the text "sells". Next, it will go through TYPE until it gets to position 3, where it finds the word "takes". It then looks for a MATCH. Since MATCH position 3 is empty, the MATCH is an "automatic" success. The last function it found was 'why_did' from position 0, so it now does a this_object()->why_did("Bill takes our taxes"; ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_friends(names, chance); names can be either a single string or a string array. Each heartbeat an npc has a chance to check whether an npc in its friends list is being attacked and join that combat. The optional chance is a percentage from 1 to 100 and defaults to 10. Use 100 to make friends always join as they did previously. set_friend_join_chance(chance); Changes the percentage chance that the npc will check and join its friends each heartbeat. Values are limited to 0 through 100; 0 disables joining. int query_friend_join_chance(); Returns the npc's current friend join chance. ----------------------------------------------------------------- catch_tell(string sStr); | | This function allows you to create responses to your monsters when a specific| string is displayed in the environment that the monster is in. You can hash | up the string anyway you like to check for matches and then call functions as| appropriate. | | ***NOTE*** | | It _IS_ possible for a monster's load_chat to get caught and matched in it's | catch_tell. If this happens the mud can crash depending on what you do with | the catch_tell. So unless you specifically desire to simulate NPC's | interacting with each other put an NPC check in the catch_tell before you do | anything with it. | | ***NOTE2*** | | One thing to remember is that a catch_tell is only looking for a string match| in the environment that the monster is in. It _IS_ possible to fool a catch | tell with an emote or something else along that line. So you will have to | put in the appropriate object checks as necessary. | ----------------------------------------------------------------- follow(str,i,ob); Using this function allows your monsters to follow other players or monsters around the mud. Str should be the exit message the monster receives. If any positive integer i is passed, then wizards in nohassle mode will be exempted from being followed. Ob is an optional object which, if present, will be the only object the monster will follow. This function is not used in reset, but should instead be called through the use of catch_tell as in the following example: catch_tell(string str) { follow(str,1,this_object()->query_attack()); } In this example, the monster is told to follow its attacker if the attacker leaves the room, but to ignore any other players/npcs or wizards with nohassle mode enabled. *Important Note* Additionally, monsters cloned through the reset() of a room will NOT follow properly. To avoid this, if you wish to add following monsters to a room through reset, use a call_out. For example: void reset(int iArg) { ::reset(iArg); call_out("make_monsters",2); etc } void make_monsters() { make_object("monster","/players/johndoe/monster",2); } ----------------------------------------------------------------- random_clone("filepath",howmany,%); this function allows you to only clone up equipment for the monster a random % of the time. it is important to always include how many of that object you want to be cloned, and to only use this function inside the reset function in your monster. The max % is 50, anything higher than 50 gets set to 50. ----------------------------------------------------------------- make_random_object("name","filepath",howmany,%); same as for random_clone, just in the make_object format. again, always include how many, and use only inside the reset function of your monster. ----------------------------------------------------------------- make_unique_and_equip("filepath"); This is used when you want your monster to wear or wield your unique item the first time it loads. Only use this inside the reset function of your monster. ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_switch_chance(d); integer d. When fighting 2 or more opponents, this is the % chance the monster will decide to switch the target of its attack for that battle round. It causes the monster's attacker_ob and alt_attacker_ob to switch places. If this is not set, it will default to 2%. ----------------------------------------------------------------- add_resistance(TYPE1|TYPE2|etc); Use this to add resistances to a monster. When getting hit by attacks of the appropriate type, the monster will take less damage. A firebreathing dragon would probably resist DAM_FIRE, for example. Use the types from 'wizhelp 4.17 (damage types)' for a complete list. Please also see /open/INCLUDE/monster_type.h to see if your monster's race already has a resistance by default. ----------------------------------------------------------------- add_weakness(TYPE1|TYPE2|etc); As add_resistance, but it makes the monster vulnerable to that type of attack instead of resistant. As an example, all monster lycanthropes are vulnerable to DAM_SILVER. 'wizhelp 4.17 (damage types)' for a complete list. Please also see /open/INCLUDE/monster_type.h to see if your monster's race already has a weakness by default. ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_no_block(int blocks) If you wish to make it so that your monster is immune to a given set of blocks, use the set_no_block() call passing the blocks you wish to have the monster ignore. For example, to have your monster be immune to blindness and paralyzation, you would use this call: set_no_block(BLK_BLIND|BLK_PARALYZE); Your monster must include <blocks.h> to use this. query_no_block(int blocks) Use the query_no_block() call to determine which blocks a monster is immune to. If you pass 0 or no argument, you'll get back the complete set of blocks. If you pass a bitmap, you'll get back whether any of those blocks are in place. reset_no_block(int blocks) Use this call to reallow a block to work against your monster. ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_no_charm() query_no_charm() set_charm() query_charm() Use these as you wish to specify whether your monster can be effected by charms type powers like fasttalk, parlay, soothe, and anything else in that family of powers. ----------------------------------------------------------------- set_death_clone(string sFilePath, status tCloneToEnv, int iQuantity); At death, the monster will clone sFilePath. If tCloneToEnv is 1 or the monster is SIZ_NONE, the object will clone to the environment. If iQuantity is not set, it will default to 1. To have any other quantity, you must also set tCloneToEnv. If tCloneToEnv and iQuanity are not set, it defaults to loading on the corpse, and 1 item. ----------------------------------------------------------------- varargs void set_monster_destruct_timer(int iTime, mixed xFunc); This function will destruct the monster in iTime seconds. If xFunc is defined and is a closure, it will apply the function before destructing it. If it's a string, it will tell_room or tell_object before destructing it. The monster will be moved to the quitroom before destruction, so anything the monster has will NOT be dropped in the room. If the monster is in combat, the call_out will be called again 30 seconds later. ----------------------------------------------------------------- varargs set_variable_level(int iBaseLevel, int iResetTime, string sMess, status tCanGoLow, status tOverrideLimit); This function will change the level of the monster to the level of the first player that it encounters, up to 50 levels above its configured base level. For example, a level 10 monster will scale to level 20 for a level 20 player, but only to level 60 for a level 70 player. After iResetTime, if not in combat, it will reset to iBaseLevel. If iBaseLevel isn't set, it will use whatever level you set_level the monster. If iResetTime isn't set, it will default to 300 seconds. sMess will default to "$N $vlook different." and is a room_message that only uses the monster, not the player when setting the string. If you set tCanGoLow to 1, then the monster can go lower than the level you set_level; otherwise it won't. Set tOverrideLimit to 1 only when the monster should preserve the old behavior and scale all the way to the player's level without the 50-level increase cap. Eg. set_variable_level(); // Will set everything to the default. Eg. set_variable_level(0,60,"$N $vlook BEEFY!"); // Will set the base level to what was set, reset time of 60 seconds, message to looks BEEFY, and won't allow the monster to go under the set_level of the monster. Eg. set_variable_level(0,0,0,0,1); // Uses the default base, reset time, and message, but preserves uncapped legacy scaling. ----------------------------------------------------------------- void set_npc_elite(status tElite); This function will change a regular monster into a slightly more elite one. It will add 25% more stats and 5% exp if set. It will also add [ELITE] to the short of the monster. Eg. set_npc_elite(1); // Makes the monster elite. RANDOM NOTES ------------ - Monsters heal at a rate of 6 HP and 6 SP every 2 minutes when they are not in battle. - Add_clone and make_object both work on monsters. - Examples of monsters can be found in the /open/MONSTER directory. REVISION HISTORY ================ Rev. 3 - Documented the 50-level variable monster increase cap and the explicit legacy scaling override. Revised 07/06/26. Rev. 2 - Moved a few functions to 4.3b (Advanced Monsters). Rev. 1 - Corrected a couple typos and added revision level. Also added in use of the catch_tell function and notes warning about the possible interaction with a monster's load_chat. Parts revised have a "|" in the right hand column. Revision made by Olgar - 10/08/04. Rev. 0 - ???
