docs.title: /public/docs/wizard/questob
docs.text: /public/docs/wizard/questob ------------------- Hmmm...So you want to know how to make a generic quest object, eh? Well, this is going to be one of the harder undertakings of your career here on Darkwind. As a matter of fact, I think that it'll probably be harder than coding your quest, even. Yeah, I'm pretty sure of that part. -------------------- The first few lines in any quest object should be: #include <mudlib.h> #include <darkwind.h> #define DESTINATION WIZROOMS+"quest_ro" inherit GEN_QUEST; The define is the pathname of the quest room underneath the adventurer's guild. When you have your quest approved and ready to be put in the game, tell an Imp+ to have it added to the mud's autoload file, and this will take care of moving it there automatically when the mud reboots. The inherit line sets up the object to be a quest object and will allow calls to the quest master object as defined below. -------------------- set_name("name"); string name. Supply the quest object a name. set_hint("hint"); string hint. This is what is printed out when a player does a "list <quest-name>" in the Adventurer's Guild. -------------------- Wow. Pretty darn hard, eh? I'll supply you with an example, just in case you didn't get it from what's been in the doc so far: Oh, another good idea is to include a long detailed comment giving specifics on how to solve your quest. Then if some wiz needs to know, the pathname of this file can be found from the object in the quest room and the file looked at. -------------------- #include <mudlib.h> #include <darkwind.h> #define DESTINATION WIZROOMS+"quest_ro" inherit GEN_QUEST; void reset(int iArg) { // NOTE: There is no ::reset(iArg); because the quest master object doesn't // have a reset() function. if (iArg) return; set_name("Pharaohs Curse"); set_hint("\ Rid Egypt of the Curse of the Pharaoh.\n\ A medium level quest - takes more brains than brawn.\n"); move_object(this_object(),DESTINATION); // this line moves it to the quest room when the object is reset, // which should happen when the mud reboots if this file is in // the mud's autoload file } /* EOF - Rodney - 11/13/95 */ // mods by AC - 11/13/95

docs.title: HOW TO MAKE GOOD QUESTS
docs.text: HOW TO MAKE GOOD QUESTS _________________________________________________________________ Perhaps the most important point about designing a quest is to think as a player and not a designer. A PLAYER SHOULD NOT TO BE KILLED WITHOUT WARNING At its most basic level, this means that a room with three exits, two leading to instant death and the third to treasure, must have a include a clearly worded warning in the long description. If death traps are thematic to the whole quest, there should be a warning in the quest hint. A PLAYER SHOULD NOT TO BE TRAPPED WITHOUT WARNING If the ground beneath your feet is likely to give way and drop you into a pit, a warning sign stating unstable ground should be in the preceding room. Having the door slam shut behind you, unexpectedly is quite frustrating. Players should not have to quit out, losing equipment and quest items, because they went east instead of west, unless there is a hint that says the road to the east looks dangerous. MAKE THE WARNINGS CLEAR A warning can be hidden hidden without being obscure. It isn't necessary to state outright: If you go east you will fall into a trap, but saying the road to the east is made of a different kind of dirt is not a warning that it is unstable. EVERYTHING REQUIRED TO SOLVE THE QUEST SHOULD BE IN THE QUEST AREA A player shouldn't have to bring some bit of information from another mud or from 'mud lore'into the area. Needing a bag to dive underwater is okay but there should be some clue that a bag lets you dive underwater, somewhere in the area. If the area is going to require torches, then there should be torches provided or the quest hint should suggest them. THE PLAYER SHOULD BE ABLE TO SOLVE THE QUEST THE FIRST TIME THROUGH For example if there is something which needs cooking for the right length of time. The only way to find out the right time is by trial and error. But you only get one try per reset. This is unfair. In principal a good player should be able to solve the entire quest without doing anything illogical. Players shouldn't have to wait out resets because they didn't "guess" the right answer. THE PLAYER SHOULD BE ABLE TO FINISH WITHOUT KNOWLEDGE OF FUTURE EVENTS For example, the quest starts near a shop. You have one coin and can buy a lamp, a magic carpet or a periscope. Five minutes later you are transported away without warning to a submarine, whereupon you need a periscope. If you bought the carpet, bad luck. THE PLAYER SHOULD NOT TO NEED TO DO UNLIKELY THINGS For example if every quest in the game either returns an object or a search fail message on the first search attempt, your quest should not make a player search a number of times in the same spot, without giving them the hint to continue searching. MAKE FORGIVING SYNTAX If you have a loose brick in the wall and the player has to pull it out in order to open a hidden door forgive them from getting only half the solution and give them a little prod to let them know they are on the right track. This is frustrating: look at wall It is made of bricks look at bricks One of them is loose look at brick Which brick do you want to look at? look at loose brick It looks loose. get brick You can't take that push brick What? pull brick What? move brick What? Seeing What? over and over is extremely frustrating. If you think the player is likely to attempt the syntax them put the response in: push brick It doesn't budge. move brick It doesn't budge. pull brick You pull gently on the brick moving it a little. pull brick hard You tug the brick right out of the wall. The wall slides open revealing a hidden exit. DON'T GIVE TOO MANY RED HERRINGS A red herring is something that looks like a clue, but is not related to the quest. They help add to the theme, and to make the quest area fuller but at some point in the quest it should become obvious that an item that the player is carrying around because it seemed important, isn't. A PLAYER SHOULD NOT TO NEED TO BE AMERICAN TO UNDERSTAND HINTS Don't require "Americanized" words to be used to solve the quest. Accept both the English and the American spelling of important responses. Not all players are Americans. Not all players have English as their first language. Making a quest dependant on obscure American syntax, American expressions or ideals, or totally dependant on American spellings makes it frustrating for non-American players. SET THE PLOT AND STICK TO IT It is a good idea to lay out clear plan on paper first. You will have to write out a description of how your quest works from start to finish when you submit it anyway. The dreaded flow chart is a useful tool when laying out your quest plan. Once you have chosen the plot and the theme. You can fill in the areas around it. Make sure that the quest doesn't deviate from the plot. If a player is questing to stop a war between the elves and the vikings in Hyper they shouldn't find themselves battling mermaids in the ocean. SET THE ATMOSPHERE The quest hint should include a general idea of what a player is expected to do and a good clue as to where to go to get the first hint. The first hint should set the atmosphere and explain the plot. Don't make a player sit through a 10 minute story to hear the plot. Do give a good overview and an idea of where to go next. GIVE ADEQUATE CLUES Wandering around finding bits and pieces is part of every quest. Make sure hint should set the plot and the atmosphere. Don't make a player sit together. This is one of the difficult parts of coding a quest. Since you are the coder, you know the ending. Don't assume that every player will do things exactly the same as you do. GIVE MILESTONES Even if a quest isn't linear, there should be some indication that the half way mark has been passed. There are few things more frustrating to a quester than to find that they gave up after 8 hours of questing yesterday when they only needed one more piece to finish. //This is adapted from an online manual that is based more on game design than //quest design. The online manual can be found under wizhelp questdesign. //--Xnedra 21/08/98--

docs.title: HOW TO CHEATPROOF QUESTS
docs.text: HOW TO CHEATPROOF QUESTS _________________________________________________________________ USE LOGS Log the time and date when a player first enters your quest area and the time and date the player solves the quest. This will tell you if a player solves the quest unusually fast. It will also tell you the average amount of time it takes a player to solve the quest. DEST QUEST ITEMS Make quest items dest on sell. Clean the players inventory of quest items upon completion. If your area is a closed quest zone, have the quest items dest upon leaving the area. If the quest isn't a party quest, dest items on give. MAKE THE WARNINGS CLEAR This statement is in quest design, because it is fair to players to do so. It is here because players will cheat without meaning to, in an attempt to keep their friends from dying to an "unfair" death. If you don't want one player warning another about a death trap in your questzone. Give the warning in the quest area. THE PLAYER SHOULD BE ABLE TO FINISH WITHOUT KNOWLEDGE OF FUTURE EVENTS Another repeat. Don't make players want to warn their friends about some minor thing they have to do at the beginning in order to avoid something going wrong later. MAKE FORGIVING SYNTAX I hate syntax! Having to come up with some obscure syntax that isn't an intuitive reaction in the room: The brick looks loose --- syntax: loosen brick Now why would I do that it is already loose? Don't use obscure syntax to make a quest more difficult. INDIVIDUALIZE THINGS Making items id to the player who found them makes it much more difficult fore players to go get them for others and give them away. There is a good example of an individualized quest item /open/OBJ/genqob.c MAKE QUESTS RANDOM Making the items load randomly in different locations depending on the player makes it more difficult for players to share quest info. Look in /open/QUEST/random for an example of how to do this. MAKE MULTIPLE SOLUTIONS If the quest is to end the war between the elves and vikings in hyper, give the players a choice. Let them choose who wins. Have more than one quest running through the same area, but only one first hint. Set the first hint to randomly send the player on one of a number of quests and have the solution dependant on which hint the player got. Cheaters will get information from more than one source and are likely to follow the wrong leads (and therefore give themselves away). CHANGE YOUR QUEST WITHOUT WARNING Here's where those logs come in handy. If you know a player is working on the quest, don't change it. But if no one has entered the area recently then change the quest slightly without notifying players. //Personally I don't think most players want to cheat. I think they get //stuck and frustrated by poorly coded quests and they go looking for "one //smallhint". It gets easier to ask for a hint everytime you do it. Make //yourself available to players who are seriously stuck and see if you can //find what they are missing. It is better that the hint comes from the //coder than from another player. //--Xnedra 21/08/98--

docs.title: The virtual room is a means of creating large areas consisting of many
docs.text: The virtual room is a means of creating large areas consisting of many similar looking rooms, without coding a separate .c file for each room. To do this, the grid needs a daemon to control it and a set of files that describe the rooms. You may have a different description for each room in the grid, or share descriptions amongst the rooms. You may also use the 8 major directions to link the rooms in the grid, as well as make links to 'real' rooms from any point in the grid. To show you how to do this, it's easiest to use an example. In the directory ~malraux/vrtest there is a rather silly one to look over. THE GRID DAEMON --------------- The first item you need for a virtual room grid is a directory to place the files in. Each grid needs a separate directory. Once you have that, create a daemon.c in that directory that inherits VRDAEMON (you will have to #include <new_virtual.h> as well). The example daemon.c should serve you well as a template. Set the variables in the file as needed: width - the east-west width of the area height - the north-south width of the area coord_dir - the directory where the daemon and its files are kept terrain - set this to set the terrain of all the rooms light - set this to 0 if you want all of your rooms to be lit. if it is set to 1, the daemon will expect you to map out the light values for the rooms (see below) numdescs - the number of descriptions your rooms will be using In daemon.c, you MUST call ::reset() after setting these values. ::reset() will load the database that you create for the rooms. Look at the example daemon, or just copy it, to do this right. THE COORD.DESCS FILE -------------------- Next, you need to create a file holding the descriptions of the rooms in the grid. This file consists of a short and long description for each separate description you want to have. Each must be one line long. If you want to have a long desc longer than one line, put the desc in a file with the extension .lf in the grid's directory. Then, on the long desc line put #<filename without the .lf extension>#. For example, look in the coord.descs file in the example directory. On line 2, you see the reference to goomba.lf (I told you it was silly). THE COORD.MAPPINGS FILE ----------------------- After you have written the descriptions to use, you need to map them onto the grid. That is, each grid point will reference a particular description. If you have enough descriptions in your coord.descs file, you can put one description per grid point. The first section of coord.mappings consists of the description mappings. For each grid point, you need to put the number of the description that goes in that room. The descriptions are numbered 0 to numdescs-1, like an array (gee, I wonder where they're kept?). I could have made it so you could number them 1 to numdescs, but this makes it faster in execution. Woo, woo. The grid is oriented with north at the top, and east to the right, like on a map. The numbering, however, is like pixels on a computer screen: 0,0 is in the top lefthand corner, and x increases to the right while y increases towards the bottom. The numbers must have one, and *only* one space between them. To take an example from the example rooms, the first line in the coord.mappings file is 3 0 1. This means that room 0,0 will have the 4th description in the coord.descs file, room 1,0 will have the 1st desc, and room 2,0 will have the 2nd desc. The next section of coord.mappings describes the exits of each point on the grid. The exits are described in binary format, where each of the exit directions has it's own bit in the number. To get the exit descriptor for a room, add up the values of each exit direction. The exit direction values are listed in /include/new_virtual.h, as well as here: North - 1 South - 2 East - 4 West - 8 Northeast - 16 Northwest - 32 Southeast - 64 Southwest - 128 So if you wanted a particular grid point to have north, south, and northeast exits, you would add up 1, 2, and 16 to get an exit descriptor of 19. Taking the first line of exits from the coord.mappings file in the example directory: 6 14 10, we find that room 0,0 has south and east exits (2 + 4 = 6), room 1,0 has east, west, and south exits (4 + 8 + 2 = 14), and room 2,0 has west and south exits (8 + 2 = 10). To connect a virtual room to a real room, make a real room that replaces one of the coordinates of the vr room. In your daemon, set up the 'rooms' var at that coordinate to point to the real room's filename. Look in the example daemon.c to see how this is done. The third section of the coord.mappings file is optional. If you decide that you want some of your rooms to be lit, and others not lit, you need to use it. It consists merely of a grid, like the desc and exit grids, with 1s and 0s to mark whether the grid point is lit or not. THE ENTRY POINT --------------- Your grid area will need at least one entry point that is a normal room. It needs to inherit VRROOM to interface with the grid. The entry room for the example is, surprisingly enough, /u/m/malraux/ctest/entry.c. It inherits VRROOM and sets up a few necessary variables. The first is the daemon that controls the grid room. Any exit to a normal room is done the same as always, but an exit to a grid room should be a number. To get this number, take the x coordinate of the destination grid room and multiply by 100, then add the y coordinate to this. In other words, make the grid coordinate into a number that looks like the coordinate with the comma removed: 2,2 -> 02,02 -> 0202. You should note that this implies that you may not have a grid area that is more than 100 rooms wide or deep. NOTE: The above has changed. If your vrroom has a width or size greater than 100, the vrdaemon will instead use a size modulo of 1000. This means that your coordinates become 002002 in the above example. Malraux, 1-18-94 Malraux, 2001-10-02: updated size modulo

docs.title: ACTION BLOCKS
docs.text: ACTION BLOCKS There is now a bitfield on all living objects to use for restricting their actions. These should be used in all spells/powers/instances where you wish to restrict the actions of another, and all abilities that would be affected by a block such as these should check for it before allowing the action. Please note that the purpose of blocks is NOT to make a guild totally ineffective. You should be able to restrict enough powers to make a character feel limited, yet leave enough powers untouched so that they have some options remaining. To use the defined block bits, #include <blocks.h> in your file. Here are the defined blocks. BLK_BLIND This is for when a character can't see. Looks, glances, searches and the like should check for this. Remember that sight is the most important sense, and things that impose this restriction should be VERY rare. BLK_CONCENTRATION This will disrupt intense concentration. Primarily this will ruin psionic abilities, but perhaps some magical spells as well. Examples might include a swarm of tiny gnats that bite all over you or get into your ears and buzz really loud. BLK_ENTANGLE_ARMS If you want to physically restrain a persons arms. Primarily this will ruin most fighting abilities, many thief abilities, and casting of spells that require physical freedom to gesture or manipulate components. BLK_ENTANGLE_LEGS For when you want to physically restrain someone from moving. Any physical movement should check for this. BLK_ENTANGLE This is just a combination of the last two, so you can set them both at once if you wish. BLK_PARALYZE When you want someone restrained magically or in some other nonphysical way, use this rather than an entangle. BLK_SILENCE If this is set on a player, he cannot use abilities that depend on the transmission of sound. These include spellcasting that requires speech, playing musical instruments, etc. Use of this block on players by other players should follow all the normal PK check rules. BLK_SILENCE_PK // As of Dec 17 2003 this block will be phased out and // BLK_HEARING should be used instead. This block was intended to be the PK version of BLK_SILENCE but was used instead for 'deafening' a player. BLK_HEARING Setting this block will stop a player from receiving normal communication. The full range of effects will be determined by the coders. USING THE BLOCKS These functions are defined for your use: set_block(int); Use this to set the block you want, using the definitions above. remove_block(int); Use this to remove a block, with the definitions given above. query_block(int); Check the status of any of the block bits, using the definitions above as arguments. With no arguments, the entire block field is returned. Antcrusher - Jan 28, 1996

docs.title: To make an autoloading object, you need to use the following code:
docs.text: To make an autoloading object, you need to use the following code: this_player()->register_auto_obj("/my/crazy/path:parameter"); To remove an autoloading object from the player's autoload mapping: this_player()->remove_auto_obj("/my/crazy/path:parameter"); If you setup an autoloading object more than once, (for example in a guild it would be setup in the join function and the guild object refresh function), that would be ok, because the code in player.c makes sure that you don't add the same object twice. If you pass the optional parameter, when the object is loaded, the function init_arg(parameter) will be called, passing the parameter to it. The ":" that follows the pathname is optional. In other words, if you have no optional parameter, you don't need to pass the ":" when you register the object with the player. Make sure that this code doesn't exist in the object's init() function. The reason for this, is that if I enter a player's inventory it'll then try to add all of his autoloading objects to me. This code should exist in places where the player first gets the object only. -Hayden, 06/22/95

docs.title: Written by Alarian@Darkwind
docs.text: Written by Alarian@Darkwind last revision 09/15/95 The following is a doc on how to use all the various calendar functions provided by the astronomy and events daemons. To use ANY of these functions, you must first: #include <daemons.h> in any file that is going to be calling a function. Next, depending on what information you want, you can call the following functions. Note, to use many of these functions, you must call them in the format shown. I.e. for many, you must pass the current time as part of the query. To get the actual names of the days of the week and months of the year, look at the help file called "calendar". I.e. "help calendar". To determine the numerical minute of the hour: minute = EVENTS_D->query_minutes(time()); To determine the numerical hour of the day: hour = EVENTS_D->query_hour(time()); Note: This will return a result on a scale of 0 to 19 hours. if you want to have it on a am, pm type of scale, you will need to add something like the following to your code: if (hour == 0) { hour = 12; tod = " Fore High-Sun"; } else if (hour > 11) { hour = hour - 12; if (hour == 0) hour = 12; tod = " Nights Watch"; } else tod = " Fore High-Sun"; write(" and the time is: "+hour+":"); if (mmnt < 10) write("0"+mmnt+tod+".\n"); else write(""+mmnt+tod+".\n"); return 1; } There are probobly better ways to do this, so if you think of one go ahead and use it. This is just here as an example. To get the Name of the day: day_name = EVENTS_D->query_day_name(time()); To get the numerical day of the month: day_number = EVENTS_D->query_day(time()); To get the Name of the month: month = EVENTS_D->query_month_name(time()); Note: There are 10 months in a year. To determine what week of the month it is: week_num = EVENTS_D->query_week(time()); Note: There are 3 weeks to a month. To get the numeric year: year = EVENTS_D->query_year(time()); To get the time of day in string format: what = EVENTS_D->query_time_of_day(); This will return one of the following strings depending on the time of day: dawn, day twilight, night. If, for some reason, you want the exact second since the the calendar system started: now = EVENTS_D->query_now(); To get the numeric phase of a given moon, (where str = the name of the moon you want to see): phase = ASTRONOMY_D->query_phase(str); The moon names are: "dailos" "markas" and "tekal". To get the string name of the phase of a given moon: phase = ASTRONOMY_D->query_phase_name(ASTRONOMY_D->query_phase(str)); where 'str' is the name of the moon you want to get the phase for. The moon names are: "dailos" "markas" and "tekal".

docs.title: An NPC is much like a MONSTER.  It can do everything that a
docs.text: An NPC is much like a MONSTER. It can do everything that a MONSTER can do, and more. An npc has the ability to hold conversations, and also allows its builders to speak through it. An NPC is created just like an ordinary monster, except that instead of inheriting MONSTER, you would inherit MONSTER_RP. Therefore, the first few lines of your file would look something like this: #include <mudlib.h> inherit MONSTER_RP; ----------------------------------------------------------------------- MONSTER_RP has a couple of functions that MONSTER does not. These functions have to do with telling your NPC how you want it to react to certain stimuli. For example, you could tell your NPC to wave whenever someone says hi. void add_response(arg1, arg2); arg1 and arg2 can be strings or arrays of strings. You can use add_response multiple times, even with the same arguments. Arg1 represents the stimuli which you want the NPC to respond to. A caution: if the word that the NPC is looking for can be contained in another word, such as "hi" in "nothing", you should make use of spacing to differentiate. The function uses catch_tell to search through everything the NPC sees on its screen, including emotes, combat spam, and even direction names. So, you can have the NPC respond to someone entering a room, getting an item, or even a particular person. Arg2 contains the responses. You can have the NPC respond in a variety of ways: with a command, an emote, an echo, or a say. If the argument is an array, it will randomly pick an element of that array to perform. In arg2, you can optionally precede the string with $C, $E, or $H. If the function does not detect one of these codes, it automatically does the entire string with a say. NPCs automatically use csay, and they understand all racial languages. Including $N anywhere in the response will cause $N to be replaced with the name of the person it is responding to. $C tells the NPC to perform the string as a command. For example, you could pass in "$Ckill $N" and the NPC would perform the kill command on the person it was triggered by. All NPCs automatically have player commands enabled. $E causes the NPC to perform an emote, like the wizard emote, using the string. It automatically puts the NPC's name in front of the string. Therefore, if arg2 = "$Elooks out the window.", the NPC would emote "<monstername> looks out the window." $H causes the NPC to perform an echo. Therefore, if second argument was "$HYou suddenly wish you lived in Northampton.", the player would see "You suddenly wish you lived in Northampton." The function uses tell_room to accomplish this. Here is a code example of the uses of add_response: /*omitted NPC code*/ add_response(" hi", "Hello there!"); add_response(({"death", "died", "killed"}), "$Csob"); add_response("Greetings", ({"$Ceast", "$Esniffs quietly.", "$Eblah"})); /*omitted NPC code*/ What if you want the NPC to do a series of commands? You would use two add_responses with the same first argument. The add_responses are executed in order, so the first add_response happen before the second add_response. For example, let's say your NPC is protecting an object in the room, and whenever someone takes that object, it says "Don't touch that" and attacks. Here is how you set up the sequence. add_response("gets axe", "Don't touch that!"); add_response("gets axe", "$Ckill $n"); ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Another function of the NPC inheritable is builder-controlled roleplaying. A wizard can take control of an NPC's actions. To do this, one would type 'roleplay <NPCname>'. A "wand of control" object is cloned to your inventory. It shows you all that your NPC sees, and allows you to send command to the NPC. To send a command, you precede the command with the word 'NPC'. As with the add_response, an NPC can do anything a player can do, since enable_player_commands() is automatic. While an NPC is being roleplayed all of its normal chat messages from add_response,load_chat,load_cmd,etc will be temporarily disabled. For example, you can type 'npc east' or 'npc say hello'. You will recieve feedback that you have caused the NPC to do something, and you will see the result of what the NPC has done. Ordinarily, only the creator of a particular NPC can roleplay it. Because some builders might want to allow other builders to roleplay their NPCs, there is a function to allow this. To add a roleplayer to your NPC, you should include this line. add_roleplayer("buildername"); add_roleplayer can only take a string, and it is important that the builder's name is in all lowercase. For each of the builders you wish to enable, you will have to have a separate add_roleplayer line. For example, if I wanted to allow Rampage and Souldancer to roleplay my NPC, I would add the lines: add_roleplayer("rampage"); add_roleplayer("souldancer"); ----------------------------------------------------------------------- Since there is obviously so much you can do with the builder-roleplaying, there are some guidelines as to how the NPC should and should not be roleplayed. 1.) 'NPC kill' IS allowed. It is no different to instruct the NPC to attack than it is to set the monster aggressive. Don't use an NPC to 'hunt' players you don't like, though. 2.) Shouting is not allowed. It is too disruptive. 3.) Joining guilds, marrying, killing monsters outside your area, and partying are NOT allowed. 4.) Helping players is not allowed. Your NPC shouldn't help the players in any way. For example, having a "guard" move out of the room to allow the players to pass through would be illegal. Also, having your NPCs kill other monsters for the players' benefit would be illegal. 5.) As for anything else, the rules will be added as they come up. Don't do anything with a NPC that you aren't allowed to do as a wizard. Your NPCs can't tell a player the weapon class of a weapon. Also, if you are roleplaying someone else's NPC, please don't do things that the creator may not want you to do. 6.) If you use an NPC as part of a quest, actual roleplaying of that NPC should not be required for the quest. Make sure any quest information you provide through roleplaying is ALSO available through add_responses. For your convenience, here is an example of an init function which would tell the builder whenever a player enters the same room as said NPC. Init is called every time an object encounters another one. void init () { ::init(); if (!controller_ob) //if not being roleplayed tell_object("persephone", "Someone is in the same room as Ananda.\n"); } Of course, this could get spammy if you have a lot of npcs. And that concludes the NPC documentation. written by Persephone Modifications by AC, 10-aug-97. NPC now defined as MONSTER_RP

docs.title: The following documentation is meant to explain the use of the vehicle
docs.text:
The following documentation is meant to explain the use of the vehicle inheritable. First, please understand what the inheritable is meant to do so you aren't using it for the wrong reason. A vehicle, in the sense of the inheritable is some object that a player or multiple players can use to travel around the mud. It can also store things for that player, and be used as a symbol of power. This actual inheritable creates the outside appearance of that vehicle. Then, using a vehicle room inheritable, you can create a single, or multiple rooms for that vehicle. The 'hull' of the vehicle actually clones the rooms to it, and then travels around with that group of objects, including players and their inventories. I will attempt to explain how to use this inheritable for one or multi-room vehicles. These vehicles will check direction hooks for all players on the vehicle at the time, and they will check for legal terrain, in the next room. Aside from those slight restrictions, it is basically something you can ride around the mud in. The vehicle consists of several files. You have to have the actual vehicle object. Then, for each 'room' within the vehicle, you will need a file. Lastly there is a sort of driver for the vehicle's rooms, that you will need to code. This is a little more complicated than your average lpc coding. If you are a little confused, you can find example files in /public/docs/vehicles: test.c == The vehicle object. front.c == A front room for the vehicle. back.c == A back room for the vehicle. standard.c == That vehicle's standard addition file. ******************************************************************************** The Vehicle Object: The vehicle will be an object that noone ever enters. That is the object that will inherit VEHICLE. This will NOT inherit ROOM or anything else. You will define all the strings there, such as the movement messages, its name, short and long descriptions, etc. Each room should not do this. Always #include <mudlib.h> and then just inherit VEHICLE; Your reset function should have a ::reset(); as should your init have ::init(); You need to init_vehicle(); at the *end* of your reset function. void set_name(string str); The string you pass is the name of the vehicle. set_name("ship"); string query_name(string str); Returns the ship's name. query_name(); void set_alias(string str); The string you pass is an alias for the vehicle. To set multiple alias's just set_alias again. Single: set_alias("ship"); Multiple: set_alias(({"ship","vehicle"})); varargs mixed query_alias(string str); Returns the array of alias' if nothing is passed. Returns 1 if str is a valid alias set for this vehicle. query_alias(); query_alias("vehicle"); void set_short(string str); This is the short description you will see outside of the vehicle. set_short("Vehicle"); string short(); Returns the vehicle's short description. short(); int id(string str); Returns 1 if the str passed is a valid id. id("vehicle"); void set_long(string str); This is the long description you will see outside of the vehicle. set_long("A great looking vehicle.
"); string query_long(); Returns the long description of the vehicle. query_long(); void long(string str); Returns the long of the vehicle or of an add_look. long("vehicle"); int query_level(); For dir_hooks it returns APPRENTICE; query_level(); void set_arrival(string str); This is the string shown when the vehicle arrives in a room. set_arrival("The vehicle arrives.
"); void set_departure(string str); This is the string shown when the vehicle leaves the room. set_departure("The vehicle leaves"); NOTE: Do not attach a '.' or a '
' because the direction which the vehicle leaves, is added to the end of this string. void set_max_players(int i); This is the maximum number of people allowed on the vehicle. You *must* set this variable. It must be an appropriate size. For example, a horse would only accept two players. set_max_players(10); void set_bad_terrain(mixed str); You use this function to set up an array of terrains that this vehicle cannot travel in. Like the set_alias function, you can pass an array for multiple bad terrains. Single: set_bad_terrain("inside"); Multiple: set_bad_terrain(({"inside","city"})); void add_look(string *name, string desc); If you describe an object on the outside of the vehicle, this would be the description for that object. You can pass an array as the first argument. add_look("mast","The mast is extremely tall.
"); add_look(({"mast","masts"}),"They are tall.
"); void set_rooms_path(string str); This is the path to the rooms of your vehicle. set_rooms_path("/players/myname/vehicle/rooms/"); string query_rooms_path(); Returns the rooms path of the vehicle. query_rooms_path(); void set_addition_path(string str); This is the path to your addition file (standard.c). set_addition_path("/players/myname/vehicle/"); string *query_additions(); Returns the array of addition files. query_additions(); void add_addition(string str); This is the 'daemon' that sets up the rooms for your vehicle. You can add as many as you want. In other words, if you want to have different vehicles, with a different set of rooms, you can have a different addition file for it. This must be called after the addition path is set. add_addition("standard.c"); NOTE: You must add_addition the file that you have setup to clone the vehicle's rooms. int query_addition(string str); Returns 1 if the str is an addition of that vehicle. query_addition("standard.c"); void remove_addition(string str); Removes that addition for that vehicle. remove_addtion("standard.c"); string query_addition_path(); Returns the addition path. query_addition_path(); void set_owner(string str); This is the name of the owner of the vehicle, if its owned. This should be used if its a player owned vehicle only. set_owner("player_name"); string query_owner(); Returns the name of the owner. query_owner(); object find_owner(); Returns the object that owns the vehicle, if its online. find_owner(); varargs void tell_vehicle(string str, string *exclude); The first argument is what to be told to the vehicle, and the second argument is an array of string, exclusions, what rooms *not* to tell the string to. You don't always have to pass the second argument. If for some reason you want to set_listen in this room, differently than the rest of the vehicle, you can set_listen(0) or 1 as needed. (1 listens) The only other special actions in the inheritable is that for 'enter_func'. It is not defined as an add_action in the inheritable, so you will have to add_action it yourself in your init of your vehicle object. The purpose here, was to allow you to define your own type of function for boarding (IE a horse would be mount.) If you wish to use your vehicle for combat, and allow it to have vehicle_points, similar to hit_points on a player, use the following functions, much like those in living.c: void set_max_vp(int iArg); int query_max_vp(); void restore_vp(int iArg); int query_vp(); Currently there is no support for vehicle vs. vehicle combat. If you wish to do something like that, you will have to prototype that yourself. There are no funtions within that will help, except for the four listed above. If you'd like to use access lists in your vehicle, use the following functions: void use_access(int iX); Set this to 1 if you want to use access lists. int add_access(string name) Add name to your access list. int remove_access(string name) Remove name from your access list. mixed query_access(string name) If name is passed it will check to see if name has access to the vehicle, returning a 1 if so, 0 otherwise. If nothing is passed it will return the array access_list containing everyone with access. ******************************************************************************** The Vehicle Room Daemon: Technically, this is not a daemon, but it sets up the rooms of the vehicle. You will be better off, calling it an 'additions' file. This file must be in the addition path you set. The reason for having a separate file to add rooms, is so you can have one file, to add a typical set of rooms, to different vehicles. Each vehicle must have a standard set of rooms, and it expects you to add_addition one file in the addition path. If you wish to only have 1 set of rooms, then just make one addition file. A typical example of the code would be this: int do_addition(object oOb) { oOb -> add_room("front","front_room"); - the first arguement is the unique name of the room, and the second - arguement is the filename of the room, in the rooms path. oOb -> set_entrance("front"); - You should set the entrance to the vehicle if this is the room you - want to be the entrance. oOb -> add_room("back","back_room"); oOb -> add_room("secret","secret_room"); } set_enter_room(n); String n. This is where you enter the vehicle. set_entrance("front"); NOTE: This should always be the only room you enter the vehicle in. ******************************************************************************** The Vehicle Rooms: The vehicle clones the 'rooms' of the vehicle to itself. These rooms should inherit VEHICLE_ROOM, *not* ROOM. Each room file has to be in the rooms path you have previously defined. Then each room adds an exit to the other rooms, and the direction function to move the player to that room. In the add_exit line of the rooms, you will do something like this: add_exit("rear","roomname"); Note: Roomname is the actual roomname of the room, that you set in the file of that room. It will then move the player to the correct room. The filename, is that actual filename, not the entire path, so if its bridge.c, just use 'bridge' for the second arguement. You will need to set the room's name as well: set_room_name("rear"); object find_room(string str); Returns the object of that name, where str is the name of the room. find_room("room_name"); Valid functions to add that are in the inheritable are: move_func() /* Moves the vehicle. */ leave_func() /* Leaves the vehicle. */ look_outside_func() /* Looks outside the vehicle. */ You can just add_action("move_func","steer"); for example, then you might code a move function to call it, if you want, so you can do your own writes and says, etc. Then you can just do move_func(str); As far as the move code is concerned, please do not use your own move function. This move function correctly checks for terrain, dir_hooks, inits and virtual rooms. You can, however, do something like add_action("move","steer"); (You will have to add_action something for the move command.) The syntax for calling move, is just move(string); The string will be the direction you want to move in.

docs.text: --=LPC Basics=-- This section handles the basics of LPC coding. Information on Intermediate LPC can be found in /public/docs/lpc/Intermediate. Note that some information in this section is outdated. 6.1 An Overview 6.2 The Coding Environment 6.3 The LPC Program 6.4 LPC Data Types 6.5 Functions 6.6 The Basics of Inheritance 6.7 Variable Handling 6.8 Flow Control 6.9 The Data Type Object 6.10 Header files To view the help file type wizhelp <number>

docs.title: -=[ LPC Basics ]=-
docs.text:
-=[ LPC Basics ]=- Introduction: The purpose of this document is to introduce to the new wizard the basic concepts of LPC coding. My experience has shown that there is a large number of wizards who are able to use configurable object files (room, armour, weapon, etc), but have little idea on why, or what they are coding. The examples shown are in my coding style, which is one of a number I have seen. I will also be coding using strict types, as this is more correct. I hope I don't make too many typo's in the lpc examples. LPC mud structure: LPC is object orientated. A sword is a complete "object", entirely separate from all other code. Actions are an interaction between one object and another. A player is interactive action between the object player and other objects. A room is an object, A player is an object placed in the room object, A sword is an object in the player object in the room object. You might already summise that you need particular functions that allow you to find the position of an object, and interaction between objects. Though not strictly true I will I will call the source file, the object. This is more convenience then anything else. Objects: The most basic object is created from a source file which is empty (0 bytes). This of course would do nothing. There are a number of "standard" functions, if placed in an object will allow it to interact with the "player" object. But before we can look at this you must understand some basic LPC language. I am going to work on the assumption that you have only very basic concepts of programming, programming algorithims, and the language C. Language: LPC is a 'block-structured' language, and like Kernighan/Ritchie C, was developed for the UNIX. The game parser is usually compiled on FSF's GNU g++. That is why LPCMuds use a unix style file, and directory system. Though there are those trying to port it to other platforms with a minimum of success. Debugging at home: Most clients have buffers that allow you to edit files at home and cut and paste into the online file editor (ed). Loading source files: update <object> if object loaded in memory, remove it. You should update an object if you make any changes to a source file. Then try to load it. load <file> load object into memory. Failure to do so will produce an error that is logged into /log/lower_case_your_name. I personally make an alias on my quicktyper, "error". (alias error tail /log/your_lower_case_name). clone <filename> make a clone of an object dest <object> destruct a clone object -=[ LPC language basics ]=- Comments: Comments are made the same way as in C, /* Comment */. It does accept the c++ commenter of '//' for one line comments. Type Declarations: LPC has six data types. These types are: status, int, string, object, mixed, and void. All variables MUST be declared, and functions SHOULD be declared. There are three basic places variables can be declared: inside functions, inside a code block (both of these constitute 'local' variables); and outside functions ('global' variables). Example: int miLast_integer; void example(int iInteger) { int iI; iI = 2 * iInteger; if(miLast_integer < iInteger) { string my_name; my_name = (string)this_player()->query_name(); say(my_name+" says: Hi.
"); } else iInteger = iI; miLast_integer = iInteger; } Example is quite an innane program but is an example of type declaration. 'miLast_integer' is a global variable of type 'int'. Its value is known throughout the program, and can be used and manipulated by any piece of code. 'void' declares that the function 'example' does not return any value. 'iInteger' is a 'formal argument' of the function example(). It has been declared as an 'int' and is treated as a local variable throughout 'example'. 'iI' is a variable declared as 'int', which can be used throughout example(). 'my_name' is declared as a 'string'. However, it can only be used within the if(){ } code block. Of note is '(string)this_player()...', the '(string)' is known as a 'cast'. Call_other and casting: Call_other allows you to call a function in another object. However, the compiler treats the return value of such a call as "unknown". So you must declare the type of a call_other by using a cast. Call_other(object|string,function,arg1,arg2,..) is equivalant to object->function(arg1,arg2,..). MAIN POINTS: Declaration of a variable MUST be done at the head of the file, function, or code block. You should declare all variables and functions. This allows you to find errors in compile time, rather then in run time. Run time errors are always harder to find. The valid declarations are: status, int, string, object, mixed, and void. Declaring Variables: -=[ Type ]=- -=[ Example of Type ]=- status example; /* example is off|on, (1|0), example = 1 */ int example; /* example = 5 */ string example; /* example = "Hi!
"; */ object example; /* example = this_player() */ mixed example; /* a mixture of int, string, or object */ Declaring Array Variables: It is important to declare variables that are arrays, as pointers(*). -=[ Type ]=- -=[ Example of Type ]=- int *aiExample; /* aiExample = ({ 1, 3, 5, 7, }); */ string *asExample; /* asExample = ({ "Bob", "Eric", "Tom", }); */ object *aoExample; /* aoExample = ({ obj1, obj2, obj3, }); */ mixed *axExample; /* axExample = ({ 1, "Bob", ({ obj2, }), }); Declaring Functions: All functions should be declared. They can be declared in the same way as variables. The type of function declaration depends upon what the function returns. void /* returns nothing */ status /* returns 0|1 */ int /* returns an int */ string /* returns a string */ object /* returns an object */ mixed /* returns an int, a string, or an object */ eg. A simple monster. inherit "inherit/monster"; void reset(status iArg) { if(iArg) return; set_name("bob"); set_level(1); set_short("Bob the Dwarf"); } Declaring Array functions: Note: If the function returns an array the function should be declared as a pointer. eg. get an array of weapons that are on a player object *get_weaoPon(object player) { int iI; object *aoInv, *aoWeapons; aoWeapons = ({}); if(!oPlayer) oPlayer = this_player(); inv = all_inventory(oPlayer); for(iI = 0; iI < sizeof(iInv); iI++) { if(iInv[iI] -> query_weapon_class()) { /* this may be invalid on some muds - see alternative */ aoWeapons = aoWeapons + ({ iInv[iI], }); } } return aoWeapons; } /* an alternative to added to arrays - this would have limits adding arrays with a total of less then 50 elements */ mixed *add_array(mixed *axArr1, mixed *axArr2) { mixed *axTemp; int iI, iSize1, iSize2; if(!(iSize1=sizeof(axArr1))) { if(!sizeof(axArr2)) return ({}); return axArr2; } if(!(iSize2=sizeof(axArr2))) return axArr1; axTemp = allocate(iSize1 + iSize2); for(iI = 0; iI < sizeof(axTemp); iI++) { axTemp[iI] = (iI < iSize1) ? axArr1[iI] : axArr2[i - iSize1]; } return axTemp; } -=[ LPC Basics ]=- Control statements: LPC has control statements the same as C. These include; if-else, switch, for-loop, while-loop, and the loop controls break, and continue; and the function control return. -=[ Selection statements ]=- LPC supports two selection statements: if, and switch. if: if(expression) { statement1; } else { statement2; } The conditional expression can be anything. C only evaluates 'expression' as false if it is 0. LPC allows an if-else-if ladder. if(expression1) { statement1; } else if(expression2) { statement2; } else { statement3; } Example: /* write the players inventory, if this_player() is a wiz, then show invisible objects */ #define WIZ 21 void inventory(object oPlayer) { object *aoInv; int iI; aoInv = all_inventory(player); for(iI = 0; iI < sizeof(aoInv); iI++) { if(aoInv[iI]->short()) { write((string)aoInv[iI]->short()+"
"); } else if(this_player()->query_level() >= WIZ) { write("*"+file_name(aoInv[iI])+"
"); } } } 'Switch' used for selection: switch(expression) { case constant1: statement1; break; case constant2: statement2; break; case constant3: statement3; break; default: statementdefault; } Switch is a multi-branch selection statement. If there is a match between the expression and 'constant'. It will execute the statement. If there is a default it will do the default statement if there are no other matches. -=[ Iteration statements ]=- The main iteration statements used are the while, and for loops. for: for(initalization;condition;increment) { statement; } while: while(expression) { statement; } Note: Unlike programmes compiled on your own machine, LPC will only allow evaluations of about 50 loops. After this you will get Too Long Evaluation errors. I think this was design so that you didn't get infinite loops, or long evaluations that lag, or crash the mud. Jump statements: return: return expression; return causes the function to jump out of the current function (routine). It may or may not have an expression. break: break; terminates the loop that the break is currently in. continue: continue; continue forces the next iteration of a loop skipping code that follows it. Operators: Operators allow processing of variables, and functions. Operator Action assignment: = assign to rvalue, lvalue arithmatic: - subtraction, unary minus + addition, add strings * multiplication / (integer) division % modulus division -- decrement ++ increment -= x -= 5; is equivelant to x = x - 5; += x += 5; is equivalent to x = x + 5; relational: > greater than >= greater than or equal to < less than <= less than or equal to == equal to != not equal to logical: && AND || OR ! NOT ternary: variable = (expr1) ? expr2 : expr3; is equivalent to, if(expr1) variable = expr2; else variable = expr3; Example: void set_msgin(string sArg) { msgin = (sArg) ? sArg : "arrives"; } Misc: -> arrow, "object -> fn()" is equivalent to "call_other(object,"fn")" [] square bracket, s[4], 5th element of array s :: scope symbol, call the function directly from the inherited object. Example: void init() { ::init(); add_action("jump","jump"); } -=[ LPC Basics ]=- directives (preprocessors): LPC allows most of the ANSI preprocessor controls. Since this is only a light brush of LPC, I will deal only with the directives, #define, #undef, and #include. I will leave an explanation of conditional directives later. #define: The #define directive allows you to do a macro substitution. The directive defines an identifier, that substitutes a string when encountered in the source file. Example: #define query_name() QN will substitute 'query_name()' whenever 'QN' is found in your code. #define can used more powerfully as a psuedo- function, #define PAY(XXX) this_player()->add_money(-XXX) if PAY(20) was called then, 20 coins would be deducted from this_player(). The macro does not have to be only one line, #define MOVE_OBJ(NN,FF) if(!present(NN,this_object())) {\ move_object(clone_object(FF),this_object());\ } However, you must be careful using pseudo-functions. They are not very leanient. For example, MOVE_OBJ("bob","players/zilanthius/monsters/bob"); would work fine. But, MOVE_OBJ( "bob", path+"/monsters/bob"); would not work. One because of the spaces, and two because of the 'path+'. #undef: #undef un-defines a macro. Why have this? There are times when you do not want a particular macro defined, that was carried through with an #include "file". example: cloning a bag into a room using room.h #include "/include/room.h" #undef EXTRA_RESET #define EXTRA_RESET if(!present("bag,this_object())) {\ move_object(clone_object("objects/bag"),this_object());\ } #include: The #include directive instructs the compiler to read another file for 'library' routines. In effect it adds the file to the 'head' file to the top of your object.'file.h' files are known as "header" files for this reason. #include "/include/array.h" Will instruct the compiler to put /include/array.h at the head of the file. For example the function, write_file_array(filename,your_array); can be used if array.h is included. (write_file_array() writes an array of strings, or ints line by line into filename). Some wizards make a "path.h" header file for directory paths. Eg. "path.h" #define PATH "/players/zilanthius/" #define OBJ "/players/zilanthius/obj/" #define MONSTER "/players/zilanthius/monsters/" #define WEAPON "/players/zilanthius/weapons/" etc. inherit: Inheritance incorporates code from one object into another thus supporting the concept of classification. Mud objects are classified into groups (such as rooms, monsters, players, etc). All of the code in the inherited file now becomes a part of the file you are writing. Therefore, you need only set the paramaters that will individualize this file. Basically this allows for a hierarchial classification system. The main files used in the creation of the mud are inherited into your files. This determines the classification of the object you are creating. Thus, to create a room you would inherit "/inherit/room.c"; The file room.c in the directory inherit has all of paramaters that make an object a room. Since this line is used in almost every room file in the mud, it is effective planning to have a header file which defines the path and file name for the room inheritable. So that if, for some reason, the path or filename is changed only one file need be updated to reflect the change. The file that defines all of the inheritables for the mud is <mudlib.h>. You must include this file before using the defines in it. Therefore now you would: #include <mudlib.h> inherit ROOM; at the start of a room file. You can create your own inheritables. If you have a monster that will have basically the same functions, but will have different longs, shorts, etc. you can create a file for that monster, and then inherit that file into each classification of that file. For example a file dwarf_guard.c might inherit MONSTER; and define all the dwarf_guards as wandering, talking, aggressive dwarves. Then red_dwarf, black_dwarf, young_dwarf, etc would inherit dwarf_guard.c and in these files you would set the paramaters that make them individual. // This is based on the original basics file, with some changes // and corrections added. The examples given in this file // include hungarian notation. All files must now use hungarian // notation. For examples that use hungarian notation look in // /open/X where X is the classification you wish an example of. //---Xnedra 21/08/98---

******************* * HEADER FILES * ******************* A header file, sometimes referred to as a "rooms.h" file, makes it easier for you to code, and easier for others to read your code. A header file (often called "rooms.h") is a file in your directory which consists of a list of #define statements. These statements define constants as a partial pathname for your code. For instance, a basic rooms.h file might contain: #define MYROOT "/players/myname/" #define MYROOM MYROOT+"rooms/" #define MYWEAP MYROOT+"weapons/" #define MYARMOR MYROOT+"armor/" #define MYNPC MYROOT+"npc/" #define MYITEM MYROOT+"objects/" If you had two separate areas, one in Kerei and one in Souvrael, you might also have: #define MYSOUV MYROOM+"souvrael/" #define MYKER MYROOM+"kerei/" You could then use those definitions to #define others. IMPORTANT: Make sure that the constants you choose aren't used elsewhere, or it will cause an error. For instance, ROOM is defined as an inheritable for the basic mudlib room. If you try to use: #define ROOM "blah" then you will get an error, because you're trying to re-define something that is already defined elsewhere. Once you've created your header file, you can use it to help you generate code for rooms and objects. Just add the following line to all your area files: #include "../rooms.h" assuming your files are one "directory level" down from your root directory. (If "/players/myname" is your root directory, then "/players/myname/rooms" is one level down, "/players/myname/rooms/blah" is two levels down, and so on.) If the file in question is more than one level down, simply add one extra "../" to the beginning of the #include statement for each additional level. Note that this is a relative path. Do not use an absolute path (for example, #include "/players/myname/rooms.h") -- if your area was ever moved, you would then have to change every file, rather than just changing the header file. You can then use the definitions in your code. For instance: add_clone(MYNPC + "demon",1); make_object("sword", MYWEAP + "sword", 1); add_exit("north", MYROOM + "room2"); "Abbreviating" filepaths in this way makes your code much easier to read, and also easier for you to type.

docs.title: LPC Basics
docs.text: LPC Basics Written by Descartes of Borg first edition: 23 April 1993 second edition: 25 May 1993 CHAPTER 1: Introduction to the Coding Environment 1.1 UNIX file structure LPMuds use basic UNIX commands and its file structure. If you know UNIX commands already, then note (with a few exceptions) options are not available to the commands. Like DOS, UNIX is hierarchical. The root directory of which all directories are sub-directories is called root(/). And from those sub-directories you may have further sub-directories. A directory may be referred to in two different ways: 1) by its full name, or absolute name, or 2) by its relative name. Absolute name refers to the directory's full path starting from / winding down the directory tree until you name the directory in question. For example: /players/descartes/obj/monster refers to the directory monster which is a sub-directory of obj which is a sub-directory of descartes which is a sub-directory of players which is a subdirectory of /. The relative name refers to the name relative to another directory. The above example is called monster relative to /players/descartes/obj, but it is also called obj/monster relative to /players/descartes, descartes/obj/monster relative to /players, and finally players/descartes/obj/monster relative to /. You can tell the difference between absolute names and relative names because absolute names always start with /. In order to know exactly which directory is being named by a relative name, you naturally must know what directory it is relative to. A directory contains sub-directories and files. LPMuds only use text files inside the mudlib. Like directories, files have both absolute and relative names. The most basic relative name is often referred to as the file name, with the rest of the absolute name being referred to as the path. So, for the file: /players/descartes/castle.c, castle.c is the file name, and /players/descartes is the path. On some muds, a file with a file name beginning with a . (like .plan) is not visible when you list files with the regular file listing command. 1.2 UNIX Commands Along with the UNIX file structure, LPMuds use many UNIX commands. Typical UNIX commands on most muds are: pwd, cd, ls, rm, mv, cp, mkdir, rmdir, more, head, cat, ed If you have never before seen UNIX commands, you probably are thinking this is all nonsense. Well, it is, but you got to use them. Before getting into what they mean though, first a discussion of current directory. If you know DOS, then you know what a current working directory is. At any given point, you are considered to be "in" some directory. This means that any relative file or directory names you give in UNIX commands are relative to that directory. For example, if my current directory is /players/descartes and I type "ed castle.c" (ed is the command to edit), then it assumes I mean the file /players/descartes/castle.c pwd: shows you your current working directory cd: changes your current working directory. You may give either relative or absolute path names. With no arguments, it changes to your home directory. ls: lists all files in the directory named. If no directory is named, it lists the files of the current working directory rm: deletes the file named mv: renames the file named cp: copies the file named mkdir: makes a new directory rmdir: deletes a directory. All files must have been first removed. more: pages the file named so that the file appears on your screen one page at a time. cat: shows the whole file to you at once head: shows you the first several lines of a file tail: shows you the last several lines of a file ed: allows you to edit a file using the mud editor 1.3 Chapter Summary UNIX uses a hierarchical file structure with the root of the tree being named /. Other directories branch off from that root directory and in turn have their own sub-directories. All directories may contain directories and files. Directories and files are referred to either by their absolute name, which always begins with /, or by their relative name which gives the file's name relative to a particular directory. In order to get around in the UNIX files structure, you have the typical UNIX commands for listing files, your current directory, etc. On your mud, all of the above commands should have detailed help commands to help you explore exactly what they do. In addition, there should be a very detailed file on your mud's editor. If you are unfamiliar with ed, you should go over this convoluted file.

docs.title: LPC Basics
docs.text: LPC Basics Written by Descartes of Borg first edition: 23 april 1993 second edition: 16 june 1993 CHAPTER 2: The LPC Program 2.1 About programs The title of this chapter of the textbook is actually poorly named, since one does not write programs in LPC. An LPC coder instead writes *objects*. What is the difference? Well, for our purposes now, the difference is in the way the file is executed. When you "run" a program, execution begins at a definite place in the program. In other words, there is a place in all programs that is noted as the beginning where program execution starts. In addition, programs have definite end points, so that when execution reaches that point, the execution of the program terminates. So, in short, execution of a program runs from a definite beginning point through to a definite end point. This is not so with LPC objects. With muds, LPC objects are simply distinct parts of the C program which is running the game (the driver). In other words, execution of the mud program begins and ends in the driver. But the driver in fact does very little in the way of creating the world you know when you play a mud. Instead, the driver relies heavily on the code created in LPC, executing lines of the objects in the mud as needed. LPC objects thus have no place that is necessarily the beginning point, nor do they have a definite ending point. Like other programming languages, an LPC "program" may be made up of one or more files. For an LPC object to get executed, it simple needs to be loaded into the driver's memory. The driver will call lines from the object as it needs according to a structure which will be defined throughout this textbook. The important thing you need to understand at this point is that there is no "beginning" to an LPC object in terms of execution, and there is no "end". 2.2 Driver-mudlib interaction As I have mentioned earlier, the driver is the C program that runs on the host machine. It connects you into the game and processes LPC code. Note that this is one theory of mud programming, and not necessarily better than others. It could be that the entire game is written in C. Such a game would be much faster, but it would be less flexible in that wizards could not add things to the game while it was running. This is the theory behind DikuMUDs. Instead, LPMUDs run on the theory that the driver should in no define the nature of the game, that the nature of the game is to be decided by the individuals involved, and that you should be able to add to the game *as it is being played*. This is why LPMUDs make use of the LPC programming language. It allows you to define the nature of the game in LPC for the driver to read and execute as needed. It is also a much simpler language to understand than C, thus making the process of world creation open to a greater number of people. Once you have written a file in LPC (assuming it is corrent LPC ), it justs sits there on the host machine's hard drive until something in the game makes reference to it. When something in the game finally does make reference to the object, a copy of the file is loaded into memory and a special *function* of that object is called in order to initialize the values of the variables in the object. Now, do not be concerned if that last sentence went right over your head, since someone brand new to programming would not know what the hell a function or a variable is. The important thing to understand right now is that a copy of the object file is taken by the driver from the machine's hard drive and stored into memory (since it is a copy, multiple versions of that object may exist). You will later understand what a function is, what a variable is, and exactly how it is something in the game made reference to your object. 2.3 Loading an object into memory Although there is no particular place in an object code that must exist in order for the driver to begin executing it, there is a place for which the driver will search in order to initialize the object. On compat drivers, it is the function called reset(). On native muds it is the function called create(). LPC objects are made up of variables (values which can change) and functions which are used to manipulate those variables. Functions manipulate variables through the use of LPC grammatical structures, which include calling other functions, using externally defined functions (efuns), and basic LPC expressions and flow control mechanisms. Does that sound convoluted? First lets start with a variable. A variable might be something like: level. It can "vary" from sitation to situation in value, and different things use the value of the player's level to make different things happen. For instance, if you are a level 19 player, the value of the variable level will be 19. Now if your mud is on the old LPMud 2.4.5 system where levels 1-19 are players and 20+ are wizards, things can ask for your level value to see if you can perform wizard type actions. Basically, each object in LPC is a pile of variables with values which change over time. Things happen to these objects based on what values its variables hold. Often, then things that happen cause the variables to change. So, whenever an object in LPC is referenced by another object currently in memory, the driver searches to see what places for values the object has (but they have no values yet). Once that is done, the driver calls a function in the object called reset() or create() (depending on your driver) which will set up the starting values for the object's variables. It is thus through *calls* to *functions* that variable values get manipulated. But create() or reset() is NOT the starting place of LPC code, although it is where most LPC code execution does begin. The fact is, those functions need not exist. If your object does just fine with its starting values all being NULL pointers (meaning, for our purposes here, 0), then you do not need a create() or reset() function. Thus the first bit of execution of the object's code may begin somewhere completely different. Now we get to what this chapter is all about. The question: What consists a complete LPC object? Well, an LPC object is simply one or more functions grouped together manipulating 0 or more variables. The order in which functions are placed in an object relative to one another is irrelevant. In other words: ----- void init() { add_action("smile", "smile"); } void create() { return; } int smile(string sArg) { return 0; } ----- is exactly the same as: ----- void create() { return; } int smile(string sArg) { return 0; } void init() { add_action("smile", "smile"); } _____ Also important to note, the object containing only: ----- void nonsense() {} ----- is a valid, but trivial object, although it probably would not interact properly with other objects on your mud since such an object has no weight, is invisible, etc.. 2.4 Chapter summary LPC code has no beginning point or ending point, since LPC code is used to create objects to be used by the driver program rather than create individual programs. LPC objects consist of one or more functions whose order in the code is irrelevant, as well as of zero or more variables whose values are manipulated inside those functions. LPC objects simply sit on the host machine's hard driver until referenced by another object in the game (in other words, they do not really exist). Once the object is referenced, it is loaded into the machine's memory with empty values for the variables. The function reset() in compat muds or create() in native muds is called in that object if it exists to allow the variables to take on initial values. Other functions in the object are used by the driver and other objects in the game to allow interaction among objects and the manipulation of the LPC variables. A note on reset() and create(): create() is only used by muds in native mode (see the textbook Introduction for more information on native mode vs. compat mode). It is only used to initialize newly referenced objects. reset() is used by both muds in compat mode and native mode. In compat mode, reset() performs two functions. First, it is used to initialize newly referenced objects. In addition, however, compat mode muds use reset() to "reset" the object. In other words, return it to its initial state of affairs. This allows monsters to regenerate in a room and doors to start back in the shut position, etc.. Native mode muds use reset() to perform the second function (as its name implies). So there are two important things which happen in LP style muds which cause the driver to make calls to functions in objects. The first is the creation of the object. At this time, the driver calls a function to initalize the values in the object. For compat mode muds, this is performed by the function named reset() (with an argument of 0, more on this later though). For muds running in native mode, this is performed by the function create(). The second is the returning of the room to some base state of affairs. This base set of affairs may or may not be different from the initial state of affairs, and certainly you would not want to take up time doing redundant things (like resetting variables that never change). Compat mode muds nevertheless use the same function that was used to create the object to reset it, that being reset(). Native mode muds, who use create() to create the room, instead use reset() to reset it. All is not lost in compat mode though, as there is a way to tell the difference between creation and resetting. For reset purposes, the driver passes either 1 or the reset number as an argument to reset() in compat mode. Now this is meaningless to you now, but just keep in mind that you can in fact tell the difference in compat mode. Also keep in mind that the argment in the creation use of reset is 0 and the argument in the reset use is a nonzero number.

docs.title: LPC Basics
docs.text:
LPC Basics Written by Descartes of Borg first edition: 23 april 1993 second edition: 17 june 1993 CHAPTER 3: LPC Data Types 3.1 What you should know by now LPC object are made up of zero or more variables manipulated by one or more functions. The order in which these functions appear in code is irrelevant. The driver uses the LPC code you write by loading copies of it into memory whenever it is first referenced and additional copies through cloning. When each object is loaded into memory, all the variables initially point to no value. The reset() function in compat muds, and create() in native muds are used to give initial values to variables in objects. The function for creation is called immediately after the object is loaded into memory. However, if you are reading this textbook with no prior programming experience, you may not know what a function is or how it gets called. And even if you have programming experience, you may be wondering how the process of functions calling each other gets started in newly created objects. Before any of these questions get answered, however, you need to know more about what it is the functions are manipulating. You therefore should thouroughly come to know the concept behind LPC data types. Certainly the most boring subject in this manual, yet it is the most crucial, as 90% of all errors (excepting misplaced {} and ()) involve the improper usage of LPC data types. So bear through this important chapter, because it is my feeling that understanding this chapter alone can help you find coding much, much easier. 3.2 Communicating with the computer You possibly already know that computers cannot understand the letters and numbers used by humans. Instead, the "language" spoken by computers consists of an "alphabet" of 0's and 1's. Certainly you know computers do not understand natural human languages. But in fact, they do not understand the computer languages we write for them either. Computer languages like BASIC, C, C++, Pascal, etc. are all intermediate languages. They allow you to structure your thoughts more coherently for translation into the 0's and 1's of the computer's languages. There are two methods in which translation is done: compilation and interpretation. These simply are differences betweem when the programming language is translated into computer language. With compiled languages, the programmer writes the code then uses a program called a compiler to translate the program into the computer's language. This translation occurs before the program is run. With interpreted languages however, the process of translation occurs as the program is being run. Since the translation of the program is occurring during the time of the program's running in interpreted languages, interpreted languages make much slower programs than compiled languages. The bottom line is, no matter what language you are writing in, at some point this has to be changed into 0's and 1's which can be understood by the computer. But the variables which you store in memory are not simply 0's and 1's. So you have to have a way in your programming languages of telling the computer whether or not the 0's and 1's should be treated as decimal numbers or characters or strings or anything else. You do this through the use of data types. For example, say you have a variable which you call 'x' and you give it the decimal whole number value 65. In LPC you would do this through the statement: ----- iX = 65; ----- You can later do things like: _____ write(iX+"
"); /* 
 is symbolically represents a carriage return */ iY = iX + 5; ----- The first line allows you to send 65 and a carriage return to someone's screen. The second line lets iYou set the value of y to 70. The problem for the computer is that it does not know what '65' means when you tell it iX = 65;. What you think of 65, it might think of as: 00000000000000000000000001000001 But, also, to the computer, the letter 'A' is represented as: 00000000000000000000000001000001 So, whenever you instruct the computer write(iX+"
");, it must have some way of knowing that you want to see '65' and not 'A'. The computer can tell the difference between '65' and 'A' through the use of data types. A data types simply says what type of data is being stored by the memory location pointed to by a given variable. Thus, each LPC variable has a variable type which guides conversions. In the example given above, you would have had the following line somewhere in the code *before* the lines shown above: ----- int iX; ----- This one line tells the driver that whatever value iX points to, it will be used as the data type "int", which is short for integer, or whole number. So you have a basic introduction into the reason why data types exist. They exist so the driver can make sense of the 0's and 1's that the computer is storing in memory. 3.3 The data types of LPC All LPMud drivers have the following data types: void, status, int, string, object, int *, string *, object *, mixed * Many drivers, but not all have the following important data types which are important to discuss: float, mapping, float *, mapping * And there are a few drivers with the following rarely used data types which are not important to discuss: function, enum, struct, char 3.4 Simple data types This introductory textbook will deal with the data types void, status, int, float, string, object, mand mixed. You can find out about the more complex data types like mappings and arrays in the intermediate textbook. This chapter deals with the two simplest data types (from the point of view of the LPC coder), int and string. An int is any whole number. Thus 1, 42, -17, 0, -10000023 are all type int. A string is one or more alphanumeric characters. Thus "a", "we are borg", "42", "This is a string" are all strings. Note that strings are always enclosed in "" to allow the driver to distinguish between the int 42 and the string "42" as well as to distinguish between variable names (like x) and strings by the same names (like "x"). When you use a variable in code, you must first let the driver know what type of data to which that variable points. This process is called *declaration*. You do this at the beginning of the function or at the beginning of the object code (outside of functions before all functions which use it). This is done by placing the name of the data type before the name of the variable like in the following example: ----- void add_two_and_two() { int iX; int iY; iX = 2; iY = iX + iX; } ----- Now, this is a complete function.
