CONCEPT closures example LAST UPDATE Mateese, 10-Dec-1994, 23:30 MET DESCRIPTION These are a small discussed examples of the usage of (lambda-)closures. For technical details see the closures(LPC) doc. For hints when to use which type of closure, see the end of this doc. Many Muds use 'details' to add more flavour. 'Details' are items which can be looked at, but are not implemented as own objects, but instead simulated by the environment. Lets assume that the function AddDetail(string keyword, string|closure desc) adds the detail 'keyword' to the room, which, when look at, returns the string 'desc' resp. the result of the execution of closure 'desc' as the detail description to the player. Now imagine that one wants to equip a room with magic runes, which read as 'Hello <playername>!
" when looked at. Obviously AddDetail("runes", sprintf( "Hello %s!
" , this_player()->QueryName())); is not sufficient, as the 'this_player()' is executed to early and just once. The solution is to use closures. First, the solution using lfun-closures: private string _detail_runes () { return sprintf("Hello %s!
", this_player()->QueryName()); } ... AddDetail("runes", #'_detail_runes); Simple? Here is the same code, this time as lambda-closure: AddDetail( "runes" , lambda(0 , ({#'sprintf, "Hello %s!
" , ({#'call_other, ({#'this_player}) , "QueryName" }) }) )); Why the extra ({ }) around '#'this_player'? #'this_player alone is just a symbol, symbolizing the efun this_player(), but call_other() needs an object as first argument. Therefore, the #'this_player has to be interpreted as function to evaluate, which is enforced by enclosing it in ({ }). The same reason also dictates the enclosing of the whole #'call_other expression into ({ }). Note also the missing #'return: it is not needed. The result of a lambda-closure is the last value computed. Another example: Task is to reduce the HP of every living in a room by 10, unless the result would be negative. Selecting all livings in a room is simply filter_array(all_inventory(room), #'living) The tricky part is to reduce the HP. Again, first the lfun-closure solution: private _reduce_hp (object liv) { int hp; hp = liv->QueryHP(); if (hp > 10) liv->SetHP(hp-10); } ... map_array( filter_array(all_inventory(room), #'living) , #'_reduce_hp) Both filter_array() and map_array() pass the actual array item being filtered/mapped as first argument to the closure. Now, the lambda-closure solution: map_array( filter_array(all_inventory(room), #'living) , lambda( ({ 'liv }) , ({'#, , ({#'=, 'hp, ({#'call_other, 'liv, "QueryHP" }) }) , ({#'?, ({#'>, 'hp, 10 }) , ({#'call_other, 'liv, "SetHP" , ({#'-, 'hp, 10 }) }) }) }) ) // of lambda() ); It is worthy to point out how local variables like 'hp' are declared in a lambda-closure: not at all. They are just used by writing their symbol 'hp . Same applies to the closures parameter 'liv . The lambda-closure solution is not recommended for three reasons: it is complicated, does not use the powers of lambda(), and the lambda() is recompiled every time this statement is executed! So far, lambda-closures seem to be just complicated, and in fact: they are. Their powers lie elsewhere. Imagine a computation, like for skill resolution, which involves two object properties multiplied with factors and then added. The straightforward solution would be a function like: int Compute (object obj, string stat1, int factor1 , string stat2, int factor2) { return call_other(obj, "Query"+stat1) * factor1 + call_other(obj, "Query"+stat2) * factor2; } Each call to Compute() involves several operations (computing the function names and resolving the call_other()s) which in fact need to be done just once. Using lambda-closures, one can construct and compile a piece of code which behaves like a Compute() tailored for a specific stat/factor combination: closure ConstructCompute (object obj, string stat1, int factor1 , string stat2, int factor2) { mixed code; // Construct the first multiplication. // The symbol_function() creates a symbol for the // lfun 'Query<stat1>', speeding up later calls. // Note again the extra ({ }) around the created symbol. code = ({#'*, ({ symbol_function("Query"+stat1, obj) }) , factor1 }); // Construct the second multiplication, and the addition // of both terms. code = ({#'+, code , ({#'*, ({ symbol_function("Query"+stat2, obj) }) , factor2 }) }); // Compile the code and return the generated closure. return lambda(0, code); } Once the closure is compiled, str_dex_fun = ConstructCompute(obj, "Str", 10, "Dex", 90); it can be used with a simple 'funcall(str_dex_fun)'. DESCRIPTION -- When to use which closure? First, a closure is only then useful if it needn't to live any longer than the object defining it. Reason: when the defining object gets destructed, the closure will vanish, too. Efun- and lfun-closures should be used where useful, as they mostly do the job and are easy to read. The disadvantage of lfun-closures is that they make a replace_program() impossible - but since such objects tend to not being replaceable at all, this is no real loss. Lambda closures are needed if the actions of the closure are heavily depending on some data available only at runtime, like the actual inventory of a certain player. If you use lfun-closures and find yourself shoving around runtime data in arguments or (gasp!) global variables, it is time to think about using a lambda-closure, compiling the value hard into it. The disadvantages of lambda closures are clear: they are damn hard to read, and each lambda() statement cost extra time to compile the closure. SEE ALSO closures(LPC)

docs.text: CONCEPT mappings LAST UPDATE Thur, 12 Jan 2006 AUTHOR Hyp, 15th Nov, 1993 DESCRIPTION A step-by-step introduction to mappings: ---------------------------------------- 1. What is a mapping? A mapping is a datatype which allows to store data associated to a key. In other languages they are also known as 'dictionaries' or 'alists'. There are also alists in LPC but they are not a seperate datatype but are implemented on top of arrays. Alists are the predecessors of mappings. The keys and the values can be of any type. But most common datatypes for keys are strings, integers and objects. Others like arrays, mappings or closures aren't a good choice because comparision between i.e. arrays often returns false even if they equal in content. This is because the driver compares i.e. two arrays by their internal pointers and not by their content. The reason for this is simple: speed. Mappings are allways treated as references when passing them to functions. This means when you pass a mapping to another object and this object modifies the mapping the modification will take place in a global scope - visible to all objects holding this mapping in a variable. 2. What are mappings good for? The term 'dictionary' probably describes the use of a mapping best. Opposed to arrays mappings don't have a specific order. They provide a mechanism to create a set of associations between values. Such an association consists of a unique key and data that is identified by the key. Think of a dictionary where you have a word and a definition of it. You use the word to lookup its definition. Mappings can be used i.e. to hold aliases for commands. The key would then be the name of the alias and the data the command(s) behind an alias. Or they can be used for the exits of a room. The keys would be the directions where one can go to and the associated data would be the file names of the rooms. But mappings can also be used as a kind of a sparse array. A sparse array is an array where most of the elements aren't used (occupied by 0). I.e. if you want to store values at the position 0, 13 and 37642 of an array you would have to create an array with a size of at least 37643. This costs a lot of memory so a mapping would be more useful because you would then use the numbers 0, 13 and 37642 as a key and not as an index to a position (actually the keys of a mapping are sometimes called indices but this is just because the way data is accessed in a mapping is similar to arrays: by the [] operator). This also allows to query all occupied positions of a sparse array by querying for all the keys of the mapping opposed to an array where you have to iterate over all elements. 3. How do I create a mapping? There are several ways to do so. The most convenient is the following: mapping map; map = ([ key0: value00; ...; value0n, ... : ... ; ...; ... , keyn: valuen0; ...; valuenn ]); As you can see, a key may have more than one value assigned. But the amount of values per key must always be equal. It is even possible to have mappings without any values! Another method is to use the efun mkmapping(). This efun gets two arguments with the first beeing an array of keys and the following beeing arrays of values: mapping map; map = mkmapping (({ key0 , ..., keyn }), ({ value00, ..., value0n }), ({ ... , ..., ... }), ({ valuen0, ..., valuenn })); If the efun only gets one argument, then this argument will be taken as an array of keys and a mapping without values will be returned. An empty mapping can be created by using the above described methods by simply ommitting the keys and values: mapping map; map = ([]); or: map = mkmapping(({}), ({})); Or by using the efun allocate_mapping(). This efun gets as first argument the amount of keys which will be added soon and an optional second argument specifying the width of the mapping: map = allocate_mapping(n, width); The value <n> may be a bit confusing since mappings shrink and grow dynamically. This value just tells the driver how 'long' this mapping is going to be so proper memory allocations will be performed to reduce the overhead of memory reallocation. I.e. if you want to read in a file and store the read data in a mapping you probably know the amount of keys. So you allocate a mapping with this efun and tell the driver how much memory should be allocated by specifing a proper <n> value. Thus causing a speedup when adding the read data to the mapping afterwards. The <width> just specifies how many values per key this mapping is going to have. If no width is given, 1 will be taken as default. It is important to note that the width of a mapping is strict and cannot shrink or grow once defined. 4. How can I modify the data of a mapping? Adding a new key is similiar to modifying the associated data of an existing key: map += ([ key: value0; ...; valuen ]); Or in case only a single value should be modified: map[key, n] = valuen; If <n> is out of range or if <key> doesn't exists and <n> is greater than 0 an "Illegal index" error will be reported. If <n> is equal to 0 or the mapping only has a single value per key one can abbreviate it with: map[key] = value; If there is no <key> (and <n> is equal to 0 or not specified at all) a new one will be added automatically. Deletion of a key is done with the -= operator or the efun m_delete(). A mapping can only be substracted by one without any values: map -= ([ key ]); or: map -= ([ key0, ..., keyn ]); The efun takes a mapping as first and a key as second argument: m_delete(map, key); The efun m_delete() returns the mapping but because mappings are handled as references there is no need of an assignment like: map = m_delete(map, key); 5. How can I access the data stored in a mapping? This can be done by: valuen = map[key, n]; Or in case of a mapping with just one value per key: value0 = map[key]; If there is no <key> in the mapping and <n> is 0 or not specified at all (which is the same) a 0 will be returned or if <n> is greater than 0 an "Illegal index" error will be reported. 6. How can I test for the existance of a key? A return value of 0 is sufficient for most applications but sometimes the ambiguity between an existing value of 0 and a nonexisting key can lead to a problem. Therefore one can use the efun member() or mapping_contains() to check if there actually is a key in the mapping: if (member(map, key)) { ... } or: if (mapping_contains(&value0, ..., &valuen, map, key)) { ... } This also shows how one can retrieve all values associated to a key from a mapping in a single step. The '&' is the reference operator which is neccesary to let the efun store the values in the variables. In case of mappings with no values, the efun member() and mapping_contains() are equal in their behaviour and their way of calling because mapping_contains() won't get any reference variables to store the values in (obviously, because there aren't any). Also normally member() is known to return the postion of an element in a list (i.e. a character in a string or data in an array) and if an element couldn't be found -1 is returned. But in the case of mappings there are no such things as order and postion. So member() only returns 0 or 1. 7. How can I copy a mapping? A mapping can be copied with the + operator or by the efun copy_mapping(): newmap = ([]) + map; or: newmap = copy_mapping(map); A mapping should only be copied when it is neccesary to get an own copy of it that must not be shared by other objects. 8. How can I get all keys of a mapping? The efun m_indices() gets a mapping as argument and returns an array holding all keys defined in this mapping: keys = m_indices(map); 9. How can I get all the values of a mapping? The efun m_values() gets a mapping as argument and returns an array holding all the first values of it. It is not possible to access the second or all following value 'columns' as a whole with this efun (or by any other efun). Not yet: values0 = m_values(map); 10. How can I determine the size of a mapping? Because a mapping is a kind of rectangle it has two sizes: a length and a width. There are two different efuns to query these values. The first is the efun sizeof() which returns the amount of key-value associations (the length of a mapping) and the second is the efun get_type_info(). get_type_info() is meant to be a function to identify a datatype. Its return value is an array of two numerical values. The first specifies the datatype of the argument and the second is a datatype dependend value. In the case of a mapping the first value is T_MAPPING (which is a value defined in <lpctypes.h>) and the second the amount of values per key (a.k.a. columns or the width of the mapping - actually it would be correct to say that the width of a mapping is the amount of columns plus one for the keys but this is uncommon). 11. What is the best method to iterate over a mapping? First of all the main purpose of a mapping is not meant to be a set of data to iterate over. Afterall the keys in a mapping have no specific but a random order (at least on the LPC side). But still it is possible and sometimes even neccesary to do so. If all key-value associations should be processed then one should use walk_mapping(). If all keys of a mapping should be processed to create a new mapping being a subset of the given one, then filter_mapping() should be used. If all keys are going to be processed and to create a new mapping with the same set of keys as the given mapping, then one would use map_mapping(). But in the case of an iteration that should/can stop even if not all data is processed it is probably wise to iterate over the mapping by first querying for the keys and then to iterate over them with a for() or a while() loop and querying the values by 'hand'. The efun walk_mapping() gets a mapping as first argument and the name of a function as second one. All the following arguments are treated as extras which will be passed to the function specified with the 2nd argument. Instead of a string for the name of a function a closure can be used, too. Nothing will be returned: ... walk_mapping(map, "func", xarg0, ..., xargn); ... void func(mixed key, mixed value0, ..., mixed valuen, mixed xarg0, ..., mixed xargn) { ... } func() will be called for all key-value associations and gets as first argument the key. The next arguments are the values behind the key and are passed as references. The rest of the passed arguments are those specified as extras. Because the values are passed as references (opposed to copies) it is possible to modify them from inside func() by simply assigning new value to the variables <value0>, ..., <valuen>. The efun filter_mapping() calls a function for each key in a mapping and creates a new mapping which only contains key-value associations for which the called function returned true (not equal 0 that is). The first argument is the mapping to iterate over and the second is a function name given as a string or a closure: ... submap = filter_mapping(map, "func", xarg0, ..., xargn); ... int func(mixed key, mixed xarg0, ..., mixed xargn) { ... } func() gets as first argument the key and the others are those passed as extras to filter_mapping(). The efun map_mapping() gets a mapping as first argument and a string as a function name (or again a closure) as second argument. Any additional arguments are again used as extras that will be passed to the iteration function. This efun returns a new mapping with the same keys as the given one. The values returned by the function that is invoked for each key will be used as the associated data behind each key of the new mapping: ... newmap = map_mapping(map, "func", xarg0, ..., xargn); ... mixed func(mixed key, mixed xarg0, ..., mixed xargn) { ... } func() gets as first argument the key and the others are those passed as extras to map_mapping(). Because a function can only return a single value (even when it is an array) it restricts the use of map_mapping() to only allow creation of mappings with a single value per key. 12. Is it possible to join/intersect/cut mappings with another? Joining mappings is only possible, if they have the same width (amount of values per key). One can use the + and += operator: map = map1 + map2 + ... + mapn; map += map1 + map2 + ... + mapn; Intersection of two mappings is only possible by using filter_mapping(). There is no efun or operator which features this. The 'easiest' way may be the following function: mapping intersect_mapping(mapping map1, mapping map2) { closure cl; cl = lambda(({ 'key }), ({ #'member, map2, 'key })); return filter_mapping(map1, cl, map2); } This function returns a new mapping which consists of all key-value associations of <map1> for which an equal key could be found in <map2>. This function uses a closure which returns 0 or 1 depending on wether a key from <map1> is contained in <map2> or not. Cutting out all key-value associations of a mapping for which a key could be found in another mapping can be done by using the - and -= operator: mapping cut_mapping(mapping map1, mapping map2) { return map1 - mkmapping(m_indices(map2)); } Because a maping can only be substracted by one without any values we first have to create such by using m_indices() and mkmapping(). 13. What are those mappings without any values (besides keys) good for? Because the way how the driver searches for a key in a mapping is rather fast, those mappings can be used as a set of elements with a fast method for testing if an element is contained in the set. This technique is called hashing (further explanation would lead too far) which is faster than searching for values in array (which is done in a linear fashion). Another (maybe more pratical) use of these mappings are to create a array of unique values out of an array with several equal values: uniques = m_indices(mkmapping(array)); mkmapping() uses <array> to create a mapping without any values but just keys. And because a mapping can only have unique keys all multiple values in <array> are taken as one. The call of m_indices() then returns an array of these unique keys. Actually we only make use of those mappings temporarily. 14. How can I convert an alist into a mapping and vice versa? There are no special efuns which handle such conversions. But it can be done by the following functions: mapping alist_to_mapping(mixed *alist) { return apply(#'mkmapping, alist); } The efun apply() takes a closure and an array of values and passes each element of the array as an argument to the closure. Because an alist consists of an array of arrays with the first beeing the list of keys and the others the values associated to each key passing them as arguments to the efun closure #'mkmapping via apply() causes the creation of a mapping out of an alist. mixed *mapping_to_alist(mapping map) { mixed *alist; symbol *vars; string var; closure cl; int width; width = get_type_info(map)[1]; alist = allocate(width + 1); vars = allocate(width + 2); for (var = "a"; width; var[0]++, width--) { alist[width] = ({}); vars[width] = quote(var); } alist[0] = ({}); vars[0] = 'key; vars[<1] = 'alist; cl = lambda(vars, ({ #'=, 'alist, ({ #'insert_alist }) + vars })); walk_mapping(map, cl, &alist); return alist; } This function is a bit more complicated than the other and detailed description would lead too far of the topic. This function has one restriction: it can only turn a mappings with up to 26 values per key into an alist. But this should be sufficient for probably all applications which use mappings. And Hyps further comment on this: The function mapping_to_alist() is also not that clever because insert_alist() allways creates a new alist. A second (optional) argument to m_values() to specify the value column would be better. Besides this, the conversion of a mapping into an alist could be done by to_array(). Version History ================ Rev. 1 - Added note about mapping width being strict and not dynamic. Change made by Olgar 1/12/06

docs.title: Area Reviews - An Introduction                                     Rev. 1.3
docs.text: Area Reviews - An Introduction Rev. 1.3 =============================== The area review process is aimed at ensuring that new and refurbished areas meet a minimum standard before becoming active. All areas, regardless of how generally competent the coder is, should be submitted for review. In software terms, an area review is analogous to an acceptance test. It is not a substitute for internal testing and debugging. For the reviewer, an area review should be a relatively painless process of verifying that the area submitted meets certain criteria characteristic of a "good" area. Too often submitted areas have too many defects, leading to long, drawn out reviews and general dissatisfaction among all parties. Submitting an area for review (for the area coder) -------------------------------------------------- When you have completed your area to the point where it is ready to be reviewed, you need to use the sumbit area command. THIS CAN ONLY BE DONE ON THE DEVELOPMENT VERSION OF THE GAME. You will be asked to provide the directory path for the area where your header file should be located. i.e. /players/violator/asgard/ You will then be asked to provide the start room for your area. This is the room which is to be connected to the game. The next part required is a simple description, which should be just a title. i.e Hyperborea Arctic Elf Camp. Do not make this title long winded. Lastly you will be required to type a description of the area, in this description we require the filenames of all uniques and any other features you may feel could be of concern. Ensure you give a decent description so that your reviewers know what to expect. These will be assigned to an appropriate reviewer. It doesn't hurt to tell higher-ups that you've done this, especially if the issues are not being assigned very fast. Conducting a review (for the area reviewer) ------------------------------------------- Reviewers will be asigned one of the three aspects of the review process. To ensure the integrity of the process a Mentor can not conduct a review on their Mentees. The process is then to go through the area to verify that the code/content/balance meets the criteria for an acceptable area. Some reviewers may find the area checklists (wizhelp sections 8.5 to 8.7 of this document) to be useful when | reviewing an area. Any defects or deficiencies should be recorded and the coder notified of these problems through the review command (see wizhelp 8.8). When the area has no remaining problems to be resolved, he/she can close that portion of the review, as completed (see wizhelp 8.8). Note that in some cases, there may need to be multiple review/repair cycles before an area is acceptable. Sometimes a reviewer will find that an area is so badly done that it is far too much work to point out all the problems. In these cases the area should be sent back to the coder for overall improvement and resubmission, instead of wasting the reviewer's time. Revision Summary ---------------- Version 1: Bob - July 02, 2003 Version 1.2: Violator - Novermber 21, 2003 'Back to the Future' Rev. 1.3: Olgar - January 16, 2006 - Updated references to checklists.

docs.title: Content Review
docs.text: Content Review ============== Content reviews take a close look at the area from a thematic point of view. This essentially covers everything cosmetic as well, from the formatting of the text to the flow of any puzzles and quest-like tasks. A content reviewer needs to look at the big picture of how the area fits into DarkWind's overall theme, and more locally to the domain. The area should be internally consistent thematically, and have a logical form in terms of room placement, inhabitants, loot etc. The content reviewer should also look at the quality of any text which is piped to a player. Ideally, text should both be correct and also have some stylistic merit. ------ Version 1: Bob - July 02, 2003

docs.title: Balance Review
docs.text: Balance Review ============== The balance review looks at an area from a balance point of view. Things to consider are the amount and quality of loot in the area, the strengths of the monsters relative to the reward, difficulty of puzzles etc. Anything that affects the players and is not cosmetic is covered under balance. The reviewer needs to consider how hard it is to get the rewards in the area, and also the effect of the rewards on the game once they are gotten. Generally, more valuable loot should be harder to get, but even the most difficult areas should not have items so powerful that they give a player godlike powers. Conversely, an area should have enough reward that there is an incentive for players to adventure there. Finally, it should be recognized that information spreads quite easily, and that once a player knows how to solve a puzzle, that puzzle is no longer so difficult. ------ Version 1: Bob - July 02, 2003

docs.title: Code Review
docs.text: Code Review =========== Code reviews try to ensure that the code in an area is up-to-date, internally consistent, consistent with mudwide standards, and have an acceptable style. There is no excuse for new code that is just as bad as the bad old stuff we already have. When doing a code review, the reviewer should recognize that the code should be in an acceptable style, not necessarily the reviewer's own. Whatever the personal style of the area coder, the format of the code should be reasonably readable to someone not familiar with the area. Note that the code should update before even getting to this stage, and it's expected that the code is already tested to work as intended. ------ Version 1: Bob - July 02, 2003

docs.title: Area Content Review Checklist
docs.text: Area Content Review Checklist ============================== General ------- __ All text has a consistent syntactic style. __ All text is free of typos or grammatical errors. __ Low level of repetitiveness in descriptions. __ Descriptions are not subjective to the player's thoughts or experience. __ Descriptions are not explanatory. __ Long descs are readable prose of sufficient detail. __ Obnoxious/hard to read color combinations are not used. Overall for the area -------------------- __ Area as a whole has a consistent thematic feel. __ Rooms should map consistently within an area. Rooms ----- __ All rooms must set: light, terrain, long and short. __ Terrain must set ALL applicable types. __ Long desc does not describe items which can be removed. __ Actions have reasonable syntax or hints. __ Nouns in the long desc for present objects have add_looks. __ Add_looks should have alternate target keys where appropriate. __ Add_looks and triggers are complete sentences. __ Extra settings should make sense. (e.g. no_teleport) Naming (monsters, objects) -------------------------- __ Proper names in name, alias and short settings are first letter capped. __ All other words in name, alias amd short settings are lowercase. __ Name, alias and short settings DO NOT start with articles. __ Aliases exist for reasonable variations of the short desc. Monsters -------- __ Monsters must set: name, long, short, size, level, alignment(al) race, gender. __ Long desc does not describe items which can be removed. __ Settings are consistent with the description of the monster. __ Monster level is reasonable given it's desc. Objects/Loot ------------ __ Items must set: name, long, short, material, weight, value. __ Armors must also set: new_type, quality, warmth. __ Weapons must also set: new_type, quality, material_composition. __ Settings are consistent with the description of the object. __ Actions have reasonable syntax or hints. ------ Version 1.1: Bob - March 02, 2004 Version 1: Bob - June 07, 2003

docs.title: Area Balance Review Checklist
docs.text: Area Balance Review Checklist ============================= Monsters -------- __ Mobs are of appropriate toughness relative to overall area difficulty. __ Mobs are of appropriate toughness relative to their own level. __ Monster toughness is hinted at in descs if unexpectedly strong/weak. Loot ---- __ Loot value (after selling) is appropriate to their owners' toughnesses. __ Getting the loot requires appropriate level of risk/action. __ Special items are not too powerful regardless of difficulty. __ Concentration of exceptional and unique items meet current standards. __ Loot should be enough to be an incentive for adventuring in the area. __ The amount of cash loot is small compared to sellable loot. Puzzles ------- __ Puzzle difficulty is based on thought required, not syntax. __ Loot acquisition is not based entirely on puzzles (access to monsters which carry the loot may be). __ Puzzles should be reasonably solvable. Traps ----- __ Traps have lethality relative to the overall area difficulty. __ Deathtraps should be avoidable if appropriate clues are heeded. ------ Version 1: Bob - July 02, 2003

docs.title: Area Code Review Checklist
docs.text: Area Code Review Checklist ============================== Structure --------- __ Files are divided into directories by type (rooms, monsters etc). __ Area directory does not contain unused files. __ Area is portable by changing a header. __ Variables are as localized as possible. Naming ------ __ File names are meaningful to a casual viewer. __ Variables use Hungarian notation. __ Variables have useful mnemonics. __ Function names have useful mnemonics. __ Aliases intended for internal use (not used by players) must begin with double underscores, and the coder name. (e.g. __bob_key). These aliases are unique to the application. Code Format ----------- __ Indentation should is clear and consistent. __ Code is not crowded (adequate spacing, blank lines etc.) __ Code is not sparse (not too many blank lines) __ Code is blocked where possible to collect similar instructions. __ Difficult/complex/obscure code is commented. __ Lines of code should 80 characters wide or less where possible. Object Creation Standard ------------------------ __ All objects use current standards for settings. __ Deprecated calls are not used. __ replace_program() is NOT used. (new standard) Code Correctness and Efficiency ------------------------------- __ All objects load. __ Sanity checks and fail outs are appropriately placed. __ All active code serves a purpose. __ Code is efficient as possible, without being unreadable. __ is_clone() checks are used wherever possible. __ Code performs the tasks intended by designer. __ All function redefinitions use all formal parameters. __ All non-void functions return a value. __ Under no circumstances will a sensitive mind error occur. ------ Version 1.1: Bob - March 02, 2004 Version 1: Bob - June 09, 2003

docs.title: Submission Commands
docs.text: Submission Commands =============================== NOTE: These commands work on DEV ONLY! ========================================================== BUILDER Commands ========================================================== Command: listtable ------------------------ Description: List of the areas that you currently have in the review process And produce a table outling who is doing what reviews. Syntax: listtable area <builders name> Command: listreview, listrev, listresponse, listresp -------------------------------------------------------------- Description: List all the reviews for a specific submission. This works for open and closed submissions. Syntax: listreview area <request number> <review type> request number is the number specific to this submission. review type is optional, and is code, content or balance. Command: respondrev, resprev -------------------------------------- Description: Respond to a review. Should be done when actions are complete. Syntax: respondrev area <request number> <review type> request number is the number specific to this submission. review type is code, content or balance Command: submit area ----------------------------- Description: This command is used to submit things for review and for the balance group to put their review comments in a central location. Its the way submissions are handled, when they are approved, and who approved the code, content and balance of the submission. ========================================================== MENTOR Commands ========================================================== Command: closesub ------------------------- Description: This command will finalise the whole area review process. The area should not be promoted until this has been done by the mentor.. Syntax: closesub area <request number> request number is the number specific to this submission. ========================================================== ARCH+ Commands ========================================================== Command: gotosub ------------------------ Description: Goto the location of a Submission. Syntax: gotosub area <request number> request number is the number specific to this submission. Command: listreviews, listrevs -------------------------------------- Description: This command is used to list submissions in table format, that are being reviewed by a specified balance member. Syntax: listreviews area <reviewer> reviewer is the person reviewing the submisson. Command: listtable area ------------------------------ Description: Provides a table outline all current area submissions and assosciated area reviewers. Command: lst ---------------- Description: List a Submission. Syntax: lst area <request number> request number is the number specific to this submission. Command: reviewsub, revsub ------------------------------------- Description: Review a submission for a certain review type. Syntax: reviewsub area <request number> <review type> request number is the number specific to this submission. review type is code, content or balance. ========================================================== IMP+ Commands ========================================================== Command: assignrev, arev Description: Assign a review to a specified person. Reviews MUST be at least ARCH + Syntax: assignreview area <request number> <review type> <name> review type is code, content or balance. request number is the number specific to this submission. name is who the review will be assigned to. NOTE: To assign a review to Noone use 'none'

docs.title: Recoding
docs.text: Recoding ========= Recoding is a code maintenance process that involves large scale changes to a body of code. Recoding can be complex and tedious, but if done well, can result in large, overall improvements to not possible by hacking code on a case by case basis. If done poorly however, recoding can exacerbate existing problems while introducing new ones. The objective of recoding is always to IMPROVE code already in play, and to do so CHEAPLY in terms of time and effort. In general, recode work is much less fun than creating new code, and involves code that works well enough for the most part anyway. There's a cost/benefit tradeoff involved in all recodes that should be considered before a serious recode effort is undertaken. 1 - Functional recode --------------------- A functional recode is a bare-bones, minimalist recode that aims to simply get the code working properly. This is really a fancy name for general bugfixing and whatnot. Where possible (i.e. doesn't cause compatibility problems), current coding standards should be used in a localized way, but the goal here is not to make the code pretty or even more maintainable. Just get it working. This approach is often taken for complex mudlib/guild code that needs a few tweaks here and there, but where complete recoding would be difficult. It can also be used for areas that break due to mudlib changes. 2 - Structural recode --------------------- A structural recode is aimed at fixing external code organization so that it is easier to maintain. This kind of recode is most commonly performed when moving old areas out of a wizard's personal directories. For this kind of recode, it is sufficient to move files into the correct structure (see wizhelp 8.7) and make sure everything works as per a functional recode. N.B. This may include fixing things that break because they were not very portable to begin with, and miscellaneous bugs that have been there from before the recode - since you're in there anyway, you may as well fix the real bugs. 3 - Full themeless recode ------------------------- This is comprehensive recode that aims to bring all aspects of the code in line with current code/balance/content standards. The aim is to bring the code up to minimum spec only, not to completely redo it into something much better than the original. This should be done periodically to all maintained code/areas to keep them in line with current coding standards. 4 - Complete recode ------------------- There are no upper bounds to what this entails. Usually complete recodes are not done on areas because it's a lot of work that's not particularly fun, for little gain. Complete recodes of guild/mudlib code are more common, and tend to include things like tightening up code in general, altering aspects of theme, adding new functionality etc. This type of recode is almost as much work as starting from scratch. ------ Version 1: Bob - June 06, 2004

docs.title: Rev. 0
docs.text:
Rev. 0 Populations General Description =================================== Introduction: ------------ Populations are a means for keeping track of groups of objects, usually NPCs, and refreshing the population via a generic generation facility. With a population, you can have a group of wandering monsters in your area keep its numbers up without having to make them all unique objects. Concepts -------- A population is a group of objects, and is held by a POPULATION object as defined in <mudlib.h>. The population has a key that should be unique on the mud, a set of filenames to clone when the population needs refreshing, a set of generators for creating the clones when necessary, and a number of parameters governing refresh time and so forth. The population should be created by a single room or object that will persist. That object doesn't need to keep track of the population; it just needs to create it. The POPULATION_D is tasked with tracking population objects. A generator is an object that places a newly created member of the population somewhere, like in a room or other object. There is a generic generator (ROOM_GENERATOR) that places new objects in a particular room and prints a message to everyone in the room. Files creating and configuring population objects should include <population.h>. Basic Functionality ------------------- POPULATION: void set_key_name(string name) - Set the name that the population daemon will use to track the population. string query_key_name() - Queries the name. void add_object_file(string filename) - Adds an object file to the list of files that can be cloned when refreshing the population. A population can be configured to pick one object file randomly when refreshing, or sequence through the object files one by one. void remove_object_file(string filename) - Removes the filename from the object file list. void add_generator(object generator) - Adds a generator to the list of generators to use when refreshing the population. A population can be configured to pick one generator randomly when refreshing, or sequence through the generators one by one. void remove_generator(object generator) - Removes the generator from the generator list. void set_clone_type(int type) - POP_CLONE_RANDOM or POP_CLONE_SEQ. RANDOM will choose one of the object files randomly when it needs to clone an object. SEQ will sequence through the object files in order, and start over at the beginning, as objects are cloned. void set_generate_type(int type) - GEN_CHOOSE_RANDOM or GEN_CHOOSE_SEQ. RANDOM will choose one of the generators randomly when it needs to generate an object. SEQ will sequence through the generators in order, and start over at the beginning, as objects are cloned. void set_auto_check(int auto) - If auto check is on, the population object will check its list of objects that it has created, determining if the object has been destructed or not. Without auto check, the objects must alert the population object manually with remove_population_object. void set_min_number(int min) - Set the minimum number of objects that should be in the population. When the number falls below the minimum, the population will use the generators to create new population members. void set_update_interval(int secs) - Sets how long between checks for population refreshes. int query_update_interval() - Query how long between checks for population refreshes. int query_generate_seq() - Queries the index of the last generation sequence. Only useful if GEN_CHOOSE_SEQ was used. int query_clone_seq() - Queries the index of the last cloning sequence. Only useful if POP_CLONE_SEQ was used. void add_population_object(object obj) - Add an object to the population for tracking. Necessary only if you wish to add objects manually. void remove_population_object(object obj) - Remove an object from the population. Necessary only if you are not using auto check. object *query_object_clones() - Returns a list of the current objects in the population. Generators: Basically, any object that has a "void generate(object obj)" function can be a generator. It should take the object and do whatever is necessary to enter the object into the game, like place it in a room or something similar. The generator can also perform additional setup of the generated object, if desired. There is a generic room generator (ROOM_GENERATOR) that will place generated objects in a given room, and print a defined message to all occupants of the room. It has the following interface: void set_room(string filename) - Sets the filename of the room where the objects will be placed. void set_room_message(string msg) - Sets the message that will be printed to the room when the newly generated object is moved there. Population daemon: The population daemon (POPULATION_D) tracks all of the populations on the mud. If a population is added of the same key as an existing population, the current population members will be moved to the new population, and the old population object will be destructed. If the population daemon is updated, all current populations will be destructed and lost. void add_population(object pop) - Adds the population to the tracking system, and calls startup() on it to initiate the refreshing call_out. void remove_population(string key) - Removes the population of that key and destructs it. Example ------- The following code will create a population that randomly selects between two types of baby demons when a population of baby demons falls below 12. The refresh check is made every 2 minutes. The two rooms, forest6 and forest8, will be selected between in order when a new baby demon is created. object pop, gen; string str; pop = clone_object(POPULATION); pop->set_key_name("malraux.newbie.demon"); pop->set_clone_type(POP_CLONE_RANDOM); pop->set_generate_type(GEN_CHOOSE_SEQ); pop->set_auto_check(1); pop->set_min_number(12); pop->add_object_file(MALNEWBIE + "obj/babydemon1"); pop->add_object_file(MALNEWBIE + "obj/babydemon2"); pop->set_update_interval(120); str = "\ The obscene flesh quivers suddenly. A quivering slit opens in the side
\ of the mound, showing a purplish interior. A small figure is pushed out,
\ and a new demon is born.
"; gen = clone_object(ROOM_GENERATOR); gen->set_room(MALNEWBIE + "forest6"); gen->set_room_message(str); pop->add_generator(gen); gen = clone_object(ROOM_GENERATOR); gen->set_room(MALNEWBIE + "forest8"); gen->set_room_message(str); pop->add_generator(gen); POPULATION_D->add_population(pop); Files ----- /objects/population/population.c - Population object. /objects/population/room_generator.c - Generic room generator object. /secure/daemons/population_d.c - Tracks all populations. Revision History: ----------------- Rev. 0 - Malraux: Initial release

docs.title: detect other objects through the use of spectrums and light
docs.text: detect other objects through the use of spectrums and light levels. It has several characteristics which can be used to finely tune how and when an object can be seen. SPECTRUMS There are currently 4 spectrums in the new system: Visible: The visible light spectrum. Acts pretty much as a stand-in for the old light system. Ultraviolet: Short wavelength light. This light is emitted by both the sun and stars, and can be used to see at night. Infrared: Long wavelength light. Emitted by living objects, this can be used to see in the dark to a limited extent. The living objects will be seen, as well as any exits, due to the difference in temperature of air currents. Sensory: Psionic sensing. Acts much like infrared. ACTIVE/PASSIVE VISION Most creatures use passive vision, meaning that they are dependent on an exterior source for the light needed to see. For example, the sun provides reflected light to see in the visible spectrum; living objects and air currents provide for difference in ambient temperature to see in the infrared spectrum. Active vision describes sight by emission; in other words, the creature that is doing the observing actually has some means of emitting light, serving as its own emission source. Races: Currently races are set up as follows: Elf, Daemon: active ultraviolet. Dwarf, gnome, halfing: passive infrared. All living creatures emit in the infrared and sensory spectrums. Garou are capable of seeing active UV and passive IR when in Crinos or Wolf form. INVISIBILITY, HIDING, ABSORPTION Invisibility in a spectrum is either on or off. Invisible items can be seen by an observer in two ways: 1) By being able to observe the object in a spectrum other than that which the object is invisible in. 2) By having the ability to see invisible objects in a spectrum by some means other than vision: magic, etc. Objects may also set a hiding, or camoflage, level. This is compared to the observers (int + wis)/2 when deciding if the object is visible or not. Finally, objects may have a level of absorption, meaning that they absorb (or fail to reflect) a certain amount of light that is cast on them. If there is not sufficient ambient light, an object may be invisible by virtue of it simply being too dark. Imagine trying to see a brown cloak in a dimly lit room. Note: Objects with shorts of 0, and objects which return a number greater than the level of the observer from the query_invis() function are also considered invisible. This supports the old method of invisibility (wiz invis). MECHANICS The light system is based on a range of 0 to 100 for all light levels. To determine if an object or its surroundings may be seen, several checks are performed for each spectrum. 1) If the object is invisible in the spectrum being checked, and the observer is not capable of seeing invisible objects in that spectrum, the object is considered invisible in that spectrum. 2) Next, the light level of the environment of the object is calculated for that spectrum. If the observer has active vision in the spectrum, the active vision level is added to the ambient light. Next, if the object has an absorption level for that spectrum, that level is subtracted from the ambient light. 3) If the viewer has passive vision, the spectrum is infrared, and the object is an emission source, then the ambient light for purposes of viewing the object is considered to be the maximum of the ambient light or the standard emission level (currently defined as 50). 4) If the result is > 0, the object is considered visible in that spectrum. Seeing environments is a little different in that if the spectrum is a detailed spectrum (visible, ultraviolet, and sensory), then objects, long descs, and exits can be seen. If the spectrum is not detailed, then only objects, short descs, and exits may be seen. Detailed means capable of distinguishing fine details. Note: when the code is finished, outside rooms will use the ambient light emitted by the sun, moons, and stars as determined by the astronomy daemon and the room's terrain type, i.e. a forest will gain less light from the moon than will an open road. The following attributes can be set by level for each spectrum (see add_visibility_level() for details) : Interior light: The ambient light inside a container. This is how rooms can have light inside them. This light is added to the light of any objects within the container which are also emanating light. Emanating light: The light given off by an object, like a torch or the like. The difference between this and interior light is subtle: interior light is cast into an object, emanated light is cast into the environment of the object. An object can emit light into itself, its environment, or both at the same time. Absorption: The amount of light NOT reflected by an object. The higher the absorption, the brighter the ambient (or interior) light of the environment needed to see the object. Camoflage: The amount of hiding being performed by an object. This really isn't a light level property, but refers more to the ability of the object to blend into its surroundings. This can be done by spectrum as well, as an object might have a great camoflage in the visible spectrum that looks like a riotous combination of bright orange and purple in the ultraviolet spectrum. Active vision: The amount of light emitted by an observer to see its surroundings. This light does NOT benefit any other observers in the same environment. Liken it to attempting to see via someone elses tight-beamed flashlight: they will never seem to hold the light where you want to look. The following attributes can be set either on or off only by spectrum (see set_visibility_flag() for details): Opacity: Whether or not a container passes exterior light to its interior, and vice versa. Passive/active vision: Whether an observer is capable of seeing in a particular spectrum, either actively or passively. Emitter: Whether or not the object emits in the spectrum, for purposes of detection with passive vision. Invisible: The invisibility of an object in the spectrum. See invisible: Whether or not an observer is capable of detecting invisible objects in the spectrum. NITTY-GRITTY All constants are defined in /secure/include/spectrum.h. Objects must inherit INH_VISIBILITY (defined in mudlib.h) in order to be either light sources, observers, or hidden/invisible. The functions used to test for visibility are defined in simul_efun, and are available to all objects: -------------------------------------------------------------------- varargs int visible_to(object oItem, object oObserver, object oEnv); Tests if an object (oItem) is visible to an observer (oObserver) in a particular environment(oEnv). oEnv is optional, and if not provided it defaults to the environment of oItem. Returns an integer containing the following bits: VIS_IS_ACTIVE - observer used active vision to see the object. VIS_IS_PASSIVE - observer used passive vision to see the object. VIS_IS_DETAILED - observer saw the object in a detailed spectrum. VIS_IS_AURA - observer saw the object in a non-detailed spectrum. VIS_IS_INVISIBLE - object was invisible in the spectrum, but was seen anyways. -------------------------------------------------------------------- varargs int environment_visible(object oObserver, object oEnv); Tests if an environment is visible to an observer. If oEnv is not provided, it defaults to the environment of the observer. Returns an integer containing the following bits: VIS_IS_ACTIVE - observer used active vision to see. VIS_IS_PASSIVE - observer used passive vision to see. VIS_IS_DETAILED - observer saw in a detailed spectrum. VIS_IS_AURA - observer saw in a non-detailed spectrum. -------------------------------------------------------------------- varargs mixed *visible(string sItem, object oEnv); Tests for the existence of a visible object matching the string, much as present() works. Returns a two-element array consisting of: 1) the object, if found. 0 otherwise. 2) the bits from visible_to(). Example: ({ object_that_was_found, VIS_ACTIVE }) -------------------------------------------------------------------- object *visible_inventory(object oContainer, object oObserver); Returns a list of the objects within a container that are visible to an observer. Returns an array of 2 element arrays as defined for visible(). -------------------------------------------------------------------- varargs void show_object_list(mixed *axTuples, object oObserver); Prints a nice inventory listing, taking into account color, numbers of items, etc. This is called by show_inventory, but may be used if needed. axTuples is an array of object/bit pairs as defined by visible(). -------------------------------------------------------------------- varargs void show_inventory(object oEnv, object oObserver); Prints an inventory listing for an environment for an observer. This should be used for all inventory lists. -------------------------------------------------------------------- The functions defined on objects which implement light are in /inherits/visibility.c (INH_VISIBILITY): -------------------------------------------------------------------- int query_visibility_level(int iType, int iSpec); Returns the level for a particular category by spectrum. Categories (iType) as defined in spectrum.h are: VIS_INTERIOR: interior light for the object VIS_ABSORPTION: amount of light the object absorbs VIS_EMANATION: amount of light the object emits VIS_HIDDEN: camoflage level of the object VIS_ACTIVE: active light ability of the object Spectrums as defined in spectrum.h are: SPCT_VISIBLE SPCT_INFRARED SPCT_SENSORY SPCT_ULTRAVIOLET SPCT_SONIC (not used currently) Returns an int. -------------------------------------------------------------------- varargs mixed *query_visibility_levels(); Returns all the visibility levels in an array. -------------------------------------------------------------------- int query_visibility_flag(); Returns the visibility flags in a single int. The individual bits should be queried using the following macros as defined in spectrum.h: VIS_GET_FLAG(flags, spectrum, flag); -------------------------------------------------------------------- void set_visibility_flag(int iSpectrum, int iFlag); Sets a visibility flag on an object. Ex. this_object()->set_visibility_flag(SPCT_INFRARED, VIS_PASSIVE_VISION); -------------------------------------------------------------------- void clear_visibility_flag(int iSpectrum, int iFlag); Clears a visibility flag on an object. -------------------------------------------------------------------- int add_visibility_level(int iType, int iSpectrum, int iAdd); Adds to a visibility level for an object. Ex. this_object()->add_visibility_level(VIS_EMANATION, SPCT_VISIBLE, 1); is the equivalent of set_light(1) for an object. Ex. this_object()->add_visibility_level(VIS_INTERIOR, SPCT_VISIBLE, 1); is the equivalent of set_light(1) for a room. -------------------------------------------------------------------- int recursive_interior_light(int iSpec); Calculates the total interior light for a container for a spectrum.

docs.title: MENU SYSTEM:
docs.text: MENU SYSTEM: The menu system allows the creation of both menu-style and wizard- style question systems, using the same menu option definitions. Menus should include <menu.h> and inherit MENU. Menu options types are: Value entry (MENU_TYPE_ENTRY) - enter an arbitrary value. Can be MENU_TYPE_STRING or MENU_TYPE_INT. Can be MENU_TYPE_MULTI_ENTRY. INT options can have an associated allowed range. Can have default values. Choice entry (MENU_TYPE_CHOICE) - enter one of a defined list of values. Can be MENU_TYPE_STRING or MENU_TYPE_INT. Can be MENU_TYPE_MULTI_ENTRY. INT options can have an associated allowed range. Can have default values. Can be either list or condensed style. Separator (MENU_TYPE_SEP) - text only separator value Sub-menu (MENU_TYPE_SUBMENU) - submenu of options Exit (MENU_TYPE_EXIT) - exit choice to leave the menu Can either completely exit, or just exit a submenu. Command (MENU_TYPE_COMMAND) - just calls the callback function as a command. Edit (MENU_TYPE_EDIT) - Calls the edit daemon like the bboards. Options can use closures for title, prompt, default value, choices, validation function, callback function, hidden, and next option (wizard mode). Regular mode: Starts out with a menu of options with numerical option selection. Wizard mode: Runs through a list of options one at a time, as determined by the option's "next" parameter. At end of list, an exit type option can be used to exit the wizard, or the wizard can drop back into normal menu mode. Menus always have a submenu defined named "default". This is the menu that will contain options that are added with no parent. It is displayed with start_menu() if no start option name is provided. NOTE: *ALWAYS* use a clone of your menu object! Otherwise, multiple people using it at the same time will step on each other. Menu Inheritable: varargs void add_option(string sName, int iType, mixed xTitle, mixed xPrompt, string sParent): Adds a menu option. sName must be unique amongst all the options defined for the menu. iType is a bitfield of: The following are mutually exclusive: MENU_TYPE_SUBMENU MENU_TYPE_ENTRY MENU_TYPE_CHOICE MENU_TYPE_SEP MENU_TYPE_EXIT The following are for ENTRY and CHOICE only: MENU_TYPE_STRING MENU_TYPE_INT MENU_TYPE_MULTI_ENTRY - keep prompting until <enter> The following are for CHOICE only: MENU_TYPE_CHOICE_STYLE_LIST - list prompt style MENU_TYPE_CHOICE_STYLE_FLAT - condensed prompt style The following is for EXIT options only: MENU_TYPE_EXIT_STYLE_POP - don't exit menu completely xTitle is either a string or closure, and is displayed in menu listings and before prompts. xPrompt is either a string or closure, and is displayed when entering a value only. sParent is the name of the submenu (defaults to "default") to which this option belongs. void set_option_title(string sOption, mixed xTitle): Sets the title for a menu option. May be a closure or a string. A closure will be passed the option info mapping. void set_option_prompt(string sOption, mixed xPrompt): Sets the prompt for a menu option. May be a closure or a string. A closure will be passed the option info mapping. void set_option_default(string sOption, mixed xDefault); Sets the default value for a menu option. May be a closure or a string. A closure will be passed the option info mapping. void set_option_choices(string sOption, string *asChoices); Sets the list of allowed values for MENU_TYPE_CHOICE options. May be a closure or a list of strings. A closure will be passed the option info mapping. void set_option_validator(string sOption, mixed xValidator); Sets the validation function for an option. Must be a closure. The validation function is passed two arguments: a string value and the option info mapping. It should return 0 if the value is valid, or a string error message if not. void set_option_integer_range(string sOption, int iMin, int iMax); Sets the valid range for an INT type option. void set_option_callback(string sOption, mixed xCallback); Sets the callback function for an option. Must be a closure. The callback function is passed two arguments: a string value and the option info mapping. void set_option_next(string sOption, mixed xNext); Sets the next option in line for wizard mode. Can be a string name or a closure that returns a string. void set_option_hiden(string sOption, mixed xHidden) Sets whether the option is visible or not. Can be a closure that returns an integer. varargs void start_menu(object oUser, string sMenu): Starts the menu at option sMenu (usually a submenu type option). varargs void start_wizard(object oUser, string sOption); Starts the menu in wizard mode at the specified option. Examples: /open/testmenu.c is an example of a way to use the menu options. It can be started in both normal and wizard mode. // Set the title and prompt for the main menu set_option_title("default", "Test Menu Title"); // The function "test_prompt" in this object will be called for the prompt. set_option_prompt("default", symbol_function("test_prompt", this_object())); // Add a string entry option add_option("test1", MENU_TYPE_ENTRY|MENU_TYPE_STRING, "Enter Name"); // The menu will call the "test_callback" function in this object each time // a value is entered for the option. set_option_callback("test1", symbol_function("test_callback", this_object())); // In wizard mode, go to option test2 after completing this option. set_option_next("test1", "test2"); // Add a string entry option with a set a allowed values that print in list // style (numbered selections). The title of the option will be returned // from the "test_test2_title" function in this object: // // <title> // 1) blue // 2) red // 3) green // Enter value: add_option("test2", MENU_TYPE_CHOICE|MENU_TYPE_STRING|MENU_TYPE_CHOICE_STYLE_LIST, symbol_function("test_test2_title", this_object())); // The menu will call the "test_callback" function in this object each time // a value is entered for the option. set_option_callback("test2", symbol_function("test_callback", this_object())); // The allowed choices are blue, red, and green set_option_choices("test2", ({ "blue", "red", "green" }) ); // In wizard mode, go to option test3 after completing this option. set_option_next("test2", "test3"); // Add a separator between options test2 and test3 add_option("testsep", MENU_TYPE_SEP, "-=-=- This Is A Separator -=-=-"); // Add an integer entry option add_option("test3", MENU_TYPE_ENTRY|MENU_TYPE_INT, "Enter Age"); set_option_callback("test3", symbol_function("test_callback", this_object())); // Note how this option chains to an option for a different submenu in wizard // mode. This lets you go through ALL of the selections in wizard mode, and // then fallback to a default hierarchical menu when all the entries have been made. set_option_next("test3", "sub1"); // Add a submenu off the main menu. add_option("testsub", MENU_TYPE_SUBMENU, "Do Some Other Stuff", "What do you want to do?"); // Add an exit option. This option will exit the menu completely when selected. add_option("test4", MENU_TYPE_EXIT, "Exit"); // Enter a normal string value entry option. add_option("sub1", MENU_TYPE_ENTRY|MENU_TYPE_STRING, "Enter Spoob", "Spoob value?", "testsub"); set_option_callback("sub1", symbol_function("test_callback", this_object())); set_option_next("sub1", "subint"); // Set the default value to "spoobalicious" set_option_default("sub1", "spoobalicious"); // Add an integer type option with an allowed range of 9 to 100, with a default // of 42. add_option("subint", MENU_TYPE_ENTRY|MENU_TYPE_INT, "Enter Spork", "Spork value?", "testsub"); set_option_integer_range("subint", 9, 100); set_option_default("subint", 42); set_option_callback("subint", symbol_function("test_callback", this_object())); set_option_next("subint", "sub2"); // Add a choice type entry using the flat style: // // Glorb: [Y/n] add_option("sub2", MENU_TYPE_CHOICE|MENU_TYPE_STRING|MENU_TYPE_CHOICE_STYLE_FLAT, "Glorb.", "Glorb:", "testsub"); set_option_callback("sub2", symbol_function("test_callback", this_object())); set_option_choices("sub2", ({ "y", "n" }) ); // Note that the default entry for a flat-style choice option gets capitalized // when displayed to signify that it is the default. set_option_default("sub2", "y"); // Add a multi-entry string option. The prompt will display based on the number // of lines entered. add_option("sub3", MENU_TYPE_ENTRY|MENU_TYPE_STRING|MENU_TYPE_MULTI_ENTRY, "Multi-Glorb.", symbol_function("count_prompt", this_object()), "testsub"); // The callback function will be sent a value of "" when the user hits <enter> to // exit the option. set_option_callback("sub3", symbol_function("test_callback_multi", this_object())); // Add an exit option. This option will exit the submenu and return to the main // menu when selected. add_option("sub4", MENU_TYPE_EXIT|MENU_TYPE_EXIT_STYLE_POP, "Back To Main Menu", 0, "testsub");

docs.title: To make use of the stat testing system, inherit STAT_TEST;
docs.text: To make use of the stat testing system, inherit STAT_TEST; in any room, object, or monster. You can perform a test with the following syntax test_<stat>(<difficulty>,<subject>);. It is an integer function which will return by how much the test was passed or failed. Remember if a player exactly makes the number needed, 0 will be returned, not 1. The difficulty should be a number between 1 and 100, with higher numbers meaning harder tests. If it is not supplied, 50 will be assumed. Subject should be the object to perform the test on. If not supplied, this_player() will be assumed. A few examples: test_str(); test_int(25); test_chr(90,this_player()->query_attack()); The first will perform a default level 50 test on this_player()'s strength. The second will perform an easier level 25 test on the player's intelligence, and the last will make an extremely difficult charisma test on the monster the player is attacking. For some examples of objects using tests, check /open/OBJ/stat_mace and stat_goblin. The inheritable stat testing system takes a number of things into account, including that no test will ALWAYS succeed or ALWAYS fail, and that the differences between a stat of 11 and 12 should be more dramatic than between 47 and 48. It can be used to reward players who have kept rell rounded characters, and make statistics not vital to combat or spell points still important. You can use charisma tests to determine the reactions of NPCs, dexterity tests to perform leaping or climbing, wisdom or intelligence tests to read books or successfully search, etc. Consider using appropriate stat tests instead of pure random numbers in your code.

docs.title: Events represent a method for functions to be called when a certain action
docs.text: Events represent a method for functions to be called when a certain action takes place. This action, we call an event. The way events are represented here on Darkwind is in a mapping, stored in each player object. This mapping has the event, the file to call, the function to call, and an optional arguement. So, to add an event for a particular player, you would do: this_player()->add_event(type, file, function, arguement); Where, type is a possible event type: login, logout, linkdeath and linkresume. File is the file to call and function is what to call in that file. The event handling routine will do: file->function(arguement); To remove an event, use the same syntax: this_player()->remove_event(type, file, function, arguement); You can also query all the events of a certain type: this_player()->query_events(type); The types are listed in <events.h>. Ask an implementor or supervisor for a current list if you need an event that isn't talked about in this document. WARNING: EVENTS ARE NOT STATIC! DO NOT USE CLONED FILENAMES UNLESS YOU EXPLICITLY REMOVE THEM BEFORE THEY ARE DESTRUCTED! -Hayden 06/25/95

docs.title: Emote System
docs.text: Emote System ============ To begin with, all emotes are handled through the emote daemon, EMOTE_D, which handles all of the visibility checks, parsing, room messaging, etc. Any emote consists of two basic parts, the 'RULE' and the 'Message String'. The RULE is a sequence of 0 or more tokens representing variable arguments passed to the emote. Valid tokens for a RULE are 'LIV', 'OBJ', and 'STR'. Any arguments given with the emote, will be compared to the known RULEs for that emote, and if a match is found, the corresponding Message String will be used. ex. (Emote: wave RULE: LIV) will match if a player types 'wave bozo' and Bozo is a living object the player has access too. The Message String is the text that is displayed with the emote, with variables in place for the words that change depending upon who is seeing the message. Note that if the variables do not match the rules, the emote may be buggy. Where applicable a variable can be modified by a number indicating who/what is the first person of referred to by the variable, followed by a modifying argument. Targets are numbered by the order they are specified in, in the rule, with the emoter being living target 0. Capitalizing the variable will capitalize the output. Valid variables are: $n ...living target - defaults to $n0s. Arguments are: b: objective [you, him] g: nominative [you, Bob] o: reflexive [yourself, himself] s: subjective [you, he] p: name [Bob, Bob] The b, o and s forms always revert to the g form when a target appears for the first time in the message. $p ...possessive [your, his]. first target appearance is named [your, Bob's]. $r ...reflexive [yourself, himself]. $t ...same as $n but default is $t1o. $o ...object for OBJ rule or string for STR rule. $v ...verb forms. Argument is the verb to be conjugated. To make different messages for every viewer, concatenate output strings with '&&' in the form: <emoter msg>&&<room msg>&&<target 1 msg>&&<target 2 msg>... ex. (Emote: wave RULE: LIV Msg: "$N $vwave at $t.") will give the message "You wave at Bozo." to you, "Clown waves at you." to Bozo, and "Clown waves at Bozo." to everyone else in the room if you were to use the emote 'wave bozo'. All emotes are added to EMOTE_D through the command 'addemote'. This information is also available in 'help addemote'. Variable Emotes =============== Some emotes return variable text depending on certain factors beyond the score of EMOTE_D to check. In order for this to work, a small command must be coded that tells EMOTE_D what message should be used. Any Variable Emote will be in the special emote directory, '/cmds/soul/'. The main function in this command will be: string get_emote(string sArg, object *aoWho) { } inside of which the emote Message String will be constructed. 'sArg' will be the matching RULE used by the player, and 'aoWho' is the array of objects involved in the emote. The return string value is the Message String EMOTE_D should use to construct the emote messages. ex. (From our wave emote, LIV rule example above.) /cmds/soul/wave.c string get_emote(string sArg, object *aoWho) { if (sArg != "LIV") return ""; // We only want LIV rules if (random(2)) return "$N $vwave in crisp military fashion at $t."; else return "$N $vwave parade-style at $t."; } This will return the first Message String 50% of the time, and the second Message String the other 50% of the time. The last thing needed for a variable emote to work is to link the small emote command you made in /cmds/soul/ to EMOTE_D itself. To do this you would still use the 'addemote' command to add the emote 'wave', for RULE LIV, but instead of giving a Message String, you would re-direct it to your emote command with '->wave'. This will cause EMOTE_D to go to the emote command for the Message String when the emote 'wave' is called with the matching 'LIV' RULE. Guild Emotes ============ Guild emotes are definitions stored in a separate, guild-scoped mapping in EMOTE_D. They use the same RULE and Message String grammar as global emotes, but only active members of the selected guild can list, preview, invoke, or use them through a channel soul. Create a static guild emote with the normal addemote flow and the -guild option: addemote -guild Street_Samurai jackin STR New message: $N $vjack into $o. The guild name is matched case-insensitively against GUILD_NAMES. Definitions are persisted in /secure/savedir/soul with the rest of the emote daemon state. Because that save data is environment-local, definitions must still be added or migrated separately wherever they are expected to exist. Use these commands to inspect and remove guild definitions: showemote -guild Street_Samurai jackin rmemote -guild Street_Samurai jackin STR rmemote -guild Street_Samurai jackin Omitting -guild operates on a global emote. A new guild-emote name may not collide with a global emote, another guild's emote, or a command available to the architect creating it. A guild emote only needs an object under /cmds/soul/ when its output must be computed dynamically. Put the get_emote() object in the lower-case guild directory, then use a guild redirect as the stored Message String: /cmds/soul/psionicist/spoon.c ->Guild_Psionicist_spoon The guild token in a redirect must use the configured guild name. Static guild emotes should store their Message String directly and do not need a redirect object. Players can discover and inspect the definitions available to them with: feelings guild [<guild>] [<prefix>] semote <emote> emoteapropos guild [<guild>] <text> See also: help guild emotes, help addemote, help showemote, help rmemote ============================= Version 1.0: 12-08-03 Aiken [Parts ripped from addemote command help] Version 2.0: 07-20-26 [Documented scoped guild emotes]

docs.title: Player stats are fun stats that you can add and display for relatively
docs.text: Player stats are fun stats that you can add and display for relatively any event on DarkWind. One rule of thumb: keep the player stats fun and light hearted. Don't use pstats to expose some underlying bit of information that may give other players tactical advantages against that player in PK. Adding player stats are really easy to do, also! Here's how: 1. Update /secure/include/playerstats.h to add your new stat. For example, let's say we want to track every time a user uses the spell "entangle". First, we'd add this to the playerstats.h file: #define CAST_ENTANGLE "cast_entangle" The important thing here is to make sure that "cast_entangle" is unique, and not used by any other stats in this header file. NOTE: If you are adding a guild stat, please group it under the appropriate area with that guild's other stats! 2. Update the PLAYER_STATS_STRING mapping at the bottom of the header file. CAST_ENTANGLE : "Entangle Spell Cast"; "Druid", \ This defines the label for this stat to be "Entangle Spell Cast", and for it to be grouped within "Druid Stats" when displayed on pstats. 3. Now update your code where that actual event happens, and put in the hook: #include <daemons.h> #include <playerstats.h> PLAYER_STATS_D->increment_stat(this_player()->query_real_name(), CAST_ENTANGLE); 4. And, finally, assuming your code from step 3 updates, update the /cmds/std/_pstats.c command for it to pick up the newly added stat! You're good to go! Your new stat is now implemented! See also: 9.15.1

docs.title: Living Status Effects
docs.text: Living Status Effects ===================== Burning, Bleeding, Chilled, Freezing, Exposed, and Sundered are stored directly on every living. Include <status_effects.h> and use the STATUS_* bit flags. The flags are saved compatibility contracts; never renumber or reuse one. Application ----------- varargs status apply_status_effect(int effect, int strength, int duration, object source, status silent) Only one STATUS_* bit may be applied per call. duration is in seconds and is rounded up to a two-second heartbeat. Burning derives its duration from its stack count and ignores duration. source is optional and is converted to a primitive identifier immediately; no object reference is saved. Set silent for a refresh or transformation that should update state and GMCP without producing application messages. Prefer the named wrappers in normal content: target->apply_burning(stacks, attacker); target->apply_bleeding(strength, seconds, attacker); target->apply_chilled(seconds, attacker); target->apply_freezing(seconds, attacker); target->apply_exposed(seconds, attacker); target->apply_sundered(strength, seconds, attacker); All functions return 1 when the effect was accepted and 0 for invalid input. Queries And Removal ------------------- int query_status_effect_mask() status query_status_effect(int mask) int query_status_effect_strength(int effect) int query_status_effect_remaining(int effect) int query_status_effect_duration(int effect) object query_status_effect_source(int effect) mapping query_status_effects() varargs status remove_status_effect(int mask, status silent) void clear_all_status_effects() Queries and removal may use combined masks. Strength and duration queries require one exact bit. Source queries resolve the stored primitive identifier to a currently loaded living, or return 0. For example, a cure for either cold tier can use: target->remove_status_effect(STATUS_COLD); query_status_effects() returns a deep copy. Do not inspect or modify the living's saved state mapping directly. Effect Contracts ---------------- Burning X Adds stacks up to max(1, target level). Each heartbeat deals X fire damage, then replaces X with floor(X/2). The 1-stack tick is final. Bleeding X Adds strength up to max(5, target level/5). X is added to melee damage before defensive modifiers and absorption. Movement has a 25 percent chance to deal X slash damage. The caller supplies the duration. Chilled / Freezing Chilled reduces final swings by 10 percent and adds 1 second to new set_spell_limit() cooldowns. Applying Chilled twice promotes it to Freezing. Freezing uses 20 percent and 2 seconds. Direct Freezing is allowed. These do not affect custom call_out or soul-owned timers. Exposed Adds 5 percentage points to incoming critical chance. It does not stack; reapplication keeps the longer duration. Sundered X Subtracts X from final armour class, after equipment and armour specialization. It stacks to 3 and reapplication refreshes duration. General acid damage has a bounded chance to apply one stack. Lifecycle And Display --------------------- State is primitive and saved on the living. Timers pause when the player object is absent and resume after restore. Death clears all effects. The `buffs` command and Char.Defences GMCP list expose them as non-clearable debuffs. Add future display names to GLOBAL_STATUS_EFFECT_MAPPING in <buffs.h>; do not put these bit flags in GLOBAL_DEBUFF_MAPPING.
